pattern: 보이다 / 들리다 (bentuk pasif dari 보다/듣다: 'bisa/tidak bisa terlihat/terdengar')
meaning: The passive forms of 'to see' (보이다) and 'to hear' (들리다), meaning 'to be seen/heard' - naturally translated as 'can/can't see/hear'.

notes.formation: 보이다 (passive of 보다) and 들리다 (passive of 듣다) are intransitive - they cannot take an object with ~를/을. A person experiencing the seeing/hearing can be added as the sentence subject, with the seen/heard thing marked ~이/가, following the Subject-Object-Passive Verb structure from Lesson 15: 저는 소방서가 보여요; 저는 소리가 안 들려요.
notes.usage: TV가 안 보여 literally 'The TV can't be seen', naturally translated 'I can't see the TV'; 소방서가 보여요 'The fire station is seen' -> 'I can see the fire station'. With a person added: 나는 TV가 안 보여 'I can't see the TV'; 나는 네 목소리가 안 들려 'I can't hear your voice'; 목소리가 잘 들려 'I hear you (your voice) well'.
notes.nuance: This is a clear illustration of how Korean intransitive/passive verbs and English transitive verbs don't map directly: the Korean sentence structurally says 'the TV isn't seen (by me)', not 'I don't see the TV' - the object of English 'see' becomes the Korean subject of 보이다, marked with ~이/가, not ~을/를, because 보이다 (like 있다 elsewhere) cannot act on an object.

examples.meaning: I can see the fire station.
Can you see the elementary school?
I can't see the mountains from here.

quiz.question: Kenapa 'TV가 안 보여' tidak memakai partikel objek ~를/을 pada TV?
options: Karena TV adalah kata benda khusus
Karena 보이다 bersifat intransitif dan tidak bisa bekerja pada objek
quiz.explanation: 보이다 is intransitive, so the seen thing is marked ~이/가 (as the grammatical subject), not ~을/를.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: I can't hear your voice. -> 나는 네 목소리가 [BLANK]
fillInTheBlank.hint: 들리다 (passive of 듣다), negated with 안.

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'I can't see the price tags.'
constructionQuiz.hint: 가격표 marked with ~이/가, since 보이다 is intransitive.

pattern: N 같이 보이다 ('terlihat seperti N')
meaning: 'To look like' a noun - attaching 같이 (adverb form of 같다) to a noun, then predicating with 보이다.

notes.formation: [Noun] + 같이 + 보이다. The noun before 같이 can also be a more complex noun phrase described by ~는 것 (a full clause turned into a noun): 네가 새로운 집으로 이사하고 싶은 것 같이 보여 'It looks like you want to move to a new house'.
notes.usage: 너는 원숭이 같이 보여 'You look like a monkey'; 저의 남자친구는 교수님 같이 보여요 'My boyfriend looks like the professor'; 그가 공연에 가고 싶지 않는 것 같이 보여 'It looks like he doesn't want to go to the performance'; 그녀가 오늘 화장을 안 한 것 같이 보여요 'It looks like she didn't do her makeup today'.
notes.nuance: In practice, it's often more common and natural to simply say something IS like something (using bare 같다, see the separate pattern) rather than explicitly saying it LOOKS like something - the meaning of 'is like a monkey' already implicitly includes looking (and acting, smelling, etc.) like one, so ~같이 보이다 is used specifically when the focus is narrowly on visual appearance.

examples.meaning: You look like a high school student.
Does it look like you won the game?
You don't look like a monkey.

quiz.question: Bagian mana yang bisa diganti frasa ~는 것 dalam pola N 같이 보이다?
quiz.explanation: The noun before 같이 can be replaced by a whole clause turned into a noun with ~는 것.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: My boyfriend looks like the professor. -> 저의 남자친구는 [BLANK]

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'It looks like she didn't do her makeup today.'
constructionQuiz.answer: 그녀가 오늘 화장을 안 한 것 같이 보여요
constructionQuiz.answerReading: geunyeoga oneul hwajangeul an han geot gachi boyeoyo
constructionQuiz.hint: Nominalize '화장을 안 하다' with ~ㄴ 것, then add 같이 보여요.

pattern: N 같다 (tanpa 같이/보이다: cara lebih alami mengatakan 'seperti N')
meaning: The more natural, common way to say something 'is like' a noun - using bare 같다 with no particle, instead of the more explicit ~같이 보이다.

notes.formation: [Noun] + 같다, with NO particle (와/과/랑/이랑/하고) attached to the preceding noun - unlike the earlier Lesson 15 usage of 같다 (comparing two named things with a connecting particle, e.g. 이 학교는 우리 학교와 같아요 'is the same as').
notes.usage: 너는 여자 같아 'You're like a girl'; 그는 여우 같아요 'He is like a fox'; 캐나다는 미국 같아요 'Canada is like the US'; 진짜 의사 같아 'You're really like a doctor'.
notes.nuance: When the intent is truly to say two things are 'the same' (identical), 똑같다 is the more natural word to use rather than bare 같다 (이 학교는 우리 학교와 똑같아요 'This school is exactly the same as our school'), whereas this particle-less N 같다 pattern is reserved for the looser 'is like/resembles' meaning covered here - the whole implied meaning of 'looking, acting, smelling, etc. like X' is packed into this single simple construction, which is why it's used more often in casual speech than the more narrowly visual ~같이 보이다.

examples.meaning: He is like a monkey.
Are you like an elementary school student?
He is not like a fox.

quiz.question: Kenapa '너는 여자 같아' tidak memakai partikel (seperti 와/과) setelah 여자?
options: Karena pola N 같다 di sini tidak memakai partikel penghubung, berbeda dari perbandingan biasa di Lesson 15
quiz.explanation: This particle-less N 같다 pattern for 'is like' differs from the Lesson 15 usage that compares two things with a connecting particle.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: Canada is like the US. -> 캐나다는 [BLANK]

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'You're really like a doctor.'

pattern: N 맛/냄새 같다 ('terasa/berbau seperti N')
meaning: 'To taste/smell like' a noun.

notes.formation: 맛 ('taste', a noun - as seen in 맛있다 'to have taste/to be delicious') or 냄새 ('smell', a noun) is placed after a noun that has that taste/smell, followed by 같다: [noun] + 맛/냄새 + 같다.
notes.usage: 김치 맛 같아 'Tastes like Kimchi'; 김치 찌개 냄새 같아 'It smells like Kimchi Jjigae'. With a subject added: 이 떡은 쓰레기 맛 같아 'This 떡 tastes like garbage'; 삼겹살은 베이컨 맛 같아요 '삼겹살 tastes like bacon'.
notes.nuance: This is structurally identical to the plain N 같다 pattern just covered, simply with 맛 or 냄새 inserted between the comparison noun and 같다 - no new grammatical mechanism is introduced, just a straightforward, practical vocabulary combination worth knowing.

examples.meaning: 삼겹살 tastes like bacon.
Does this smell like Kimchi Jjigae?

examples.hangul: 이 떡은 쓰레기 맛 같지 않아요
examples.romaja: i tteogeun sseuregi mat gatji anhayo
examples.meaning: This 떡 doesn't taste like garbage.

quiz.question: Kata benda mana yang dipakai untuk 'rasa' dalam pola ini?
quiz.explanation: 맛 means 'taste', while 냄새 means 'smell' - both are placed before 같다.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: This 떡 tastes like garbage. -> 이 떡은 [BLANK]

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'It smells like Kimchi Jjigae.'

pattern: Adj~아/어 보이다 ('terlihat Adj')
meaning: 'To look' + an adjective, e.g. 'to look happy/sad/strong'.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어 to an adjective stem (following the usual vowel-harmony rule), then 보이다: 행복하다 -> 행복해 보이다 'to look happy'; 슬프다 -> 슬퍼 보이다 'to look sad'; 강하다 -> 강해 보이다 'to look strong'.
notes.usage: 왜 그렇게 행복해 보여요? 'Why do you look so happy?'; 저의 여자친구는 어제 너무 슬퍼 보였어요 'My girlfriend looked really sad yesterday'; 그 남자 종아리가 아주 강해 보여요 'That man's calf looks very strong'; 이 원룸은 깨끗해 보여요 'This studio apartment looks clean'; 화장이 예뻐 보여요 'Your makeup looks pretty'; 소방 훈련이 힘들어 보여요 'Firefighting training looks difficult'; 무릎이 아파 보여요 'Your knee looks sore'.
notes.nuance: This construction is specifically for adjectives, complementing the noun-based ~같이 보이다 covered earlier in this lesson - together, the two patterns cover both 'looks like a NOUN' and 'looks ADJECTIVE', giving a complete way to describe appearance-based impressions in Korean.

examples.meaning: It looks like that man has a lot of willpower/drive.
Does your knee look sore?
This studio apartment doesn't look clean.

quiz.question: Bentuk yang benar dari 행복하다 (bahagia) + 보이다 ('terlihat bahagia') adalah...
quiz.explanation: Attach ~아/어 (following vowel harmony, 하 -> 해) to the adjective stem before 보이다.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: Why do you look so happy? -> 왜 그렇게 [BLANK]

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'That man's calf looks very strong.'
constructionQuiz.answer: 그 남자 종아리가 아주 강해 보여요
constructionQuiz.answerReading: geu namja jongarriga aju ganghae boyeoyo

pattern: V/Adj~아/어서 (karena/oleh sebab itu) + aturan partikel klausa ganda
meaning: 'Because/therefore' - connecting a reason clause to a result clause, with Korean's clause order reversed from English.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어서 to the stem of the REASON clause (following the usual vowel-harmony rule), then follow with the result clause: 배고프다 -> 배고파서. Following the multi-clause rule from Lesson 24, the reason (sub-)clause's subject takes ~이/가, while the main (result) clause's subject can take either ~는/은 or ~이/가 depending on the nuance wanted (Lessons 2/22). If both clauses share the same subject, it's stated only once, in the main clause, and dropped from the reason clause.
notes.usage: English says 'I want to eat because I am hungry' (result first, reason second); Korean reverses this: 저는 배고파서 밥을 먹고 싶어요, literally 'Because I am hungry, I want to eat' - it can help to mentally translate ~아/어서 as 'therefore' instead of 'because', which keeps the clause order matching: 'I am hungry, therefore I want to eat'. Full example with differing subjects: 제가 배고파서 저는 밥을 먹고 싶어요 (제가 = reason-clause subject with ~이/가; 저는 = main-clause subject with ~는).
notes.nuance: ~아/어서 attached to 가다/오다 specifically (가서/와서) was already taught in Lesson 17 to mean 'go/come, and then...' rather than 'because I go/come...' - although both meanings are technically possible, native speakers essentially never intend the 'because' reading with these two particular verbs, since it would rarely make sense to say something like 'the reason I went to sleep is because I came home' as a because-statement; context and convention make the 'and then' meaning by far the default for 가서/와서.

examples.meaning: I am hungry, therefore I want to eat.

examples.hangul: 그 여자가 너무 예뻐서 저는 그녀를 만나고 싶어요?
examples.romaja: geu yeojaga neomu yeppeoseo jeoneun geunyeoreul mannago sipeoyo?
examples.meaning: That girl is very pretty, so do I want to meet her? (used to show the pattern)

examples.hangul: 고속도로가 막혀서 일반 길로 안 갈 거예요
examples.romaja: gosokdoroga makhyeoseo ilban gilro an gal geoyeyo
examples.meaning: I won't take the normal road, even though the highway is blocked up. (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: Urutan klausa mana yang benar untuk menerjemahkan 'I want to go to the park because I am bored' ke bahasa Korea?
options: 저는 공원에 가고 싶어서 저는 심심해요 (hasil dulu, alasan kedua)
저는 심심해서 공원에 가고 싶어요 (alasan dulu, hasil kedua)
quiz.explanation: Korean reverses the English order: the reason clause comes first, then the result clause.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: I am bored, therefore I want to go to the park. -> 저는 [BLANK] 공원에 가고 싶어요

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'I want to get plastic surgery because I am so ugly.'
constructionQuiz.answer: 저는 너무 못생겨서 성형수술을 받고 싶어요
constructionQuiz.answerReading: jeoneun neomu mossaenggyeoseo seonghyeongsusureul batgo sipeoyo

pattern: ~아/어서 di waktu lampau (waktu klausa pertama disimpulkan dari konteks)
meaning: The reason clause before ~아/어서 is NEVER itself conjugated into the past tense - the past meaning is inferred entirely from context.

notes.formation: It is grammatically WRONG to conjugate the reason clause into the past before adding ~아/어서 (배고팠아서 is incorrect). Instead, always attach ~아/어서 directly to the plain stem (배고파서), and let the surrounding sentence/context establish whether the reason happened in the past.
notes.usage: 저는 배고파서 밥을 먹었어요 'I was hungry, so I ate' (the past-tense main clause 먹었어요 implies the reason was also in the past, even though 배고파서 itself carries no past marker). The final clause doesn't even need to be past tense to imply the first clause is: 점심을 안 먹어서 지금 먹고 있어요 'I didn't eat lunch, so I'm eating now' (present-tense main clause, but the reason is clearly past); 거기에 안 가 봐서 내일 갈 거예요 'I haven't been there yet, so I will go tomorrow' (future-tense main clause, reason clause still understood as past/perfect).
notes.nuance: This can feel confusing at first because there's no visible tense marker on the ~아/어서 clause itself to rely on - but as the lesson emphasizes, you are not actually guessing: Korean simply relies on the logical context of the whole sentence to make the timing clear, and this becomes increasingly natural with more exposure rather than through a fixed rule to apply mechanically.

examples.hangul: 학생들이 너무 시끄러워서 저는 교수님의 말을 못 들었어요
examples.romaja: haksaengdeuri neomu sikkeureowoseo jeoneun gyosunimui mareul mot deureosseoyo

examples.hangul: 저는 화장을 하지 않아서 안 못생겨 보여요
examples.romaja: jeoneun hwajangeul haji anhaseo an mossaenggyeo boyeoyo
examples.meaning: I don't look ugly, even though I didn't do my makeup. (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: Manakah yang secara gramatikal SALAH?
options: 점심을 안 먹어서 지금 먹고 있어요
거기에 안 가 봐서 내일 갈 거예요
quiz.explanation: The reason clause before ~아/어서 is never itself conjugated into the past - 배고팠아서 is incorrect.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: I was hungry, so I ate. -> 저는 [BLANK] 밥을 먹었어요
fillInTheBlank.hint: Use the plain stem + ~아/어서, no past marker here.

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'I haven't been there yet, so I will go tomorrow.'
constructionQuiz.answer: 거기에 안 가 봐서 내일 갈 거예요
constructionQuiz.answerReading: geogie an ga bwaseo naeil gal geoyeyo
constructionQuiz.hint: 가 보다's stem + ~아/어서, no past marker despite the implied past meaning.

pattern: N이다 + ~아/어서 (이어서/여서 atau 이라서/라서, 'karena adalah N')
meaning: Attaching ~아/어서 to 이다, with two equally-valid but differently-common forms.

notes.formation: Since 이다's stem always ends in the vowel 이, ~어서 (never ~아서) is added: 일요일이다 -> 일요일이어서. When the preceding noun ends in a vowel, 이+어 merges into 여: 의사이어서 -> 의사여서. An entirely separate but equal-meaning alternative uses ~이라(서)/라(서) instead: ~이라(서) after a consonant-final noun, ~라(서) after a vowel-final noun: 일요일이라서; 의사라서. For 아니다, either ~어서 or ~라(서) can be added: 아니어서/아니라서.
notes.usage: 일요일이어서 저는 공원에 가고 싶어요 = 일요일이라서 저는 공원에 가고 싶어요 'It is Sunday, so I want to go to the park'. 예쁜 여자여서 = 예쁜 여자라서 똑똑하지 않을 것 같아 'She is a pretty girl, so she is probably not smart'. 최신 핸드폰이 아니어서 = 최신 핸드폰이 아니라서 이 앱이 아주 느려요 'This isn't the latest cell phone, so the app is really slow'.
notes.nuance: Both ~이어서/여서 and ~이라서/라서 mean exactly the same thing, but ~(이)라(서) is heard far more often in actual speech (though ~이어서/여서 does appear in writing) - purely a matter of what flows more naturally off the tongue, not a difference in meaning. It's enough to be comfortable using just one of these forms consistently (most learners settle on ~(이)라서) while still recognizing the other when it's heard or read.

examples.hangul: 이번 주말이 연휴라서 우리 엄마 집에 갈 거예요
examples.romaja: ibeon jumari yeonhyurraseo uri eomma jibe gal geoyeyo
examples.meaning: This weekend is a long weekend, so I will go to our mom's house.
Is this room too small because it's a studio apartment?

examples.hangul: 그것이 최신 정보가 아니라서 안 맞는 것 같아요
examples.romaja: geugeosi choesin jeongboga aniraseo an matneun geot gatayo
examples.meaning: It's probably not correct because that's not the latest information.

quiz.question: Bentuk mana yang lebih umum terdengar dalam percakapan sehari-hari?
quiz.explanation: ~(이)라(서) is heard far more often in speech, even though both mean exactly the same thing.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: It is Sunday, so I want to go to the park (using ~이라서). -> [BLANK] 저는 공원에 가고 싶어요
fillInTheBlank.hint: 일요일 ends in a consonant, so ~이라서 attaches.

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate using ~여서: 'She is a pretty girl, so she is probably not smart.'
constructionQuiz.answer: 예쁜 여자여서 똑똑하지 않을 것 같아
constructionQuiz.answerReading: yeppeun yeojayeoseo ttokttokaji anheul geot gata
acceptableVariants: 예쁜 여자라서 똑똑하지 않을 것 같아
constructionQuiz.hint: 여자 ends in a vowel, so 이+어 merges into 여: 여자여서.

pattern: ~아/어서 di waktu depan (것이어서/거여서/것이라서/거라서)
meaning: Attaching ~아/어서 to a future-tense clause - handled exactly the same as attaching it to 이다, since ~ㄹ/을 것이다 is itself built on 것 + 이다.

notes.formation: Since the future tense ~ㄹ/을 것이다 is literally ~ㄹ/을 것 (describing 것) + 이다, adding ~아/어서 to a future clause follows exactly the same rules as adding it to 이다 (previous pattern). This gives four equally valid options, since 것 can shorten to 거, and 이다 can take either the ~이어서/여서 or ~이라서/라서 form: 올 것이어서, 올 거여서, 올 것이라서, 올 거라서 (all meaning 'because [it/he] will come').
notes.usage: 나중에 밥이 없을 거라서 저는 지금 먹고 싶어요 'There will not be any food later, therefore, I want to eat now'; 친구가 거기에 많을 거라서 그 파티에 가고 싶어요 'Many of my friends will be there, so I want to go to that party'; 입장료가 너무 비쌀 거라서 저는 안 갈 거예요 'The price of admission will be so expensive, so I am not going to go'.
notes.nuance: Despite there being four technically valid forms, it's enough to comfortably master just one for everyday speech (the lesson author says they personally always use ~이라(서)/라(서) and never ~이어서/여서) while still being able to recognize all four when encountered - there's no need to actively practice producing every variant.

examples.meaning: Many of my friends will be there, so I don't want to go to that party.

constructionQuiz.answer: 입장료가 너무 비쌀 것이라서 저는 안 갈 거예요

pattern: 그래서 ('oleh sebab itu/karena itu', dari 그렇다 + ~아/어서)
meaning: 'Therefore/that's why' - built by attaching ~아/어서 to 그렇다 ('to be like that').

notes.formation: 그렇다 + ~아/어서 -> 그래서 (following the ㅎ irregular pattern already seen elsewhere with this word).
notes.usage: 그래서 refers back to a previously mentioned situation and links it as the reason for what follows, commonly translated 'therefore' or 'that's why': 비가 왔어요? 'Did it rain?' -> 응, 그래서 나가기 싫어요 'Yeah, that's why I don't want to go out'; 우리 학교가 영어회화 수업이 없어요? 'Our school doesn't have an English Conversation class?' -> 네, 없어요. 그래서 제가 다음 학기부터 개설할 거예요 'Right, there isn't any. That's why I'm going to start one beginning next semester'.
notes.nuance: 그래서 functions as a standalone conversational connector referring to an entire previously stated situation, rather than attaching directly to a specific verb/adjective stem within the same sentence - it's the natural way to link back to something already said in a separate sentence or turn of conversation, distinct from the clause-internal ~아/어서 covered in the rest of this lesson.

examples.hangul: 비가 왔어요? 응, 그래서 나가기 싫어요
examples.romaja: biga wasseoyo? eung, geuraeseo nagagi sireoyo
examples.meaning: Did it rain? Yeah, that's why I don't want to go out.
Our school doesn't have an English Conversation class?
That's why I didn't go outside.

quiz.question: 그래서 dibentuk dari kata dasar apa?
quiz.explanation: 그래서 comes from 그렇다 ('to be like that') plus ~아/어서.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: Right, there isn't any. That's why I'm going to start one. -> 네, 없어요. [BLANK] 제가 개설할 거예요
fillInTheBlank.hint: Use 그래서 to link back to the previously mentioned situation.

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'Did it rain? Yeah, that's why I don't want to go out.'
constructionQuiz.answer: 비가 왔어요? 응, 그래서 나가기 싫어요
constructionQuiz.answerReading: biga wasseoyo? eung, geuraeseo nagagi sireoyo
constructionQuiz.hint: 그래서 links the rain fact to not wanting to go out.

pattern: N 때문에 ('karena/gara-gara N')
meaning: 'Because of' a noun.

notes.formation: Simply place 때문에 directly after a noun: 일 때문에 'because of work'; 남자 친구 때문에 'because of (my) boyfriend'.
notes.usage: 일 때문에 나는 너를 못 만날 것 같아 'Because of work, I probably won't be able to meet you'; 남자 친구 때문에 새로운 남자를 못 만나 'Because of my boyfriend, I can't meet another man'.
notes.nuance: This is NOT the same as attaching ~아/어서 to 이다 (covered in Lesson 37): 남자 친구 때문에 새로운 남자를 못 만나 ('Because of my boyfriend...') is different in feel from 남자 친구라서 새로운 남자를 못 만나 ('Because he IS my boyfriend...', a sentence that rarely makes practical sense). 때문에 states 'because of [that noun itself]', with no implied 'to be' verb, whereas ~이다+아/어서 specifically means 'because [something] IS that noun'. That said, this distinction is sometimes irrelevant in practice, since 우리는 제사 때문에 할아버지 집에 갔어요 ('because of 제사') and 우리는 제사라서 할아버지 집에 갔어요 ('because it is 제사') can effectively convey the same idea in some contexts.

examples.meaning: I'm really hot because of my school uniform.

pattern: V/Adj~기 때문에 ('karena...', klausa penuh, setara ~아/어서)
meaning: 'Because' - attaching ~기 to a stem to nominalize the reason clause before 때문에, with the exact same meaning as ~아/어서.

notes.formation: Attach ~기 to the stem of the verb/adjective immediately before 때문에: 배고프다 -> 배고프기 때문에. Works for verbs, adjectives, and 이다 alike, exactly like ~아/어서.
notes.usage: 저는 배고프기 때문에 밥을 먹고 싶어요 = 저는 배고파서 밥을 먹고 싶어요 'I want to eat because I am hungry' - completely identical in meaning. 저는 행복하기 때문에 죽고 싶지 않아요 'I don't want to die because I am happy'; 무릎이 아프기 때문에 저는 걸어가기 싫어요 'I don't want to walk because my knee is sore'; 내가 남자이기 때문에 그런 영화를 좋아해 'I like those kinds of movies because I am a man' (이다 taking ~기, giving 이기).
notes.nuance: ~기 때문에 and ~아/어서 are essentially interchangeable, both meaning 'because' with no meaningful difference - the choice between them is largely a matter of style/preference rather than grammar. Both follow the same multi-clause particle rules from Lesson 24 for their subjects.

pattern: ~았/었기 때문에 (klausa alasan BISA dikonjugasikan ke lampau, berbeda dari ~아/어서)
meaning: Unlike ~아/어서, the clause before ~기 때문에 CAN be directly conjugated into the past tense.

notes.formation: Attach ~았/었 to the stem first, then add ~기 (not the plain stem alone): 먹다 -> 먹었기 때문에.
notes.usage: 내가 밥을 벌써 먹었기 때문에 지금 먹고 싶지 않아 'Because I already ate, I don't want to eat now' - this is the SAME meaning as 내가 밥을 벌써 먹어서 지금 먹고 싶지 않아 (Lesson 37), but here the past tense is directly visible in the reason clause itself, unlike with ~아/어서 where it must never be conjugated and is only inferred from context.
notes.nuance: This is a genuine, meaningful structural difference between the two 'because' constructions: ~아/어서 categorically forbids conjugating its clause into the past (내가 밥을 먹었어서 is wrong), while ~기 때문에 not only allows but requires the past marker to be included directly when the reason is meant to be understood as past (먹었기 때문에, not 먹기 때문에, when the eating already happened) - so despite meaning the same thing overall, the two constructions handle past tense completely differently.

pattern: ~ㄹ 것이기 때문에 (waktu depan sebelum 때문에)
meaning: Attaching ~기 때문에 to a future-tense clause, by attaching it to the 이다 at the end of ~ㄹ/을 것이다.

notes.formation: Since the future tense is ~ㄹ/을 것 + 이다, simply attach ~기 때문에 to that 이다: 먹을 것이다 -> 먹을 것이기 때문에. 것 can shorten to 거, in which case 이 merges with it: ~ㄹ/을 거기 때문에.
notes.usage: 내가 나중에 먹을 것이기 때문에 지금 먹고 싶지 않아 'Because I am going to eat later, I don't want to eat now'; 나는 내년에 대학교에 갈 것이기 때문에 지금 열심히 공부하고 있어 'Because I will be going to university next year, I am studying hard now'; 그녀가 그 셔츠가 거기에 없는 것을 깨닫지 못할 거기 때문에 저는 그냥 가져갈 거예요 'She won't notice that shirt is gone, so I'm just going to take it' (거기 때문에, the shortened form).
notes.nuance: This directly parallels how ~아/어서 attaches to future-tense clauses (Lesson 37) - both future-tense 'because' constructions are really just their normal present-tense form applied to the word 이다, since ~ㄹ/을 것이다 is fundamentally built on 이다 to begin with.

pattern: 그렇기 때문에 ('oleh sebab itu/karena itu', dari 그렇다 + ~기 때문에)
meaning: 'Therefore/because of that' - built from 그렇다 ('to be like that') plus ~기 때문에.

notes.formation: Attach ~기 to 그렇다's stem (dropping ㅎ as usual), then 때문에: 그렇다 -> 그렇기 때문에.
notes.usage: Used to link back to a previously mentioned situation as the reason for what follows, just like 그래서 (from Lesson 37, built with ~아/어서 instead): 요즘에 사람들은 그 제품을 안 사요 'These days, people aren't buying that product' -> 네, 그렇기 때문에 그 회사의 주식이 떨어지고 있어요 'Yes, because of that, that company's stocks are falling'.

pattern: N이/가 V~는 이유는 ~기 때문이다 ('alasan ... adalah karena...')
meaning: 'The reason ___ is because ___' - combining a noun-clause subject (이유 'reason') with a noun-clause predicate (~기 때문 + 이다).

notes.formation: 때문 can end a sentence as a noun, but a bare noun cannot end a sentence, so 이다 must be attached: 사람들이 너무 많이 있기 때문이야 'It's because there are too many people' (literally '[it] is [the reason of] there being too many people'). This '때문+이다' noun phrase can then serve as the predicate for a sentence whose SUBJECT is 이유 ('reason'), itself described by a ~는/ㄴ/은 verb clause (from Lesson 26): 내가 방에 들어가지 않은 이유는 [사람들이 너무 많이 있기 때문]이야 'The reason I didn't go into the room is because there are too many people'. The past can be marked either on 때문 (있었기 때문) or on the final 이다 (때문이었어), or both together, to indicate the reason happened in the past: 사람들이 너무 많이 있었기 때문이었어 'It was because there were too many people'.
notes.usage: 내가 한국에 간 이유는 한국어를 배우고 싶기 때문이었어 'The reason I went to Korea was because I wanted to learn Korean'; 내가 여기서 일하고 싶은 이유는 새로운 경험을 하고 싶기 때문이야 'The reason I want to work here is because I want to have a new experience'.
notes.nuance: These 'reason is because' sentences are technically equivalent in meaning to the much simpler ~아/어서 sentences already known: 한국어를 배우고 싶어서 한국에 갔어 'Because I wanted to learn Korean, I went to Korea' says essentially the same thing as the more elaborate 이유는...때문이다 version. This more complex structure is genuinely difficult to master at first (combining two separate noun-forming principles, 이유 as subject and 때문+이다 as predicate, within one sentence) - full comfort with it develops naturally with more exposure to Korean, and there's no need to force it before it feels natural.

pattern: ~(으)시 (honorifik subjek: menghormati orang yang MELAKUKAN tindakan)
meaning: A subject honorific marker added to a verb/adjective when the person DOING the action deserves respect - independent of who the speaker is talking to.

notes.formation: Attach ~시 to a vowel-final stem, ~으시 to a consonant-final stem. Irregulars: ㅅ/ㄷ/ㅂ follow their Lesson 7 rules exactly (짓다 -> 지으시; 걷다 -> 걸으시; 돕다 -> 도우시). ㅡ/르 are unaffected, simply taking ~시 since their stems already end in a vowel (잠그다 -> 잠그시; 자르다 -> 자르시). ㄹ irregular: the ㄹ is dropped and ~시 added (살다 -> 사시). ㅎ irregular: ㅎ is dropped and ~시 added, following the same rule as ㄹ (그렇다 -> 그러시). Once ~(으)시 is added, the word becomes an unconjugated stem that must then take a normal conjugation ending, exactly as if the stem itself ended in ~(으)시: 지으시 + 어요 -> 지으셔요; + ㅂ니다 -> 지으십니다; + 았다 -> 지으셨다.
notes.usage: ~(으)시 is chosen based on who is ACTING in the sentence, completely separate from the honorific level chosen based on who is being SPOKEN TO (Lesson 6). This creates four possible combinations: speaking to someone of low respect about someone of low respect (친구는 미용실에 갔어? 'Did your friend go to the salon?'); speaking to low respect about high respect (어머님은 미용실에 가셨어? 'Did your mother go to the salon?' - 으시 added because mother acts, but 어 ending because listener is casual); speaking to high respect about low respect (친구는 미용실에 갔습니까?); and speaking to high respect about high respect (어머님은 미용실에 가셨습니까?).
notes.nuance: This is genuinely tricky for English speakers because English has no equivalent - respect in English is shown only through vocabulary/tone, not through a grammatical marker tied specifically to the actor rather than the listener. The two honorific systems (formality-to-listener from Lesson 6, and respect-to-actor via ~(으)시 here) operate completely independently and can be mixed in any of the four combinations depending on the actual social relationships involved in a given sentence.

pattern: 드리다 (memberi, honorifik) + ~께 (bentuk formal dari ~에게/한테)
meaning: 'To give' when the recipient deserves high respect, paired with ~께 as the formal equivalent of ~에게/한테.

notes.formation: Use 드리다 in place of 주다 when giving to someone deserving high respect, with the recipient marked by ~께 (formal version of ~에게/한테) instead: [recipient]께 [object]를/을 드리다.
notes.usage: 할아버지께 선물을 드리고 싶어 'I want to give my grandfather a present'; 저는 항상 손님들께 봉지를 드려요 'I always give bags to the customers'; 저는 스님께 돈을 드렸어요 'I gave money to the monk'.
notes.nuance: Korean speakers do NOT say 드리시다 - one might expect ~(으)시 to also be added when the GIVER (not just the recipient) deserves respect, but 드리다 is apparently already formal enough to cover both the acting person and the receiving person in these situations, so the extra ~시 layer is simply not used.

pattern: 말씀하다 / 말씀 (bicara, honorifik: bisa untuk PELAKU tinggi ATAU pembicara ke PENDENGAR tinggi)
meaning: 'To speak' when the speaker deserves respect (말씀하다), and also the honorific noun for 'words' used when addressing someone who deserves respect.

notes.formation: Use 말씀하다 in place of 말하다 when the person speaking deserves high respect - 하다 typically combines with ~(으)시다 to give 말씀하시다. Separated, 말씀 alone is the honorific form of the noun 말 ('words/speech').
notes.usage: As a verb for a high-respect speaker: 모든 사람들은 교수님이 말씀하시기 시작하는 것을 기다렸다 'Everybody was waiting for the professor to start talking'; 선생님이 하시는 말씀을 잘 들었어요? 'Did you listen carefully to what your teacher said?'. As a noun for words YOU are saying to someone who deserves respect (note the reversal - here it's used because of who is being SPOKEN TO, not who is speaking): 제가 드리고 싶은 말씀이 있습니다 'I have something that I want to say' (literally 'I have words that I want to give you'), commonly paired with 드리다 to indicate the words are being 'given' to the high-respect listener.
notes.nuance: This is genuinely a bit unusual: 말씀하다 (verb) elevates the person doing the speaking, but 말씀 (bare noun) is instead used specifically because YOU (the speaker) are addressing someone deserving respect - the same honorific word ends up applying based on two different roles (speaker vs. listener) depending on whether it's used as a conjugated verb or as a standalone noun.

pattern: 드시다 / 잡수시다 (makan, honorifik)
meaning: 'To eat' when the eater deserves respect - two words with different levels of formality.

notes.formation: 들다 combined with ~(으)시다 gives 드시다. 잡수시다 is a separate, even more elevated word.
notes.usage: 아버지! 다 드셨어요? 'Dad! Have you finished eating?'; 점심을 드셨어요? 'Did you have lunch?'; 뭐 드시고 싶어요? 'What do you want to eat?'
notes.nuance: 잡수시다 shows a genuinely extreme level of respect - using it toward anyone who doesn't specifically deserve that much can come across as ridiculous or funny (the author recounts using it with his girlfriend's parents on first meeting them, and them finding it amusing). He personally reserves 잡수시다 only for occasions like dinner with his girlfriend's grandparents: 잘 잡수셨어요? 'Did you have a good meal?' - so 드시다 is the standard, broadly appropriate honorific choice, while 잡수시다 is reserved for unusually high-respect situations.

pattern: 계시다 (berada di/memiliki, honorifik dari 있다)
meaning: The honorific equivalent of 있다 when a high-respect person is located somewhere, or (with 있으시다 specifically) when they possess something.

notes.formation: 계시다 replaces 있다 for LOCATION ('to be at/in') when the person deserves respect: 아버지가 집에 계셔요 'Dad is (at) home'. It can also substitute for 있다 within ~아/어 있다 (Lesson 14) and ~고 있다 (Lesson 18): 아버지가 아직 서 계셔요 'Dad is still standing'; 아버지가 아직 드시고 계셔요 'Dad is still eating'. However, when 있다 means 'to have (possess)', the honorific form is instead 있으시다 (simply attaching regular ~(으)시 to 있다), NOT 계시다: 할아버지! 지금 시간이 있으셔요? 'Grandpa! Do you have time now?'
notes.usage: 할아버지가 여기에 계신지 몰랐어요 'I didn't know you were here, grandpa'; 교장선생님이 학교에 안 계셔요 'The principal isn't in the school'; 거기에 언제까지 계실 거예요? 'Until when will you be there?'; 선생님이 안 계셔서 학생들은 다 자고 있어요 'The teacher isn't here, so all the students are sleeping'.
notes.nuance: This mirrors the exact same split already learned for plain 있다 (Lesson 5/14): location-있다 and possession-있다 are different underlying usages, and that distinction carries straight through to their honorific forms - 계시다 for location, 있으시다 for possession - rather than one single honorific word covering both meanings.

quiz.explanation: For possession, the honorific is 있으시다 (regular ~(으)시 attached to 있다), not 계시다.

pattern: 주무시다 (tidur, honorifik dari 자다)
meaning: The honorific equivalent of 자다 ('to sleep').

notes.formation: 주무시다 is a completely separate word substituting for 자다 when the sleeper deserves respect (not a regular ~(으)시 derivation of 자다).
notes.usage: 잘 주무셨어요? 'Did you sleep well?'; 아버지가 지금 주무시고 있어요 'Dad is sleeping now'.

pattern: Kalimat perintah: V~아/어(요) (paling santai/semi-sopan)
meaning: The easiest, least formal way to give a command, by simply attaching ~아/어 (or ~아/어요 for more politeness) to a verb stem.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어 to a verb stem exactly as for the informal present tense: 먹다 -> 먹어; add ~요 for more politeness: 먹어요. ~(으)시 can also be inserted for extra respect toward the person being commanded: 가다 -> 가시다 -> 가셔요.
notes.usage: 밥을 천천히 먹어 'Eat your food slowly'; 열심히 공부해! 'Study hard!'. As with regular sentences, the subject (the person being commanded) is normally omitted, since it's obviously the listener. ~아/어 is appropriate for someone younger, the same age, or close to you; using it toward a superior (like saying 빨리 가! to a boss) would be highly inappropriate.
notes.nuance: These imperative forms are structurally IDENTICAL to ordinary present-tense conjugations - 저는 월요일마다 운동해요 ('I exercise every Monday', a statement) uses the exact same ending as an imperative command. Only context tells listeners whether a sentence is a statement or a command; this seems confusing at first, but becomes natural with more exposure to real conversational situations.

quiz.explanation: Imperative and statement forms with ~아/어(요) are structurally identical - context alone distinguishes them.

pattern: Kalimat perintah: V~(으)세요 (dari ~(으)셔요, bentuk sopan standar)
meaning: The standard, widely-used polite command form, technically a shortened pronunciation of ~(으)셔요.

notes.formation: ~(으)셔요 (= ~(으)시 + ~아/어요) is, in modern speech and writing, almost always pronounced/written as ~(으)세요 instead: 가셔요 = 가세요; 공부하셔요 = 공부하세요. This swap ONLY works when the form is exactly ~(으)셔요 - it cannot be applied to other conjugations of ~(으)시다 (가셨어요 cannot become 가셨으세요; 가셔 cannot become 가세; 가시다 cannot become 가세다). Irregulars follow the same rules as elsewhere: 걷다 -> 걸으세요; 짓다 -> 지으세요; 열다 (ㄹ irregular) -> 여세요; 눕다 -> 누우세요.
notes.usage: 이것을 보세요 'Look at this'; 빨리 올라오세요 'Come up quick'; 수고하세요! 'Work hard!' (a common parting greeting); 칠판을 올려다보세요 'Look up to the board'. ~(으)세요 can also be added to 있다 (as a verb, meaning 'to stay'): 집에 있어! 'Stay at home!' can also become more formal via 계시다 (Lesson 39) -> 계셔요 -> 계세요, the source of the greeting 안녕히 계세요 ('stay in peace').
notes.nuance: It is oddly uncommon to say ~(으)세요 attached directly to 먹다 - instead, ~(으)세요 is much more naturally attached to 들다 (the formal word for 'eat'), which as a ㄹ-irregular becomes 드세요 ('Eat!'). Also worth noting: this same ~(으)셔요/~(으)세요 swap applies not just to commands but to ANY sentence using this ending, including ordinary statements and questions with no imperative meaning at all: 저의 엄마는 매일 운동하셔요 = 저의 엄마는 매일 운동하세요 ('My mother exercises every day'); 선생님, 어디 가셔요? = 선생님, 어디 가세요? ('Teacher, where are you going?').

pattern: Kalimat perintah: V~아/어라 (dipakai orang tua ke yang lebih muda)
meaning: Another way to command, similar in formality to ~아/어 but with a distinctly different register - typically used by much older people toward younger people.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어라 to a verb stem: 가다 -> 가라; 듣다 -> 들어라; 먹다 -> 먹어라.
notes.usage: 빨리 가라! 'Go fast!'; 그렇게 해라! 'Do it like that!'; 내 말을 들어라 'Listen to what I say'; 밥을 먼저 먹어라 'Eat first'.
notes.nuance: Despite being technically similar in formality level to ~아/어, ~아/어라 carries a distinctly parental/grandparental feel and sounds odd or even funny coming from a peer - the lesson author recounts saying 가라 to his girlfriend and being teased for sounding like her grandfather. In practice, it's safer and more natural for most learners to simply use ~아/어 instead of ~아/어라 in everyday peer-to-peer commands.

pattern: Kalimat perintah: V~(으)십시오 (sangat formal)
meaning: A very formal command form, reserved for situations demanding an extreme level of respect.

notes.formation: Attach ~(으)십시오 to a verb stem, following the exact same irregular-change rules as ~(으)세요.
notes.usage: 여기서 내리십시오 'Get off here' (the kind of announcement broadcast in the Seoul subway at every stop). This form is typically reserved for meeting a partner's grandparents for the first time, or seen on signs in government buildings, stores, or restaurants (e.g. 'please come again').
notes.nuance: Because of its very narrow, high-formality use case, most learners will encounter ~(으)십시오 far more often as a listener (on announcements, signs) than as something they need to actively produce in daily conversation.

pattern: ~지 말다 (kalimat perintah negatif: 'jangan...')
meaning: 'Don't' - the negative imperative, built with the irregular word 말다, at all the same formality levels as the positive imperative.

notes.formation: Attach ~지 to a verb stem, then 말다, then a normal imperative ending: 가지 말다 + ~아/어 = 가지 말아! -> irregularly shortened to 가지 마! (dropping ㄹ before ~아/어, ~아/어라, ~아/어요 specifically - 말다 is the only verb known to behave this way for these three endings; in every other situation it follows the regular ㄹ irregular pattern). The five levels: 가지 마! / 가지 마라! / 가지 마요! / 가지 마세요! / 가지 마십시오!
notes.usage: By far the two most commonly heard forms are 가지 마 (informal) and 가지 마세요 (polite formal): 너무 빨리 먹지 마세요 'Don't eat your food too fast!'; 부끄러워하지 마세요 'Don't be shy!'; 집에 가지 마! 'Don't go home!'; 앉지 마! 'Don't sit down!'; 여기에 오줌을 싸지 마세요 'Don't pee here'.
notes.nuance: Numbers 1-3 (마/마라/마요, dropping ㄹ before a vowel-starting ending) go against Korean's normal grammatical rules - 말다 is a genuinely unique irregular in this specific respect, with no other verb known to behave this way for these particular endings. This irregularity applies ONLY to these specific imperative additions; in every other grammatical context, 말다 simply follows the regular ㄹ irregular pattern like any other verb ending in ㄹ.

pattern: ~지 말고 ('jangan..., dan...' - menghubungkan larangan dengan perintah positif)
meaning: 'Don't ___, and ___ instead' - connecting a negative command to a following positive command using ~고 (Lesson 17's connector).

notes.formation: Attach ~고 (the ordinary clause-connecting ~고 from Lesson 17) to 말다 instead of a normal imperative ending: [verb]~지 말고 + [positive command clause].
notes.usage: 매일 같은 운동을 하지 말고 많이 쉬세요 'Don't do the same exercise every day, and get lots of rest'; 그렇게 하지 말고 내 말을 들어봐 'Don't do it like that, and listen to what I have to say'; 한 사람에게 다 주지 말고 사람들과 동등하게 나누세요 'Don't give them all to one person, and divide them out evenly'.
notes.nuance: This is simply the regular clause-connecting ~고 already known (Lesson 17, e.g. 저는 밥을 먹고 갈 거예요 'I will eat then go') applied on top of the negative imperative 말다, rather than a brand-new grammatical mechanism - it's specifically useful for the common real-life need to tell someone both what NOT to do and what TO do instead in one sentence.

pattern: Kalimat perintah dengan ~아/어 보다 (mencoba/melunakkan perintah)
meaning: Attaching an imperative ending to ~아/어 보다 ('to try', Lesson 32), softening a command into a suggestion, though the 'try' meaning is often barely noticeable.

notes.formation: Attach any imperative ending (~아/어, ~아/어요, ~(으)세요, etc.) to the already-known ~아/어 보다 construction: 확인하다 -> 확인해 보다 -> 확인해 봐! 'Try checking that!'.
notes.usage: 이것을 먹어 봐! can be translated either 'Try eating this!' or simply 'Eat this!' - both are valid depending on how literally the 'try' nuance should come through. 여기 와 보세요 'Come here'; 지금 앉아 봐 'Sit down'; 문을 열어 봐 'Open the door'; 이것을 드셔 보세요 'Eat this' (formal, with 드시다); 그 강아지가 온순해 보여서 한 번 만져 보세요 'That dog looks calm/gentle, so try touching it'.
notes.nuance: Especially in the least formal command form (~아/어 봐), this construction is very commonly used simply as a plain command with essentially no remaining sense of 'trying/attempting' - the 'try' meaning is often so subtle it barely changes the sentence's overall meaning, making ~아/어 봐 feel like a softer, friendlier alternative to a bare command rather than a literal request to 'attempt' something.

pattern: N을/를 주세요 dll. (perintah dengan 주다: 'berikan saya N')
meaning: Using an imperative ending on 주다 ('to give') to ask/tell someone to give you an object.

notes.formation: Attach any imperative ending from the previous lesson to 주다: 줘 (informal, from 주 + 어); 주라 (from ~아/어라, usually pronounced this way rather than 줘라); 주세요 (polite formal).

notes.nuance: This is simply the imperative mood (Lesson 40) applied directly to the already-familiar verb 주다 when the thing being requested is a concrete OBJECT - the next pattern in this lesson extends 주다 to also request that an ACTION be done for the speaker, which is a distinct (though related) usage.

pattern: V~아/어 주다 ('melakukan V untuk saya/seseorang', tindakan sebagai jasa/kebaikan)
meaning: Attaching ~아/어 주다 to a verb stem to indicate the action is done AS A FAVOR for someone, or (in commands) to politely ask someone to do something for you.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어 to the verb stem, then 주다: 가르치다 -> 가르쳐 주다. ~(으)시 can be inserted when the acting person deserves respect: 가르쳐 주다 -> 가르쳐 주시다.
notes.usage: 그 선생님은 한국어를 저에게 가르쳤어요 'That teacher taught me Korean' (plain) vs 그 선생님은 한국어를 저에게 가르쳐 줬어요 'That teacher taught me Korean' (emphasizing the teaching was a favor/service). 할머니가 오늘 멀리에서 와 주셨어요 'Grandma came from far away (for me) today'. In commands, ~아/어 주세요 softens/politely frames a request as 'please do X for me': 빨리 오세요 'Come quick' (plain command) vs 빨리 와 주세요 'Come quick (for me)/Please come quick'; 점심을 요리해 주세요! 'Please make me lunch'. ~아/어 주다 is often added to 보이다 to ask something be shown (얼굴을 보여주세요/보여 주세요 'Please show me your face', both spacings acceptable).
notes.nuance: The difference between 점심을 요리하세요 ('Make lunch') and 점심을 요리해 주세요 ('Please make me lunch') is that only the latter frames the action as a specific service done for the speaker - without 주다, it's simply an instruction, while with 주다, the listener is understood to be doing a favor for the speaker's benefit. The word 좀 (a shortened, softer version of 조금 'a little') is very commonly inserted in these imperative-with-주다 sentences to make the request sound gentler, with no direct English translation: 밥을 좀 많이 주세요; 이것을 좀 만들어 주세요; 그 책을 제자리에 좀 둬 주세요.

pattern: ~지 말아 주다 ('tolong jangan...', larangan dilunakkan sebagai permintaan)
meaning: Combining the negative imperative ~지 말다 with ~아/어 주다 to politely ask someone not to do something, as a favor.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어 주다 after ~지 말다 (using 말아, not the shortened 마, since 주다 follows): [verb]~지 말아 주세요.
notes.usage: 그것을 말하지 마세요 'Don't say that' (plain negative command) vs 그것을 말하지 말아 주세요 'Please don't say that' (framing the non-action as a favor); 수업 시간 동안 자지 말아 주세요 'Please don't sleep in class'; 저를 쳐다보지 말아 주세요 'Please don't stare at me'; 저를 감옥에 넣지 말아 주세요! 'Please don't put me in prison!'
notes.nuance: Just as with the positive ~아/어 주다 pattern, adding 주다 here emphasizes that the listener is doing the speaker a service specifically by refraining from the action - the meaning shift from plain ~지 마세요 to ~지 말아 주세요 parallels exactly the shift from plain ~(으)세요 to ~아/어 주세요 covered in the previous pattern.

pattern: V~아/어 줘서 감사합니다 ('terima kasih sudah/atas V')
meaning: 'Thank you for ___-ing' - combining ~아/어 주다 (a favor), ~아/어서 (because), and 감사하다 (to be thankful) into one layered construction.

notes.formation: Build it up step by step: (1) take a verb stem, e.g. 요리하다; (2) add ~아/어 주다: 요리해 주다; (3) add ~아/어서 (Lesson 37, 'because'): 요리해 줘서; (4) add 감사하다 ('to be thankful'): 요리해 줘서 감사합니다 'thanks for cooking' (literally 'because you cooked (as a favor for me), I am thankful').
notes.usage: 열심히 공부해 줘서 감사합니다 'Thanks for studying hard'; 이것을 가르쳐 줘서 감사합니다 'Thanks for teaching that to me'; 문을 열어 줘서 감사합니다 'Thanks for opening the door for me'.
notes.nuance: Since thanking someone is usually done in a formal context, ~(으)시 is very often inserted as well, adding yet another layer: 가르치다 + ~아/어 주다 + ~(으)시 + ~아/어서 + 감사합니다 -> 이것을 가르쳐 주셔서 감사합니다 'Thanks for teaching that to me' (more formal/respectful than without ~(으)시). This construction deliberately combines several previously separate grammar points (the imperative-adjacent ~아/어 주다 from this lesson, ~아/어서 from Lesson 37, and ~(으)시 from Lesson 39) into a single sentence, which is why it's introduced only this late - understanding each piece individually beforehand is what makes the combined form manageable.

pattern: N 때 ('selama/pada masa N')
meaning: 'During' - placed directly after a noun naming an event or period to refer to the time during it.

notes.formation: [Noun] + 때, e.g. 저녁 때 'during dinner/evening time'; 방학 때 'during the school vacation'; 회의 때 'during the meeting'; 고등학교 때 'during high school'; 대학교 때 'during university'.

notes.nuance: This simple form is a bare noun-to-noun combination with no additional grammar - the more complex use of 때 (describing it with a full clause via ~ㄹ/을) is covered in the next pattern, building on this basic noun usage.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 때 ('saat/ketika V', waktu umum/depan)
meaning: 'When' - describing 때 with a full clause via ~ㄹ/을, indicating the precise moment an action happens, not a result afterward.

notes.formation: 때 is described by a preceding clause using the ~는 것 principle, with the future/general form ~ㄹ/을 (not ~는): 내가 밥을 먹을 때 'the time that I eat'. When both clauses share a subject, it's stated only once.
notes.usage: 내가 밥을 먹을 때 음악을 듣는 것을 좋아해 'When I eat I like to listen to music'; 뼈마디가 아플 때 이 약을 드세요 'When your joints hurt, take this medicine'; 대통령을 만날 때 저는 아주 예의가 바를 거예요 'When I meet the president I will be very polite'.
notes.nuance: Despite using the future-looking ~ㄹ/을, this form describes a GENERAL or timeless moment (not necessarily tied to past/present/future) unless context specifies otherwise. Critically, the main clause's action must occur PRECISELY DURING the time indicated by 때, not as a result afterward - so 집에 갈 때 아빠를 전화할 거예요 does NOT mean 'when I get home, I will call my father' (that would require ~(으)면, covered in the next lesson, or ~아/어서: 집에 가서 아빠를 전화할 거예요 'I will go home and [then] call my father'); it instead means the calling happens DURING the going-home trip itself. This precision matters especially with 가다/오다, where the timing distinction is easy to get wrong.

pattern: V~았/었을 때 ('saat/ketika V dulu', waktu lampau)
meaning: 'When' referring to a specific point in the past.

notes.formation: Attach ~았/었 to the stem first, then ~ㄹ/을 때: 먹다 -> 먹었을 때 'when I ate'; 가다 -> 갔을 때 'when I went'; 공부하다 -> 공부했을 때 'when I studied'.
notes.usage: 내가 밥을 먹었을 때 말하고 싶지 않았어 'When I ate, I didn't want to talk'; 엄마가 갔을 때 저는 울었어요 'When mom left, I cried'; 가방을 처음 봤을 때 가짜인 것을 알았어요 'When I first saw the bag, I knew that it was fake'.
notes.nuance: This is the standard way to describe what used to happen or how things were when you were younger: 제가 어렸을 때 곤충을 먹었어요 'When I was young I used to eat bugs'; 제가 열 살이었을 때 아주 뚱뚱했어요 'I was really fat when I was 10 years old' (이다 + ~았/었을 때, following its usual past-tense conjugation pattern).

pattern: 때 + partikel (~까지, ~부터, ~마다, ~는/은, dan penanda subjek/objek)
meaning: 때 combines with various particles to add nuances like 'until', 'since', 'every time', or to serve as the subject/object of a sentence.

notes.formation: ~에 can technically be added to 때 in all the previous patterns, but is normally omitted when 때 simply refers to a time. Other particles CAN be added when 때 (with its describing clause) is used as a subject or object: ~가 (우리가 지난 번에 만났을 때가 아주 재미있었어요 'The last time we met was really fun'), ~를 (저는 사막에서 살았을 때를 잊어버리고 싶어요 'I want to forget the time I lived in the desert'). More complex particles: ~까지 ('until': 키가 클 때까지 얕은 수영장에서만 수영할 거예요 'I'm only going to swim in shallow pools until I am taller'); ~부터 ('since': 저는 그 팀을 어렸을 때부터 응원했어요 'I've been cheering for that team since I was young'); ~마다 ('every time': 내가 한국에 있을 때마다 한국어로 말하고 싶어 'Every time I am in Korea, I want to speak Korean'); ~는/은 (contrastive/topic: 제가 집에 있을 때는 TV를 봐요 'I watch TV when I'm at home [but not elsewhere]'); ~에만 ('only when': 저의 여자 친구는 우리가 같이 있지 않을 때에만 저를 좋아해요 'My girlfriend only likes me when we are not together'); ~나 (from Lesson 25/55: 아무 때나 좋아요 'Anytime is good').
notes.usage: These particles attach to 때 exactly as they would to any other noun, layering their individual meanings onto the basic 'time when' concept established by ~ㄹ/을 때.
notes.nuance: This confirms that 때 (once described by a clause) behaves as a genuine, fully flexible noun, just like 것 in the ~는 것 principle - any particle appropriate for a noun's grammatical role can be attached, not just the time-marking ~에 that gets dropped in the simplest 'when' sentences.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을 때가 있다/많다 ('ada kalanya/sering kali...')
meaning: Using 있다/없다/많다 with 때 to indicate that there are (or aren't, or are many) occasions/cases when something happens.

notes.formation: [Clause]~ㄹ/을 때 + 가 + 있다/없다/많다: 그 친구를 죽이고 싶을 때가 있어요.
notes.usage: 그 친구를 죽이고 싶을 때가 있어요 'There are times when I want to kill that friend'; 밤 늦게 배고플 때가 많아요 'There are many cases/times where I am hungry at night'. In this usage, ~ㄹ/을 때 CAN appropriately be attached to 가다/오다 (unlike the timing-precision concern in the earlier 'when' pattern), since the focus here is on 'occasions/cases', not on precisely matching two simultaneous actions: 그 학생이 늦게 올 때가 많아요 'There are many times where that student comes late'.
notes.nuance: In this usage, 때 shifts meaning slightly from 'the time when' to something closer to 'a case/occasion' - the best English translation moves away from 'when' and toward 'there are times/cases where...', a distinct nuance from the straightforward temporal 'when' meaning covered in the earlier patterns of this lesson.

pattern: V/Adj~(으)면 (pemakaian 1: dugaan/asumsi - 'kalau/saat X terjadi, Y akan terjadi')
meaning: 'When/if' - the first clause is a supposition that hasn't happened yet, and the second clause is an assumption of what will happen once it does.

notes.formation: Attach ~면 to a vowel-final stem, ~으면 to a consonant-final stem. Irregulars: ㅅ/ㄷ/ㅂ follow Lesson 7 rules exactly (짓다 -> 지으면; 걷다 -> 걸으면; 돕다 -> 도우면). ㅡ/르 are unaffected, taking plain ~면 (잠그다 -> 잠그면; 자르다 -> 자르면). ㄹ-final stems take ~면 directly with no change (살다 -> 살면). ㅎ irregular: ㅎ is dropped, ~면 added (그렇다 -> 그러면).
notes.usage: 집에 도착하면 빨래를 할 거예요 'When I arrive at home, I will do laundry' - here arriving home is inevitable/certain, so 'when' fits naturally. 집에 일찍 도착하면 빨래를 할 거예요 'IF I arrive home early, I will do laundry' - here the earliness is uncertain, so 'if' fits better. 학교에 가면 알려 주세요 'When/if you go to school, let me know' can be translated either way depending on context; 내일 비바람이 오면 경기가 취소될 거예요 'If it storms tomorrow, the match will be cancelled'.
notes.nuance: Whether 'when' or 'if' is the better English translation depends entirely on how certain the first clause's event is - Korean ~(으)면 covers both without distinguishing them grammatically, so it's best not to fixate on picking the 'correct' English word and instead focus on understanding that the second clause is always a supposition about what happens once/if the first clause occurs.

pattern: ~았/었으면 ... ~았/었을 것이다 ('seandainya ... pasti sudah ...')
meaning: The past-tense version of ~(으)면, expressing a hypothetical about what WOULD HAVE happened if something HAD occurred (but didn't).

notes.formation: Attach ~았/었 to the stem, then ~으면: 공부하다 -> 공부했으면 'if I had studied'. The result clause typically ends in ~았/었을 것이다 ('would have ___').
notes.usage: 내가 공부했으면 시험을 합격했을 것이다 'If I had studied, I would have passed the test'; 내가 밥을 먹었으면 배고프지 않았을 것이다 'If I had eaten, I wouldn't have been hungry'; 돈을 다 쓰지 않았으면 그것을 샀을 거예요 'If I hadn't spent all my money, I would have bought that'.
notes.nuance: Here 'if' is clearly the more appropriate English translation (rather than 'when'), because using 'when' would wrongly imply the action actually happened - the whole point of this past-tense construction is that the condition did NOT actually occur. This pattern is also a common way to express a wish/hope, a usage explored further in a later lesson.

pattern: V~ㄴ/는다면 / Adj~다면 / N이라면 (alternatif dari ~(으)면 dengan penekanan lebih pada dugaan)
meaning: An alternative to ~(으)면, formed by attaching ~면 to the plain/diary form conjugation, which places extra emphasis on the hypothetical nature of the clause.

notes.formation: First conjugate the word to its plain/diary form (Lesson 5), then add ~면: verbs present tense 가다 -> 간다면, 먹다 -> 먹는다면; adjectives present tense 행복하다 -> 행복하다면, 길다 -> 길다면; verbs/adjectives past tense 가다 -> 갔다면, 먹다 -> 먹었다면, 행복하다 -> 행복했다면; 이다 present -> 이라면, past -> 이었다면; 아니다 present -> 아니라면, past -> 아니었다면.
notes.usage: All the earlier ~(으)면 example sentences can be re-expressed with ~ㄴ/는다면 with the same overall meaning: 집에 도착한다면 빨래를 할 거예요; 학교에 간다면 알려 주세요; 내가 공부했다면 시험을 합격했을 것이다; 친구를 만났다면 재미있었을 것이다.
notes.nuance: Using ~ㄴ/는다면 places a bit more emphasis on the fact that the preceding clause is a genuine supposition/assumption (might or might not happen) than plain ~(으)면 does - as a result, 'if' becomes the more fitting English translation more often with ~ㄴ/는다면 than with ~(으)면. Both forms are otherwise interchangeable in meaning for the sentences covered so far in this lesson.

pattern: ~았/었더라면 (varian lain dari 'seandainya' waktu lampau)
meaning: Another way to express the past-tense 'if had' meaning, essentially interchangeable with ~았/었으면.

notes.formation: Attach ~더라면 to a stem already conjugated with ~았/었: 공부하다 -> 공부했더라면. Best treated as a single fixed unit for now.
notes.usage: 내가 공부했더라면 시험을 합격했을 것이다 'If I had studied, I would have passed the test'; 친구를 만났더라면 재미있었을 것이다 'If I had met my friend, it would have been fun' - both convey the same meaning as their ~았/었으면 counterparts.
notes.nuance: The ~더~ portion of this construction has its own deeper grammatical purpose explored in much later lessons (Lessons 117-119) - for now, it's enough to treat ~았/었더라면 as one interchangeable unit alongside ~았/었으면, without needing to analyze why it's built the way it is.

pattern: V/Adj~(으)면 (pemakaian 2: fakta umum/sebab-akibat, bukan dugaan)
meaning: Using ~(으)면 to state a general fact/common-knowledge cause-and-effect relationship, not a supposition about a specific future event.

notes.formation: Same ~(으)면 attachment as before, but here the final clause is conjugated in the PRESENT tense, since it describes a general truth rather than a specific past/future event.
notes.usage: 비가 오면 날씨가 추워져요 'When/if it rains, the weather gets colder' - a general, commonly-known fact, not a specific assumption about one rain event. 잠을 못 자면 다음 날에 몸이 피곤해져요 'When you don't sleep well, the next day you will be tired'; 콜라를 매일 마시면 건강이 나빠져요 'When you drink cola every day, your health deteriorates'; 오후가 되면 햇살이 강해져요 'When it becomes afternoon, the sun gets stronger'.
notes.nuance: The distinction from Usage 1 (supposition) is that these sentences describe events that are NOT tied to a specific occurrence in the past or future - they're general cause-and-effect statements that hold true generally, which is why the resulting clause naturally takes the present tense rather than a future/past conjugation.

pattern: V/Adj~(으)면 (pemakaian 3: 'setiap kali', tindakan berulang)
meaning: Using ~(으)면 to mean 'whenever' - the second clause happens every time the first clause is repeated, essentially the same as ~ㄹ/을 때마다.

notes.formation: Same ~(으)면 attachment, used for actions that repeat frequently. The result clause is typically in the present tense, since these are recurring facts, not one-time past/future events.
notes.usage: 피자를 먹으면 저는 콜라를 마셔요 'Whenever I eat pizza, I drink cola'/'Every time I eat pizza, I drink cola'; 아버지가 운전하면 습관으로 담배를 피워요 'Whenever my dad drives, he smokes cigarettes out of habit'; 일요일이면 그 가족이 기도하러 교회에 가요 'Whenever it is Sunday, that family goes to church to pray'.
notes.nuance: This usage is nearly identical in meaning to attaching ~마다 to 때 (Lesson 42): 피자를 먹을 때마다 저는 콜라를 마셔요 conveys the same 'whenever' idea. Just as English has multiple ways to say the same thing ('whenever' and 'every time'), Korean offers ~(으)면 and ~ㄹ/을 때마다 as two roughly interchangeable ways to express repeated cause-and-effect.

pattern: 만약 (kata keterangan penanda ketidakpastian/hipotesis)
meaning: An adverb with no direct English translation, used to signal that a sentence's outcome is uncertain, typically preceding a ~(으)면 clause.

notes.formation: Simply placed at the beginning of a sentence (or before the ~(으)면 clause), with no conjugation of its own.
notes.usage: 만약 내가 공부했으면 시험을 합격했을 것이다 'If I studied, I would have passed the test'; 만약 내일 비바람이 오면 경기가 취소될 거예요 'If it storms tomorrow, the match will be cancelled'; 만약 지금 환경을 보존하지 않으면 미래에 더 큰 문제가 생길 것 같아요 'If we don't preserve the environment now, there will probably be bigger problems in the future'.
notes.nuance: 만약 belongs to a small group of Korean adverbs that carry no real standalone meaning of their own - they exist to add a feeling to the sentence and help the listener anticipate what kind of statement is coming (here, a hypothetical), rather than to translate into any specific English word. It naturally pairs with the FIRST usage of ~(으)면 (supposition/assumption) covered in this lesson, since that's precisely the context where the sentence's outcome is genuinely uncertain.

pattern: 그러면/그렇다면 ('kalau begitu') dan 아니면 ('kalau tidak/atau')
meaning: 'If so' (from 그렇다 + ~(으)면 or ~ㄴ/는다면) and 'if not/or' (from 아니다 + ~면).

notes.formation: 그렇다 + ~(으)면 = 그러면 (ㅎ dropped, as usual); 그렇다 + ~ㄴ/는다면 = 그렇다면 (NOT 그렇는다면, since 그렇다 is an adjective and the plain-form conjugation rule for adjectives doesn't add ~는). 아니다 + ~면 = 아니면.
notes.usage: 그러면/그렇다면 refers back to a situation just mentioned, meaning 'if (that situation happens/is true)...', commonly translated 'if so': 내일 비가 올 것 같아요 'It will probably rain tomorrow' -> 그러면/그렇다면 공원에 안 갈 거예요 'If so, I'm not going to the park'. 아니면 ('if not') can start a sentence referring back to the previous one: 저는 밥을 먹고 싶어요. 아니면 죽을 것 같아요 'I want to eat rice. If not, I will probably die'. 아니면 can also appear mid-clause between two nouns to mean 'or': 저는 밥 아니면 사과를 먹고 싶어요 'I want to eat rice, if not, apples' (i.e. 'rice or apples').
notes.nuance: 아니면's 'or' meaning is one of several ways to express 'or' in Korean - an alternative using ~이나/거나 is introduced in a later lesson, giving learners more than one tool for this common connective idea.

pattern: V~자 ('Ayo...', informal) + ~지 말자 ('Ayo jangan...')
meaning: 'Let's...' - suggesting an action be done together, informally, plus its negative counterpart.

notes.formation: Attach ~자 directly to a stem ending in either a vowel or consonant, always in the present tense form, with no irregular changes triggered: 먹다 -> 먹자; 가다 -> 가자. For 'let's not', attach ~자 to 말다 (from ~지 말다, Lesson 40) instead of a normal imperative ending: 가지 말다 -> 가지 말자.
notes.usage: 밥을 먹자! 'Let's eat!'; 내일 공원에 가자! 'Tomorrow, let's go to the park!'; 무대에 같이 올라가자 'Let's go onto the stage together'. Negative: 내일 공원에 가지 말자 'Let's not go to the park tomorrow'; 우리 애기를 위해 그것을 사지 말자 'Let's not buy that for our baby'.
notes.nuance: ~자 is strictly informal - unlike most imperative-family endings, ~요 is simply never added to ~자 in Korean. This means ~자 can only be used with people who don't deserve high respect, like friends or people younger than the speaker.

pattern: V~ㅂ/읍시다 ('Ayo...', sedikit lebih formal daripada ~자)
meaning: 'Let's...' - a slightly more formal alternative to ~자, common in workplace settings among coworkers.

notes.formation: Attach ~읍시다 to a consonant-final stem, ~ㅂ시다 directly to a vowel-final stem: 먹다 -> 먹읍시다; 가다 -> 갑시다.
notes.usage: 밥을 먹읍시다! 'Let's eat!'; 내일 공원에 갑시다! 'Tomorrow, let's go to the park!'; 그 규정을 내일부터 시행합시다 'Let's enforce that rule starting tomorrow'; 연수를 받으러 갑시다 'Let's go to receive the training'.
notes.nuance: ~ㅂ/읍시다 is commonly heard in offices - a boss speaking to subordinates, or coworkers speaking to each other - situations where some respect toward the listener is appropriate but extreme formality isn't required. However, it should NOT be used toward someone deserving very high respect (like a father-in-law or a boss you're especially deferential to) - in those cases, it's better to simply phrase the suggestion as a polite question instead (e.g. 같이 먹고 싶습니까? 'Do you want to eat together?').

examples.meaning: Let's enforce that rule starting tomorrow.
Let's go to receive the training? (used to show the pattern)
Let's not enforce that rule yet.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을래(요) (pemakaian 1&2: 'Bagaimana kalau kita...' dan ancaman kosong)
meaning: Asking if the listener wants to do something together ('Shall we...'), or (with two fixed words) making an empty threat.

notes.formation: Attach ~ㄹ/을래(요) to a verb stem, following the usual vowel/consonant split. Unlike ~자 and ~ㅂ/읍시다, ~요 CAN be added to make it more formal.
notes.usage: Usage 1 - asking if the listener wants to do something together, translated 'Shall we...' or 'Would you like to...': 내일 공부하러 독서실에 갈래요? 'Shall we go to the library tomorrow to study?'; 영화를 볼래요? 'Shall we see a movie together?'. Works with question words too: 뭐 먹을래? 'What shall we eat?'. Usage 2 - two specific fixed expressions, 맞을래? ('Do you want to be hit?') and 죽을래? ('Do you want to die?'), used as empty threats when the speaker is annoyed at someone, not meant literally.
notes.nuance: These two usages share the same underlying mechanism - asking whether the listener wants a certain thing to happen - but Usage 1 is a genuine, friendly suggestion, while Usage 2 is a narrow, idiomatic pair of threat expressions that shouldn't be taken as a general pattern for making threats with other verbs.

examples.meaning: Shall we go to see the show in Seoul?
Do you want to die? (empty threat)
Shall we not eat dinner together tomorrow? (used to show the pattern)

quiz.explanation: These are typically empty threats used when the speaker is annoyed, not meant literally.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을래(요) + 주다 (pemakaian 3: permintaan sopan, 'bisakah kamu tolong...')
meaning: Attaching ~ㄹ/을래(요) to 주다 (either standalone or ~아/어 주다) to softly ask someone to do something for you.

notes.formation: [verb stem]~아/어 주다 (or bare 주다) + ~ㄹ/을래(요). ~(으)시 is often inserted before ~ㄹ/을래(요) to soften and formalize the request further: 주다 -> 주실래요.
notes.usage: 김치를 더 줄래요? 'Can you give me more kimchi?'; 문을 닫아 줄래요? 'Can you close the door?'. With ~(으)시 added: 김치를 더 주실래요? 'Could you please give me more kimchi?'; 환불해 주실래요? 'Could you please give me a refund?'; 이 숙어가 무슨 뜻인지 설명해 주실래요? 'Could you please explain what this idiom means?'
notes.nuance: This is a softer alternative to the direct imperative endings from Lesson 40 - by framing the request as a question about what the listener would like/be willing to do, rather than a direct command, ~ㄹ/을래(요) sounds gentler, almost like a request rather than an order.

examples.meaning: Could you please turn on the air conditioner?
Could you please pick up the phone that is ringing?
Won't you please write all of this up for me? (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: Apa fungsi ~(으)시 saat disisipkan sebelum ~ㄹ/을래요 dalam permintaan?
quiz.explanation: ~(으)시 makes the request softer and more formal, e.g. 주다 -> 주실래요.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을래(요) (pemakaian 4: 'saya mau/akan V', kalimat sederhana)
meaning: Stating that the speaker wants to or will do something, similar to ~고 싶다 or a simple future-tense conjugation, but typically limited to simple sentences.

notes.formation: Attach ~ㄹ/을래(요) directly to a verb stem, exactly as in the earlier usages, but here with no listener-directed question meaning - it simply states the speaker's own intention.
notes.usage: 나는 집에 갈래 'I'm going home/I want to go home' - roughly equivalent to both 나는 집에 갈 거야 ('I'm going home') and 나는 집에 가고 싶어 ('I want to go home'). ~안 or ~지 않다 negates it to show the speaker doesn't want to do something: 나는 안 할래 'I'm not going to do it/I don't want to do it'; 나는 안 먹을래 'I'm not going to eat/I don't want to eat that'.
notes.nuance: Unlike the regular future tense or ~고 싶다, which can be used in complex sentences, ~ㄹ/을래(요) in this usage is typically reserved for simple, short sentences (like 나는 먼저 할래 'I want to do it first') - it isn't the natural choice for elaborate or multi-clause statements of intent.

examples.meaning: I'm going to eat that/I want to eat that.
Do you want to do it first? (used to show the pattern)
I'm not going to eat/I don't want to eat that.

options: Baik 나는 집에 갈 거야 maupun 나는 집에 가고 싶어
quiz.explanation: ~ㄹ/을래(요) in this usage roughly equals both the plain future tense and ~고 싶다.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 수 있다 ('bisa V')
meaning: 'Can/is able to' - expressing ability or possibility, using the pseudo-noun 수 ('ability/capability').

notes.formation: 수 is a 'pseudo-noun' like 지 (Lesson 30) and 적 (Lesson 32) - it means 'ability/capability' by dictionary definition but can never stand alone; it must be described by a preceding verb clause using the ~ㄹ/을 attributive: 공부하다 -> 공부할 수, literally 'the ability to study'. Attach 있다 to complete the meaning 'to have the ability to ___': 공부할 수 있다.
notes.usage: 저도 그것을 할 수 있어요 'I can do that too'; 저는 이 수학문제를 술술 풀 수 있어요 'I can solve this math question without any issue'; 저는 몇몇 한국사람들보다 한국어를 더 잘 말할 수 있어요 'I can speak Korean better than some Korean people'. Also used to ask if someone is able to do something: 오늘 밤에 만날 수 있어요? 'Can you meet tonight?'. When the action would be done for the speaker, ~아/어 주다 (Lesson 41) can be inserted before ~ㄹ/을 수 있다, and 좀 can soften the request: 그것을 좀 빨리 해 줄 수 있어요? 'Can you do it a little bit faster (for me)?'
notes.nuance: As with other pseudo-nouns, 수 only ever appears in this specific slot (after a ~ㄹ/을-conjugated clause, before 있다/없다) - it's grammatically a noun but not a freely usable one, so it should be thought of as a fixed building block rather than a word you can place anywhere a normal noun goes.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 수 없다 ('tidak bisa V')
meaning: 'Cannot/is not able to' - the negative counterpart of ~ㄹ/을 수 있다.

notes.formation: Same structure as the positive form, but with 없다 instead of 있다: 공부할 수 없다 'to not have the ability to study'.
notes.usage: 제가 너무 아파서 많이 먹을 수 없어요 'I can't eat much because I am very sick'; 저 사람은 한국어를 말할 수 없어요 'That person can't speak Korean'; 여기가 너무 시끄러워서 저는 집중할 수 없어요 'I can't concentrate here because it is too loud'; 그런 일을 하면 장기 휴가를 갈 수 없어요 'If you do that kind of job, you can't go on any long holidays'.
notes.nuance: Just like ~ㄹ/을 수 있다, this is built on the same pseudo-noun 수, simply completed with the negative existential/possessive 없다 instead of 있다, following the exact same rule set already established.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을 수 있었다/없었다 dan ~ㄹ/을 수 있을/없을 것이다 (waktu lampau dan depan)
meaning: Conjugating ~ㄹ/을 수 있다/없다 into the past or future tense - only 있다/없다 itself is conjugated, never the preceding verb.

notes.formation: Only 있다 or 없다 is conjugated for tense; the verb before ~ㄹ/을 수 stays in its ~ㄹ/을 attributive form regardless of the overall sentence's tense: past 있었다/없었다; future 있을 것이다/없을 것이다.
notes.usage: 어렸을 때 저는 햄버거 다섯 개를 먹을 수 있었어요 'When I was younger, I could eat five hamburgers'; 저는 다음 번에 더 잘 할 수 있을 거예요 'I will be able to do better next time'; 저는 그 여자를 볼 수 없었어요 'I couldn't see that girl'; 내년에 캐나다에 갈 수 없을 거예요 'I won't be able to go to Canada next year'.
notes.nuance: This mirrors a pattern already seen elsewhere in the course: the pseudo-noun/attributive-clause part of the construction (~ㄹ/을 수) stays fixed, and only the final predicating word (있다/없다 here) receives tense conjugation - similar in spirit to how 것이다 alone gets conjugated in other ~ㄹ/을 것 constructions.

pattern: 이해할 수 없다 vs 이해하지 못하겠다 ('tidak bisa mengerti' umum vs spesifik)
meaning: Two ways to say 'I don't/can't understand', with a subtle difference between a general, permanent inability versus a specific, potentially fixable one.

notes.formation: 이해하다 ('to understand') + ~ㄹ 수 없다 gives 이해할 수 없다. Alternatively, ~지 못하다 (Lesson 22) attaches to 이해하다, and specifically with the future-looking ~겠다 ending: 이해하지 못하겠어요 (though the plain past 이해하지 못했어요 is also possible).
notes.usage: 이해할 수 없다 fits a general, sweeping topic that the speaker fundamentally can't grasp and likely never will: 나는 화학을 이해할 수 없어 'I can't understand Chemistry'; 나는 한국어를 이해할 수 없어 'I can't understand Korean'. 이해하지 못하겠다 fits something specific that the speaker doesn't currently get, but could probably understand if someone explained it better: 이 문제를 이해하지 못하겠어요 'I don't understand that question/problem'; 네가 무슨 말을 하고 있는지 이해하지 못하겠어 'I don't understand what you are trying to say'.
notes.nuance: This distinction mirrors the English difference between 'I can't understand [a whole subject]' (permanent, sweeping) and 'I don't understand [this specific thing]' (potentially temporary, fixable with better explanation). The author notes these two forms are essentially interchangeable in practice and the distinction doesn't need to be worried about too heavily, though it's worth being aware of.

examples.meaning: I can't understand Chemistry.
Do you not understand this question/problem?
I didn't understand this question/problem.

quiz.explanation: 이해할 수 없다 fits sweeping, general topics the speaker fundamentally can't grasp.

pattern: ~수가 있다/없다 (menambahkan ~가 ke 수 untuk penekanan)
meaning: Adding the particle ~가 to 수, which native speakers say adds no formal difference in meaning, but is often felt to add emphasis.

notes.formation: Insert ~가 directly after 수, before 있다/없다: ~ㄹ/을 수가 있다/없다.
notes.usage: 우리는 그것을 정확이 알 수가 없어요 'We can't know that for sure' (or, with the emphasis nuance, 'There's no way we can even know that for sure'); 이 사진을 보여줄 수가 없어요 'I can't show you that picture'; 그것을 어떻게 할 수가 있어요? 'How can you do that?' (or 'How can you POSSIBLY do that?').
notes.nuance: Korean grammar teachers report that ~가 adds no formal meaning difference to these sentences - the pairs with and without ~가 are considered grammatically identical. However, based on personal experience with the language, ~가 tends to appear more often specifically when the speaker wants to emphasize the situation (an even stronger sense of 'can't/can'), an intuition that can only really be developed through continued exposure to natural Korean conversation rather than a fixed rule.

examples.meaning: There's no way I can even look at my brother in the eyes.

pattern: V~아/어야 하다/되다 ('harus V' - must/have to/should)
meaning: 'Must/have to/should' - all covered by a single Korean construction, since the English distinction between these words is smaller than it seems.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어야 to a verb/adjective stem (following the usual vowel-harmony rule), then 하다 or 되다: 공부하다 -> 공부해야 하다/공부해야 되다.
notes.usage: 저는 밥을 먹어야 해요 'I have to eat'; 저는 지금 공부해야 해요 'I have to study now'; 대학교에 가고 싶다면 열심히 공부해야 돼요 'If you want to go to university, you have to/must/should study hard' (all three English translations are equally valid). 친구를 만나러 지금 가야 해요 'I have to go now to meet my friend'; TV를 켜고 싶으면 이것을 TV에 연결해야 해요 'If you want to turn on the TV, you need to connect this thing to the TV'.
notes.nuance: English speakers often feel 'must/have to' and 'should' carry meaningfully different strengths of obligation, but this same single Korean construction covers all of them - rather than trying to force a specific English word choice, it's better to recognize that Korean doesn't grammatically distinguish these levels of obligation the way English speakers instinctively want to. Swapping 하다 for 되다 makes no difference in meaning, though 되다 is reportedly more common in speech.

pattern: V~아/어야지/죠 (variasi percakapan dari ~아/어야 하다/되다)
meaning: Using ~지 (or its formal equivalent ~죠) in place of 하다/되다 in this construction, mostly heard in conversation, with no space before 지/죠.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어야 to the stem, then directly attach 지 (informal) or 죠 (formal) with NO space in between: 가다 -> 가야지/가야죠.
notes.usage: 우리가 빨리 가야지! 'We have to go fast!'; 우리는 빨리 가야죠! 'We have to go fast!' (more formal) - both mean the same as 우리는 빨리 가야 해요/돼요. More examples: 먹어야지! 'You have to eat!'; 신입생들에게 반말을 해야지 'You should speak in 반말 to the freshmen students'; 운명을 믿어야지 'You need to trust (in) fate'.
notes.nuance: This ~지/죠 addition is mainly a conversational alternative, and 지/죠 here has a separate, broader grammatical role introduced in a much later lesson - for now it's enough to recognize it as another interchangeable ending for the 'must/have to' meaning.

pattern: ~아/어야 했다/될 것이다 (waktu lampau/depan dari 'harus V')
meaning: Conjugating 하다/되다 at the end of ~아/어야 into the past or future tense, to express something 'had to have' happened or 'will have to' happen.

notes.formation: Conjugate only 하다/되다 for tense, keeping ~아/어야 fixed on the preceding stem: past 되었어요/했어요; future 될 거예요/할 거예요.
notes.usage: 그때 열심히 일해야 되었어요 'At that time I had to work really hard'; 복사기를 수리해야 되었어요 'We had to repair the photocopier'; 10분 후에 가야 될 거예요 'We will have to go in 10 minutes'; 신입생들을 위해 선물을 준비해야 할 거예요 'We will have to prepare a present for the freshmen'.
notes.nuance: This follows the same principle already seen with other multi-part constructions in the course (like ~ㄹ/을 수 있다/없다): the fixed 'core' of the expression (~아/어야) doesn't change with tense, and only the final predicating word receives the tense conjugation.

pattern: ~아/어야겠다 (singkatan dari ~아/어야 하겠다, 'sepertinya harus...')
meaning: A contraction of ~아/어야 하겠다, used when the speaker has just received some information/signal that prompts a reactive decision.

notes.formation: 밥을 먹어야 하겠다 -> commonly shortened in speech to 밥을 먹어야겠다.
notes.usage: 나는 지금 가야겠다 - said right after checking the time and realizing you have to go; best translated something like 'I'd better get going now' or 'I guess I'll have to go now' rather than a flat 'I will have to go'. 남자친구랑 내일 헤어져야겠다 'I'll have to break up with my boyfriend tomorrow'; 이 사실을 부장님께 알려 줘야겠어요 'I'll have to tell the boss about that fact'; 그녀를 위해 선물을 사야겠어요 'I'll have to buy her a present'.
notes.nuance: Unlike a plain future-tense 'will have to', ~아/어야겠다 specifically implies the decision is a REACTION to something the speaker just noticed, heard, or realized - it's not a pre-planned obligation but a spontaneous conclusion. No single English translation captures this perfectly, so it's best to focus on the underlying meaning (a just-realized, reactive necessity) rather than force a fixed English equivalent.

pattern: N이/가 필요하다 ('membutuhkan N')
meaning: 'To need' something - 필요하다 is an adjective (like 있다), so the needed thing is marked ~이/가, never ~을/를.

notes.formation: [needed thing] + ~이/가 + 필요하다. As an adjective, its plain/diary form conjugation follows the adjective rule (dictionary form = plain form): 필요하다, NOT 필요한다 (which would be the incorrect verb-style form).
notes.usage: 나는 밥이 필요하다 'I need food/rice'; 나는 여자 친구가 필요하다 'I need a girlfriend'; 우리 회사는 새로운 복사기가 필요해요 'Our office needs a new photocopier'; 그 영화가 영웅 캐릭터가 필요해요 'That movie needs a hero character'.
notes.nuance: The common beginner error is copying English's transitive-verb feel and writing 나는 밥을 필요하다 with the object marker ~을/를 - this is grammatically incorrect precisely because 필요하다, despite its verb-like English translation ('to need'), is actually an adjective in Korean, following the same particle logic already seen with 있다.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 필요가 있다/없다 ('perlu/tidak perlu V')
meaning: 'To need to' do a verb, using the noun 필요 ('necessity') described by a verb clause, paired with 있다/없다.

notes.formation: Describe the noun 필요 with a verb using the ~ㄹ/을 attributive: 밥을 먹다 -> 밥을 먹을 필요 'the necessity to eat'. Attach 있다 for 'to have that necessity' (i.e. 'need to') or 없다 for 'not need to': 밥을 먹을 필요가 있다/없다.
notes.usage: 저는 그 여자랑 결혼할 필요가 있어요 'I need to marry that girl'; 시험공부를 곧 할 필요가 있어요 'I need to study soon'; 강한 캐릭터를 만들 필요가 있어요 'We need to make a strong character'. With 없다: 제자리에 놓을 필요가 없어요 'You don't need to put it back in its place'; 그렇게 가까이 앉을 필요가 없어요 'There's no need to sit that close'.
notes.nuance: The literal 'to have the necessity to ___' translation is technically accurate but rarely used in practice - especially in speech, the more natural rendering is simply 'I need to ___', which is why this pattern conveys essentially the same practical meaning as ~아/어야 하다/되다, just built from a different underlying structure (a described noun + 있다/없다, rather than a direct verb-to-verb attachment).

pattern: V/Adj/이다~지만 ('meski/tapi', waktu sekarang)
meaning: 'But/even though' - connecting two clauses where the first is true, and the opposite/contrasting idea follows in the second.

notes.formation: Attach ~지만 directly to the stem of a verb, adjective, or 이다. Since the addition starts with ㅈ (a consonant that doesn't trigger any of the Lesson 7 irregulars), no irregular changes ever occur here.
notes.usage: This shortens the more explicit two-sentence version using 하지만 ('but', usually starting a new sentence): 저는 먹고 싶어요. 하지만 배고프지 않아요 becomes 저는 먹고 싶지만 배고프지 않아요 'I want to eat but I am not hungry' / 'Even though I want to eat, I am not hungry' (both English translations mean exactly the same thing). 부산에 가고 싶지만 차가 없어서 못 가요 'Even though I want to go to Busan, I can't because I don't have a car'; 그 연예인이 돈이 많지만 왜 그렇게 행복하지 않아 보여요? 'That celebrity has a lot of money, but why doesn't he look happy?'
notes.nuance: In every example in this lesson, the clause before ~지만 is something TRUE or already/certainly happening (not a hypothetical) - this distinguishes ~지만 from a related 'even though/even if' construction (~아/어도) covered in the next lesson, which can apply to hypothetical situations as well.

pattern: ~았/었지만 ('meski/tapi sudah...', waktu lampau)
meaning: The past-tense version of ~지만.

notes.formation: Attach ~았/었 to the stem first, then ~지만: 먹다 -> 먹었지만.
notes.usage: 밥을 먹었지만 배고파요 'Even though I ate, I am hungry'; 상처를 치료했지만 아직 고통이 있어요 'I treated the wound, but there is still pain'; 원래 한국에 여행하러 가고 싶었지만 돈이 없어서 못 갔어요 'Originally I wanted to go to Korea to travel, but because I didn't have any money, I couldn't go'.
notes.nuance: This is a straightforward application of the general ~았/었 past-tense marker to the already-known ~지만 connector, with no special irregular behavior beyond the regular past-tense conjugation rules.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을 것이지만 / ~ㄹ/을 거지만 / ~겠지만 ('meski/tapi akan...', waktu depan)
meaning: The future-tense version of ~지만, formed by removing the final 다 from a future-tense conjugation before attaching ~지만.

notes.formation: Take the future tense form (~ㄹ/을 것이다, ~ㄹ/을 거다, or ~겠다), remove the final ~다, then add ~지만: 갈 것이다 -> 갈 것이지만; 갈 거다 -> 갈 거지만; 가겠다 -> 가겠지만. All three are equally valid alternatives with the same meaning.
notes.usage: 한국에 안 갈 것이지만 여전히 한국어를 배우고 싶어요 = 한국에 안 갈 거지만 여전히 한국어를 배우고 싶어요 = 한국에 안 가겠지만 여전히 한국어를 배우고 싶어요, all meaning 'Even though I will not go to Korea, I still want to learn Korean'. 오늘 선생님이 안 올 거지만 우리는 선생님이 준비하신 내용을 공부해야 돼요 'Even though the teacher won't come today, we need to study the material that she prepared'.
notes.nuance: This follows the general pattern seen elsewhere with future-tense constructions built on 것이다/것이다 or 겠다: the '다' ending is simply swapped out for whatever grammatical addition is needed (here, ~지만), while the core future meaning is preserved regardless of which of the three underlying future forms is chosen as the starting point.
