pattern: 그렇지만 ('namun/akan tetapi', dari 그렇다 + ~지만)
meaning: 'However' - built by attaching ~지만 to 그렇다, referring back to a previously mentioned situation.

notes.formation: 그렇다 + ~지만 = 그렇지만 (no ㅎ-dropping this time, since ~지만 begins with a consonant that doesn't trigger the ㅎ irregular the way ~(으)-starting additions do).
notes.usage: Used to introduce a contrasting point about a situation already under discussion, most naturally translated 'however': 주차를 이 선 안에 해야 되지 않아요? 'Don't you have to park between these lines?' -> 그렇지만 차가 너무 커서 그렇게 할 수 없어요 'However, the car is too big so I can't do it like that'; 지금 가야 되지 않아요? 'Don't you have to go now?' -> 네, 그렇지만 할 게 많아서 지금 못 가요 'Yes, however I can't go now because I have a lot of things to do'.
notes.nuance: 그렇지만 stands as its own connector referring to the whole preceding situation, parallel to how 그래서 (Lesson 37) and 그렇기 때문에 (Lesson 38) work - all three attach a different piece of familiar grammar (~아/어서, ~기 때문에, ~지만) to the same base word 그렇다 to create a conversational connector with a distinct meaning ('therefore', 'because of that', 'however' respectively).

pattern: V/Adj~아/어도 ('terlepas dari apakah/kalaupun...')
meaning: 'Regardless of if/whether' - the second clause happens no matter what happens with the first (uncertain, supposed) clause.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어도 to a verb/adjective stem, following the usual vowel-harmony rule: 오다 -> 와도; 예쁘다 -> 예뻐도.
notes.usage: 밥이 있어도 저는 안 먹을 거예요 'Regardless of if there is food, I am not going to eat'; 태풍이 와도 내일 박람회에 가야 돼요 'Regardless of whether there is a typhoon, I have to go to the trade show tomorrow'; 여자들이 예뻐도 똑똑하지 않으면 매력이 없어요 'Regardless of how pretty girls are, if they are not smart, they have no charm'. Because the first clause is a genuine supposition (uncertain), question words can naturally appear in it: 네가 어디 가도 나는 가고 싶지 않아 'Regardless of where you are going, I don't want to go'; 우리 엄마가 무엇을 사도 산 다음 날에 항상 교환해요 'Regardless of what my mother buys, she always exchanges it the day after'.
notes.nuance: The key difference from ~지만 (previous lesson) is certainty: ~지만's first clause is an already-accepted fact (밥이 있지만 저는 안 먹을 거예요 'Even though there IS food...'), while ~아/어도's first clause is a genuine, uncertain supposition (밥이 있어도... 'Regardless of WHETHER there is food or not...'). This is also why question words work naturally with ~아/어도 but sound unnatural with ~지만 (네가 어디 가지만... is odd) - an accepted fact can't logically contain an unresolved 'where/what/when'.

pattern: 아무리 (kata keterangan penanda ~아/어도, menggantikan 얼마나)
meaning: An adverb that both replaces 얼마나 ('how much') in ~아/어도 sentences, and signals to the listener that ~아/어도 is coming later in the sentence.

notes.formation: Placed before the clause that will end in ~아/어도, replacing 얼마나 when the meaning is 'no matter how much...'.
notes.usage: 네가 나를 아무리 사랑해도 우리는 헤어져야 돼 'Regardless of how much you love me, we need to break up' (아무리 replaces what would otherwise be 얼마나); 애기를 안으려고 아무리 노력해도 애기가 나를 안고 싶지 않은 것 같이 보여요 'Regardless of how much I try to hug the baby, it looks like the baby doesn't want to hug me'.
notes.nuance: Beyond its 'how much' replacement role, 아무리 has a second function similar to 만약 (Lesson 43): it's placed early in a sentence purely to give the listener a feeling that a ~아/어도 clause is coming, helping them anticipate the sentence's structure - 아무리 often appears in ~아/어도 sentences even when 'how much' isn't the specific meaning being conveyed: 아무리 그 제품을 반값으로 줘도 저는 안 살 거예요 'Regardless of if you give me that product at half price, I'm not going to buy it' (here 아무리 is just signaling the ~아/어도 clause is coming, not replacing a 'how much' meaning).

pattern: N이다 + ~아/어도 (여도/라도, 'terlepas dari apakah adalah N')
meaning: Attaching ~아/어도 to 이다, following the same pattern already seen when attaching ~아/어서 to 이다 (Lesson 37).

notes.formation: Attach ~어도 directly to 이다's stem (이다 -> 이어도), since 이다's stem always ends in the vowel 이. Alternatively, ~라도 can be used instead of ~어도 (이다 -> 이라도), an equal-meaning alternative. When the preceding noun ends in a vowel, 이 merges with the addition: 이+어 -> 여, giving 여도; 이+라 -> 라, giving 라도 (identical either way since the 이 simply disappears into the merge).
notes.usage: 그 남자가 마법사라도 그 문을 열 수 없을 거예요 'Regardless of if that man is a magician, he is not going to be able to open that door'; 그 사람이 네 엄마여도 나는 그녀와 말을 안 할 거야 'Regardless of if that person is your mother, I'm not going to talk to her'; 그 일을 하는 사람이 누구라도 창피할 거예요 'Regardless of who does that job, they will be embarrassed'.
notes.nuance: This mirrors exactly the same ~이어서/여서 vs ~이라서/라서 choice already learned for 이다 + ~아/어서, just applied to ~아/어도 instead - the same two equally-valid alternative forms exist here (~이어도/여도 vs ~이라도/라도), and either is acceptable to use.

pattern: 그래도 ('meski begitu/tetap saja', dari 그렇다 + ~아/어도)
meaning: 'Regardless/it doesn't matter' - built by attaching ~아/어도 to 그렇다.

notes.formation: 그렇다 + ~아/어도 = 그래도 (following the same ㅎ-dropping pattern as 그래서/그러면).
notes.usage: Used as a standalone response referring back to a previously mentioned situation, meaning 'regardless of if (that situation) occurs': 같이 가자! 사람이 많을 거야! 'Let's go together! There will be so many people!' -> 그래도 가기 싫어요 'Regardless. I'm not going.'; 선생님! 배가 좀 아파요! 'Teacher! My stomach is a little sore!' -> 그래도 수업에 와야 돼 'Regardless, you have to come to class'.
notes.nuance: 그래도 completes the set of connectors built from 그렇다: 그래서 ('therefore', ~아/어서), 그렇기 때문에 ('because of that', ~기 때문에), 그러면 ('if so', ~(으)면), 그렇지만 ('however', ~지만), and now 그래도 ('regardless', ~아/어도) - each attaches a different, already-learned grammar point to the same base word to create a distinct conversational connector, all sharing the underlying idea of referring back to something just said.

pattern: 되다 (makna lain: 'berjalan baik/berfungsi/selesai')
meaning: Another meaning of 되다 - indicating something is going well, working, or finished, distinct from its earlier 'to become' and passive-sentence uses.

notes.formation: Place 되다 after a noun to indicate 'no problem' with that noun, often paired with the adverb 잘 ('well').
notes.usage: 사업이 잘 되고 있어요? 'Is your business going well?'; 여기서 Wi-Fi가 잘 돼요 'The Wi-Fi here works well'; 밥이 됐어요? 'Is the rice ready?/Has the rice finished cooking?' (indicating something has finished). To say the opposite (not going well/not working/not finished), use 안 (not 못, the usual opposite of 잘): 밥이 아직은 안 됐어요 'The rice still isn't ready'; 컴퓨터가 안 돼요 'The computer isn't working'; 로그인이 안 돼요 'I can't log in'. 됐어(요)! alone can mean 'That's enough!' (e.g. telling someone to stop pouring water into your glass).
notes.nuance: 됐어요 is also commonly used to decline an offer or say something 'doesn't work' for you in a scheduling sense: 저는 가고 싶지만 내일은 안 돼요 'I want to go, but tomorrow doesn't work for me' - a natural, idiomatic way of declining without a flat 'no'.

examples.meaning: The heart surgery went well.

pattern: V/Adj~아/어도 되다 ('boleh V')
meaning: 'One may/is allowed to' - combining ~아/어도 ('regardless of', Lesson 48) with 되다 ('no problem') to say an action is permitted.

notes.formation: Attach ~아/어도 to a verb/adjective stem, then 되다: 가다 -> 가도 되다, literally 'regardless of if you go, there is no problem'.
notes.usage: 네가 일찍 가도 돼 'You may go early/You are allowed to go early'; 아무거나 해도 돼요 'You can do whatever you want'; 지금 문을 열어도 돼요 'You may open the door now'; 학생들이 들어가도 되지만 부모를 동반해야 돼요 'Students may enter, but they must be accompanied by a parent'. As a question, asking if there's a 'problem' with doing something, naturally translated 'May I...?': 제가 일찍 가도 돼요? 'May I go early?'; 화장실에 가도 돼요? 'May I go to the bathroom?'. The final 되다 can be conjugated to past or future tense: 그때 나가도 되었어요 'It would have been okay if you left at that time'; 문을 열어도 될 거예요 'It will be okay if you open the door'.
notes.nuance: This construction directly builds on two previously learned pieces (~아/어도 and this lesson's 'no problem' meaning of 되다) rather than introducing anything fundamentally new - the permission meaning ('may/is allowed to') emerges naturally once you recognize it as literally 'regardless of if you do X, there's no problem'.

pattern: 안 ~아/어도 되다 ('tidak perlu/tidak harus V')
meaning: 'It's okay if one doesn't/one doesn't have to' - negating the verb before ~아/어도 되다, the near-opposite of ~아/어야 하다.

notes.formation: Add 안 (or ~지 않다) to the verb before ~아/어도 되다: 가다 -> 안 가도 되다/가지 않아도 되다, literally 'regardless of if you don't go, there's no problem'.
notes.usage: 네가 빨리 안 가도 돼 'You don't have to go quickly'; 내일까지 다 안 해도 돼요 'You don't need to do it all by tomorrow'; 이 음식에 소금을 안 넣어도 돼요 'You don't need to put salt on this food'; 이 학교가 과학 고등학교라서 인문학을 공부하지 않아도 돼요 'You don't need to study the humanities at this school because it is a science high school'. As a question: 지금 밥을 안 먹어도 돼요? 'You don't need to eat now?'; 수염을 안 깎아도 돼요? 'You don't need to shave your beard?'
notes.nuance: This construction can be thought of as roughly the logical opposite of ~아/어야 하다 (Lesson 46, 'must/have to'): 그 시험을 합격하기 위해 공부를 해야 돼요 'In order to pass that test, I need to study' vs 그 시험을 합격하기 위해 공부를 안 해도 돼요 'In order to pass that test, I don't need to study' - the same underlying situation, described from the 'obligation' side or the 'no obligation' side.

pattern: 좋다 / 괜찮다 sebagai pengganti 되다 dalam ~아/어도
meaning: Two words that can substitute for 되다 in the ~아/어도 construction, with the exact same 'it's okay if' meaning.

notes.formation: Simply swap 되다 for 좋다 or 괜찮다 at the end of the ~아/어도 construction, with no change to the rest of the sentence.
notes.usage: 지금 문을 열어도 돼요 = 지금 문을 열어도 좋아요 = 지금 문을 열어도 괜찮아요, all meaning 'You may open the door now'; 밥을 많이 먹어도 돼요? = 밥을 많이 먹어도 좋아요? = 밥을 많이 먹어도 괜찮아요?, all meaning 'May I eat a lot?'
notes.nuance: All three words (되다, 좋다, 괜찮다) carry the identical core meaning of 'it is okay if/there is no problem if' in this specific construction - the choice between them is purely stylistic, with no difference in permission strength or formality implied by which one is picked.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 예정이다 ('dijadwalkan untuk V')
meaning: 'To be scheduled to' - describing the noun 예정 ('schedule') with a future-tense verb clause, then predicating with 이다.

notes.formation: Describe 예정 with the future ~ㄹ/을 attributive, then add 이다 to complete the sentence (since a bare noun can't end a sentence): 하다 -> 할 예정 -> 할 예정이에요.
notes.usage: 우리는 10시에 만날 예정이에요 'We are scheduled to meet at 10:00'; 수업이 4시쯤에 시작될 예정이에요 'The class is scheduled to start at about 4:00pm'; 비행기가 9시에 출발할 예정이지만 눈이 많이 와서 못 출발할 것 같아요 'The plane is scheduled to depart at 9:00, but it probably won't because it is snowing a lot'.
notes.nuance: This is a direct extension of the ~는 것 principle (Lesson 26) already known - just as 것 can be replaced by any noun (제가 먹는 음식 'the food I eat'), here 예정 fills that slot, and since a schedule is inherently about the FUTURE, only the ~ㄹ/을 attributive is used, never ~는 or ~ㄴ/은.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 계획이 있다 ('punya rencana untuk V')
meaning: 'To have plans to' - describing the noun 계획 ('plan') with a future clause, then completing with 있다 ('to have').

notes.formation: Describe 계획 with the future ~ㄹ/을 attributive, then add 있다 to say the plan is 'had': 가다 -> 갈 계획 -> 갈 계획이 있다.
notes.usage: 참치를 잡으러 그 섬에 갈 계획이 있어요 'I have plans to go to that island to catch tuna'; 우리 사업규모를 내년에 늘릴 계획이 있어요 'We have plans to increase the scale of our business next year'; 제가 친구를 만날 계획이 있었지만 친구는 안 왔어요 'I had plans to meet my friend, but he didn't come'; 원래 대학교에 갈 계획이 있었지만 수능을 잘 못 봐서 대학교에 갈 수 없었어요 'I had plans to go to university, but I couldn't get in because I did poorly on the SAT test'.
notes.nuance: Just like English says 'I HAVE plans to...', Korean completes this construction with 있다 ('to have') rather than 이다 - a small but important structural difference from the 예정이다 pattern just covered, even though both describe a future-oriented noun with the ~ㄹ/을 attributive.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 준비가 되다 ('siap untuk V')
meaning: 'To be ready to' - describing 준비 ('preparation') with a future clause, then using 되다 ('going well') in the past tense to indicate the preparation has been completed.

notes.formation: Describe 준비 with the future ~ㄹ/을 attributive, mark it with ~가, then attach 되다 conjugated to the PAST tense (되다's 'going well' meaning from the previous lesson): 가다 -> 갈 준비 -> 갈 준비가 됐다, literally 'the preparation of going went well'.
notes.usage: 저는 지금 갈 준비가 됐어요 'I am ready to go now'; 저는 아무 때나 일을 시작할 준비가 됐어요 'I am ready to start working any time'; 우리는 소규모 장소에서 시작할 준비가 됐어요 'We are ready to start in a small location'. Negated to say NOT ready: 저는 아직 결혼할 준비가 되지 않았어요 'I'm still not ready to get married'. As a question: 파티에 갈 준비가 됐어요? 'Are you ready to go to the party?'
notes.nuance: In casual speech, 준비가 되다 is sometimes written/spoken as the fused passive verb 준비되다 (갈 준비됐다), technically considered incorrect since ~ㄹ/을 should describe a noun, not merge into a verb - but because ~가 is frequently dropped in speech, these two forms become indistinguishable by ear, so 준비되다 is commonly seen in practice despite the theoretical objection.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 준비를 하세요 (perintah: 'bersiaplah untuk V') + perbedaan ~를 vs ~가
meaning: Using an imperative ending on 준비하다 to tell someone to get ready to do something, illustrating why active 하다 takes ~를/을 while passive 되다 takes ~이/가.

notes.formation: Describe 준비 with the future ~ㄹ/을 attributive as before, but here attach the OBJECT particle ~를 (since 하다 is an active verb that CAN act on an object), then use 하다 with any imperative ending: 갈 준비 -> 갈 준비를 하세요.
notes.usage: 갈 준비를 하세요 'Get ready to go'; 먹을 준비를 하세요 'Get ready to eat'; 몸을 굽힐 준비를 하세요 'Get ready to bend your body'; 수능을 볼 준비를 하세요 'Get ready to write the 수능 test'; 증상이 계속 나타나면 병원에 올 준비를 하세요 'Get ready to come to the hospital if symptoms persist'. For a simple, direct 'get ready/prepare', 준비하세요 can be used with a plain object noun (not a verb clause): 밥을 준비하세요! 'Get the food ready!'; 모든 것을 준비하세요! 'Get everything ready!'
notes.nuance: The particle choice here (~를 with 하다 vs ~가 with 되다, seen in the previous pattern) isn't arbitrary - it follows directly from whether the predicating verb is active or passive (Lesson 14): 하다 is active and can take an object with ~를/을 (밥을 준비했어요 'I prepared rice'), while 되다 is passive and cannot act on an object, requiring ~이/가 instead (밥이 준비되었어요 'The rice was prepared'). As with 준비가 되다, the fused-looking 갈 준비하세요 (dropping ~를) is commonly heard in speech even though it's technically the same kind of theoretical inconsistency noted for 준비되다.

pattern: V/Adj~기도 하다 ('juga/pun', menambahkan ~도 ke klausa lewat ~기)
meaning: 'Also/too' applied to an entire verb/adjective clause, by first nominalizing it with ~기 (Lesson 29), then attaching ~도, then predicating with 하다.

notes.formation: Turn the clause into a noun with ~기 (그녀가 예쁘다 -> 그녀가 예쁘기), attach ~도 (그녀가 예쁘기도), then add 하다 as the predicating verb to complete the sentence: 그녀가 예쁘기도 해요 'She is pretty too'.
notes.usage: Only the noun ~도 is attached to carries the 'also/too' meaning - here that's the ENTIRE clause (turned into a noun via ~기), not just one word within it. Compare: 그녀도 예뻐요 'SHE too is pretty' (other people are pretty, and she is too) vs 그녀가 예쁘기도 해요 'She is pretty TOO' (she may have other qualities, but prettiness is also one of them). Similarly: 나도 밥을 먹었어 'I TOO ate rice' (others ate, I did too) vs 내가 밥을 먹기도 했어 'I ate rice TOO' (I did other things, and eating rice was also one of them).
notes.nuance: These sentences almost always need context/a preceding statement to feel natural, since 'she is pretty too' sounds odd walking into a room out of nowhere - it needs a prior comment about her other qualities to make sense: Person 1: 그녀가 매우 똑똑하고 친절해요 'She is very smart and kind' -> Person 2: 네, 그녀가 예쁘기도 해요 'Yeah, she is pretty too'.

pattern: ~기도 하고 ~기도 하다 ('baik...maupun...' / 'kadang...kadang...')
meaning: Attaching ~기도 하다 twice in one sentence (connected by ~고) to stress that two actions/descriptions both happen, OR to say something happens 'sometimes X, sometimes Y'.

notes.formation: Attach ~기도 하다 to both of two clauses, connecting them with ~고: 그녀가 예쁘다 + 똑똑하다 -> 그녀가 예쁘기도 하고 똑똑하기도 해요. This is a more emphatic version of the simpler 그녀가 예쁘고 똑똑해요 'She is pretty and smart'. The first 하다 (not the word right before ~기) can optionally be conjugated to match the tense of the final 하다, with no meaning difference according to native speakers: 양파를 썰기도 하고 물을 끓이기도 했어요 = 양파를 썰기도 했고 물을 끓이기도 했어요.
notes.usage: 제가 치약을 사기도 하고 칫솔을 사기도 했어요 'I bought toothpaste and a toothbrush too' (emphasizing BOTH purchases happened, useful e.g. if someone assumed you only bought one); 아르키메데스는 철학을 가르치기도 하고 중요한 발명품을 발명하기도 했어요 'Archimedes taught philosophy and also invented important inventions too'. The same structure can instead mean 'sometimes X, sometimes Y' rather than 'both X and Y': 제가 피자를 먹을 때 콜라랑 먹기도 하고 물이랑 먹기도 해요 'When I eat pizza, sometimes I eat it with cola, and sometimes I eat it with water'; 저는 그 친구를 좋아하기도 하고 싫어하기도 해요 'I like that friend sometimes, and I hate him sometimes too'.
notes.nuance: The 'both happened together' meaning and the 'sometimes one, sometimes the other' meaning cannot be reliably distinguished by the grammar itself - only context tells you which is meant, exactly as with the ambiguous English sentence 'When we used to meet, we used to watch movies and have dinner too' (did both happen on the same date, or alternately?). Rather than treating these as two separate grammar points, it's best to consider them one flexible usage whose precise meaning depends entirely on context.

pattern: V~ㄴ/는다고 (mengutip kata kerja: 'mengatakan bahwa...')
meaning: Quoting a clause ending in a verb by conjugating it into the plain/diary form, then attaching ~고, before a verb like 말하다 ('to say').

notes.formation: Counter-intuitively for English speakers, quoting is NOT done with the ~는 것 principle - instead, the quoted clause is conjugated into its own plain/diary form (Lesson 5: 하다->한다, 가다->간다, 먹다->먹는다 present; 했다/갔다/먹었다 past; 하겠다/가겠다/먹겠다 future), then ~고 is attached directly: 한다고, 간다고, 먹는다고. The final predicating verb (usually 말하다) can be conjugated to any tense/level to show WHEN the quote was said, independent of the quoted clause's own tense.
notes.usage: 나는 그가 너를 좋아한다고 말했어 'I said that he likes you' (quoted clause present tense); 나는 그가 너를 좋아했다고 말했어 'I said that he liked you' (quoted clause past); 나는 그가 너를 좋아하겠다고 말했어 'I said that he will like you' (quoted clause future). The person being spoken TO is marked with ~에게/한테/께: 나는 엄마에게 그가 너를 좋아한다고 말할 거야 'I will tell mom that he likes you'. Since ~ㄴ/는다고 already signals a quote, 말하다 is very commonly shortened to just 하다: 그는 공부하지 않았다고 했어요 'He said that he didn't study'.
notes.nuance: The quoted clause's tense and the final verb's tense are completely independent of each other - each can be past, present, or future regardless of the other, since one describes WHAT was said and the other describes WHEN the saying happened: 선생님은 학생들이 늦게 도착했다고 말했다 'The teacher said (past) that the students arrived (past) late' vs 선생님은 학생들이 늦게 도착하겠다고 말했다 'The teacher said (past) that the students will arrive (future) late'.

pattern: Adj~다고 (mengutip kata sifat, termasuk 있다/없다/싶다)
meaning: Quoting a clause ending in an adjective, using the same principle as verbs but with the adjective's own plain-form rule (dictionary form = present-tense plain form).

notes.formation: Since an adjective's plain-form present tense IS its dictionary form (Lesson 5), simply add ~고 directly: 행복하다 -> 행복하다고 (never 행복한다고). Past and future follow the same rule as verbs: 행복했다고, 행복하겠다고.
notes.usage: 밧줄의 길이가 너무 부족하다고 했어요 'I said that the length of this rope is not enough'; 우리 아빠는 자기가 어렸을 때 너무 행복했다고 했어요 'My dad said that he was very happy when he was young'; 대부분 사람들이 이 영화의 주인공이 아주 잘생겼다고 말해요 'Most people say that the main character of this movie is very handsome'. Since 있다/없다 (Lesson 5), including 있다/없다 inside ~ㄹ/을 수 있다/없다, and 싶다 (Lesson 12) all conjugate as adjectives, they follow this same rule when quoted: 학생이 이해할 수 없다고 했어요 'The student said he can't understand'; 저는 여자 친구에게 같이 가고 싶은 데가 있다고 말했어요 'I told my girlfriend that there is a place that I want to go with her'; 나는 새로운 차를 사고 싶다고 했어 'I said that I want to buy a new car'.
notes.nuance: This is the same distinction already drilled elsewhere in the course between verb and adjective plain-form conjugation - the only new piece here is remembering to apply that existing rule correctly when quoting, since it's easy to mistakenly add ~는다 to an adjective by analogy with verbs.

pattern: N이다 + ~(이)라고 (mengutip kopula 이다, waktu sekarang & lampau)
meaning: Quoting a clause ending in 이다 - present tense uses the special ~(이)라고 form, past tense simply adds ~고 to the past-tense conjugation.

notes.formation: Past tense: simply add ~고 to 이다's past plain form: 선생님이었다 -> 선생님이었다고. Present tense: 라 replaces 다 (의사이다 -> 의사이라고, NEVER 의사이다고). When the preceding noun ends in a vowel, 이 can be omitted: 의사이라고 or 의사라고, both correct. When the noun ends in a consonant, 이 CANNOT be omitted: 학생이라고 is correct, but 학생라고 is not.
notes.usage: 그가 의사이라고/의사라고 했어요 'He said he is a doctor' (vowel-final noun, 이 optional); 우리 선생님은 제가 나쁜 학생이라고 했어요 'Our teacher said I am a bad student' (consonant-final noun, 이 required). Past: 그가 선생님이었다고 했어요 'He said he was a teacher'; 경찰관은 거리에 있었던 사람들이 시위자들이었다고 했어요 'The police officer said that the people who were on the street were protesters'.
notes.nuance: This same vowel/consonant-dependent 이-omission rule already applies broadly whenever anything is attached to 이다 (Lesson 12's ~고/~(으)면, and later ~거든/~잖아): after a vowel-final noun, 이 can blend into the following sound and be dropped without changing pronunciation (의사이고/의사고 sound nearly identical); after a consonant-final noun, dropping 이 would create an unpronounceable or drastically different sound (선생님이고 vs the impossible 선생님고), so 이 must stay. Quoting with ~(이)라고 is simply one more instance of this general principle already seen elsewhere.

pattern: Mengutip waktu depan (~ㄹ/을 것이라고 / 거이라고 / 거라고)
meaning: Quoting a future-tense clause by applying the 이다-quoting rules to the 이다 hidden inside ~ㄹ/을 것이다.

notes.formation: Since the future tense ~ㄹ/을 것이다 is literally the noun 것 (often shortened to 거) + 이다, quoting it means applying the ~(이)라고 rule to that hidden 이다: 나는 밥을 먹을 것이다 -> 나는 밥을 먹을 것이라고 했어 / 나는 밥을 먹을 거이라고 했어 / 나는 밥을 먹을 거라고 했다 - all three are equally correct.
notes.usage: 저는 밖에 갈 수 없을 거라고 했어요 'I said I can't go outside/won't be able to go outside'; 저는 우리 가족에게 이 사람이 저의 여자 친구라고 했어요 'I told my family that this person is my girlfriend' (present-tense 이다 example for contrast); 제가 제일 좋아하는 여자를 가리킬 거라고 했어요 'I said that I will point to the girl that I like the most'.
notes.nuance: This directly confirms, once more, that ~ㄹ/을 것이다 is fundamentally built on 것/거 (a noun) + 이다 - because quoting always targets whatever word is functioning as 이다 in a sentence, and here that's the 이다 attached to 것/거, the exact same vowel/consonant-dependent 이-omission rules from the previous pattern apply, just with 것/거 (always vowel-final) as the noun in question, which is why 이 is always optional here (것이라고/거이라고 vs 거라고).

pattern: N을/를 N(이)라고 부르다 ('menyebut N sebagai N') + memperkenalkan diri dengan ~(이)라고 합니다
meaning: 'To call something X', using ~을/를 for the object being named and ~(이)라고 for the name it's called - also the natural, idiomatic way to introduce your own name.

notes.formation: [object]을/를 [name](이)라고 부르다.
notes.usage: 사람들은 그 건물을 한국타워라고 불러요 'People call that building "Korea Tower"'; 밥을 많이 먹을 수 있는 사람들을 식신이라고 불러요 'People who can eat a lot are called "식신"'. This same ~(이)라고 structure, paired with 하다 instead of 부르다, is the more natural way to introduce your own name than a direct '제 이름은 ___입니다' translation: 안녕하세요, 저는 캐나다에서 온 김의지라고 합니다 'Hi, my name is 김의지, and I come from Canada'; 안녕하세요, 저는 강남고등학교 2학년 3반 김의지라고 합니다 'Hi, my name is 김의지, and I am in class 3, in the second grade of 강남 high school'.
notes.nuance: Introducing yourself with ~(이)라고 합니다 (rather than the literal '내 이름은...') is considered the more natural, idiomatic Korean way to state your name, especially when adding a bit of self-description (like where you're from or your school/class) before the name itself.

pattern: 약속하다 dengan klausa kutipan waktu depan ('berjanji akan...')
meaning: 'To promise' - typically paired with a future-tense quoted clause describing the action being promised.

notes.formation: Quote the future-tense action (using ~겠다고 or ~ㄹ/을 거라고), then attach 약속하다.
notes.usage: 현금을 내일 주겠다고 약속했다 'I promised to give you (the) cash tomorrow'; 지금부터 열심히 하겠다고 약속했다 'I promised to work hard from now on'; 제가 아빠에게 숙제를 다 할 거라고 약속했어요 'I promised dad that I would do all my homework'; 이 정보를 내일까지 다 입력해 줄 거라고 약속했어요 'I promised that I would input all of this information by tomorrow'.
notes.nuance: Since a promise is inherently about a future action, the quoted clause here is virtually always in the future tense - this is a natural, practical application of the future-tense quoting rules already covered (~겠다고, ~ㄹ/을 거라고).

pattern: 그렇다 sebagai kata akhir kutipan (그랬어, alternatif dari 말했어/했어)
meaning: Ending a quoted sentence with 그렇다 (conjugated) instead of 말하다 or 하다, with no detectable difference in meaning.

notes.formation: After the quoted clause, use a conjugated form of 그렇다 (already known, Lesson 23) instead of 말하다/하다: 오빠가 이거를 안 한다고 그랬어.
notes.usage: 오빠가 이거를 안 한다고 말했어 = 오빠가 이거를 안 한다고 했어 = 오빠가 이거를 안 한다고 그랬어, all meaning 'My older brother said he wasn't going to do this'.
notes.nuance: All three final-verb choices (말하다, 하다, 그렇다) are heard often in speech with no detectable difference in meaning or nuance - this is simply another available option, alongside the already-known shortening of 말하다 to 하다.

pattern: 뭐라고(요)? ('apa katamu?') dan mengulang kutipan untuk klarifikasi
meaning: Attaching ~(이)라고 to 뭐 to ask what someone said, and repeating part of what was heard as a quoted clause (usually as a question) to ask for clarification.

notes.formation: 뭐 + ~(이)라고 = 뭐라고?/뭐라고요? (more formal). 하다/말하다 can optionally be added: 뭐라고 했어요?/뭐라고 말했어요?. To ask for clarification about part of what someone else just said, quote it back (without needing to attach a final 말하다/하다), usually ending in a question: [their quoted clause]~다고/~냐고 등 + ~(요)?.
notes.usage: 아빠가 뭐라고 말했어요? 'What did dad say?'. For clarification: Person 1: 밥을 먹기 싫어 'I don't want to eat' -> Person 2: 밥을 먹기 싫다고? '(You said that) you don't want to eat?'; Person 1: 저는 내일 캐나다에 갈 거예요 'I'm going to Canada tomorrow' -> Person 2: 내일 캐나다에 갈 거라고요? '(You said that) you're going to Canada tomorrow?'. You don't need to repeat the whole sentence - just the unclear part: Person 1: 저의 몸이 몹시 피곤해요 'My body is really tired' -> Person 2: 피곤하다고요? '(You said) tired?'
notes.nuance: If the first person's original statement is misheard/misunderstood, they can respond by simply stressing the correct quoted word: Person 1: 그는 돈이 없다고 했어요 'He said that he doesn't have money' -> Person 2: 돈이 있다고? '(Did you say) he has money?' -> Person 1: 아니요, 없다고요 'No, (I said that) he doesn't have money' - here the correction is delivered purely through the quoting mechanism, with no need for a full restated sentence.

examples.meaning: What did you say? (formal)
What did the doctor say?
No, (I said that) he doesn't have (money).

pattern: ~ㄴ/는다는 것 (singkatan dari ~ㄴ/는다고 하는 것, kutipan sebagai kata benda dengan 사실/소문)
meaning: A shortened form of '(quoted clause) + 고 하는 것', turning a quoted statement into a noun phrase - often paired with 사실 ('fact') or 소문 ('rumor') instead of 것.

notes.formation: 간다는 것 is short for 간다고 하는 것; 갔다는 것 for 갔다고 하는 것; 가겠다는 것 for 가겠다고 하는 것. The verb before ~는 것 is conjugated to the plain form as in regular quoting. For adjectives, the plain present form (= dictionary form) is used directly: 예쁘다는 것. For the future tense, the quoting rule for 이다 (hidden inside 것/거+이다) applies: 먹을 것이라는 것/먹을 거라는 것.
notes.usage: 그가 나를 싫어한다는 것을 알아 'I know that (it is said that) he doesn't like me' (compare to the plain, non-quoted 그가 나를 싫어하는 것을 알아, which has essentially the same practical meaning/translation but doesn't specifically flag that this was SAID by someone). 것 is very commonly replaced by 사실 ('fact') or 소문 ('rumor') in these constructions, since those nouns already inherently imply something was said: 그 여자가 다른 남자랑 애기가 있다는 소문이 있습니다 'There is a rumor that that woman has a baby with another man'; 그녀가 시험에 떨어졌다는 소문을 들었어요 'I heard a rumor that she failed the test'; 그녀는 아이가 죽었다는 사실을 숨겼어요 'She hid the fact that her child died'; 그녀가 곧 결혼할 거라는 사실을 잊어버렸어요 'I forgot the fact that she will be getting married soon'; 너의 여자 친구가 예쁘다는 것을 잊어버렸어 'I forgot the fact that your girlfriend was pretty' (adjective example).
notes.nuance: The exact source of the quoted statement (who said it) is often left ambiguous and simply understood from context - the sentence 그가 나를 싫어한다는 것을 알아 could theoretically mean 'I know he said he doesn't like me' or 'I know someone said he doesn't like me', but in practice it's usually just translated the same as the non-quoted version, since English doesn't always need to mark this distinction explicitly.

pattern: V~자고 (mengutip ajakan 'ayo...')
meaning: Quoting a suggestion sentence ('let's...', Lesson 44) by attaching ~고 to ~자.

notes.formation: Attach ~고 directly to the already-known ~자 suggestion ending: 먹자 -> 먹자고; 가자 -> 가자고.
notes.usage: 아빠가 밥을 먹자고 했어 'Dad said "Let's eat"'; 선생님이 수업 시간 동안 열심히 공부하자고 했어요 'The teacher said "let's study hard during class time"'; 우리 아들은 나한테 자꾸 부산에 가자고 졸랐어 'My son kept pestering me and said "let's go to Busan"'; 여자친구가 산책하자고 했지만 저는 너무 피곤해서 안 갔어요 'My girlfriend said "let's go for a walk," but I was too tired, so I didn't go'.
notes.nuance: This follows exactly the same overall quoting pattern as verbs/adjectives/이다 (attach ~고 after the relevant conjugation) - here the 'conjugation' being quoted is simply the ~자 suggestion form itself, with no extra irregularity to worry about.

pattern: V~(느)냐고 (mengutip pertanyaan dengan kata kerja)
meaning: Quoting a question ending in a verb - officially ~느냐고, though ~냐고 (without 느) is far more common in everyday speech.

notes.formation: Attach ~느냐고 to a verb stem (or its past ~았/었 or future ~겠 form): 좋아하다 -> 좋아하느냐고; 갔다 -> 갔느냐고; 가겠다 -> 가겠느냐고. In practice, ~냐고 (dropping 느) is heard and even accepted as correct by Korean teachers, despite being technically non-standard.
notes.usage: 그가 무엇을 좋아하느냐고 물어봤어요 'I asked him what he likes'; 우리 아빠는 나에게 어디 가느냐고 물어봤어 'My dad asked me where I am going'; 나는 여자 친구에게 뭐 먹었느냐고 물어봤어 'I asked my girlfriend what she ate'. 물어보다/묻다 ('to ask') can itself be conjugated to any tense to show when the asking happens: 나는 여자 친구에게 뭐 먹었느냐고 물어보고 있어 'I am asking my girlfriend what she ate'.
notes.nuance: 있다/없다 are a special irregular here: regardless of whether they're being used as adjectives (to have) or verbs (~고 있다/~아/어 있다), they ALWAYS take the verb-style ~느냐고 (or its common shortening ~냐고) when quoting a question - Korean grammar teachers themselves describe this simply as 'an irregular' with no deeper explanation: 저는 그에게 수영할 수 있느냐고 물어봤어요 'I asked him if he could swim'; 동생에게 환경을 왜 파괴하고 있느냐고 물어봤어요 'I asked my brother why he is destroying the environment'.

pattern: Adj~(으)냐고 (mengutip pertanyaan dengan kata sifat, termasuk 싶다)
meaning: Quoting a question ending in an adjective, using ~으냐고 (consonant-final, except ㄹ) or ~냐고 (vowel-final or ㄹ-final).

notes.formation: ~으냐고 attaches to a consonant-final adjective stem (except ㄹ); ~냐고 attaches to a vowel-final stem or one ending in ㄹ: 예쁘다 -> 예쁘냐고 (vowel-final); 편안하다 -> 편안하냐고; 춥다(irregular) -> 추우냐고 (vowel after irregular change); 많다 -> 많으냐고 (consonant-final). 싶다 (Lesson 12/17) is an adjective too, so it follows this same rule: 먹고 싶다 -> 먹고 싶으냐고.
notes.usage: 저는 친구에게 그 여자가 예쁘냐고 물어봤어요 'I asked my friend if that girl was pretty'; 이런 반팔이 집에 많으냐고 물어봤어 'I asked if there were many of these types of t-shirts at home'; 그는 뭐 먹고 싶으냐고 물어봤어 'He asked what do you want to eat'.
notes.nuance: As with verbs, the officially-correct ~으냐고 (after a consonant-final stem) is often heard shortened to just ~냐고 in casual speech (많으냐고 -> 많냐고) - most Korean speakers can't reliably say which is 'more correct' and would consider both acceptable.

pattern: N이다 + ~(이)냐고 (mengutip pertanyaan dengan 이다, termasuk waktu depan dan kata tanya)
meaning: Quoting a question ending in 이다 - since 이다's stem always ends in the vowel 이, only ~냐고 is used (never ~으냐고), with the same optional 이-omission rule as elsewhere.

notes.formation: 의사이다 -> 의사이냐고 (or, with 이 omitted since 의사 ends in a vowel, 의사냐고). If the noun ends in a consonant, 이 must stay: 선생님이냐고 (never 선생님냐고). This same ~(이)냐고 attaches naturally to question words already paired with 이다 (누구, 뭐, 어디, 언제): 언제(이)냐고, 어디(이)냐고, 뭐(이)냐고, 누구(이)냐고. For the future tense (~ㄹ/을 것이다), the same 이다-quoting rule applies to the 이다 hidden in 것/거: 갈 거냐고 물어봤어 'I asked if he is going to go'.
notes.usage: 나는 그 사람이 의사냐고 물어봤어 'I asked if that person is a doctor'; 이 신사가 누구냐고 물어봤습니다 'I asked who this gentleman is'; 저는 제 친구에게 한국으로 이사하고 싶은 이유가 뭐냐고 물어봤어요 'I asked my friend "what is the reason you want to move to Korea?"'; 나는 그들에게 결혼식에 갈 거냐고 물어봤어 'I asked if they were going to go to the wedding'; 그는 저한테 여자친구랑 언제 결혼할 거냐고 물어봤어요 'He asked me when I will marry my girlfriend'.
notes.nuance: This confirms once more that questions with 이다 follow the same general 이-omission logic seen throughout this and the previous lesson - the only real novelty here is that ~(으)냐고's consonant/vowel split collapses to just ~냐고 for 이다, since its stem 이 is always a vowel, so there's never a need for the ~으 form with this particular word.

quiz.question: Kenapa 이다 tidak pernah memakai bentuk ~으냐고 (hanya ~(이)냐고)?

pattern: Kutipan langsung dengan ~라고 (mengutip kalimat persis sesuai aslinya)
meaning: A direct quote - conjugating the quoted sentence exactly as it was originally said (rather than converting to plain form), then attaching ~라고.

notes.formation: Unlike an indirect quote (which converts everything to plain form), a direct quote keeps the ORIGINAL conjugation of the quoted sentence exactly as spoken, then attaches ~라고 (usually ~라고 rather than ~이라고, since most complete sentences end in a vowel) - the whole quoted sentence functions like a noun being described by ~라고.
notes.usage: Indirect: 그는 하고 싶지 않다고 했다 'He said he doesn't want to do it' (plain form 하고 싶지 않다). Direct: 그는 "제가 하고 싶지 않습니다"라고 했어요 'He said "I don't want to do it"' (keeps the original formal 습니다 exactly as spoken). Another pair - Indirect: 그는 너를 사랑한다고 했어 'He said I love you' (plain form 사랑한다). Direct: 그는 "너를 사랑해"라고 했어 'He said "I love you"' (keeps the original informal 사랑해 exactly as spoken). Quotation marks are needed in writing but not necessary in speech.
notes.nuance: It helps to think of the entire directly-quoted sentence as functioning like a noun, which is why ~라고/이라고 (the same addition used for 이다) attaches to it - the quote itself is being 'named' or 'labeled' by ~라고, exactly as any other noun would be, rather than being grammatically transformed the way an indirect quote's clause is.

pattern: V~(으)라고 (mengutip perintah: 'menyuruh untuk...')
meaning: Quoting a command sentence - none of the regular imperative endings (~아/어, ~아/어라, ~(으)세요, ~(으)십시오) are used; instead, a special quoting-only ending ~(으)라고 attaches directly to the verb stem.

notes.formation: ~으라고 attaches to a consonant-final verb stem (except ㄹ); ~라고 attaches to a vowel-final stem or one ending in ㄹ. Note this uses the ~(으) vowel/consonant split, NOT the ~아/어 split - this can produce a genuinely different result than ~아/어라 for many irregular verbs: 먹다 -> 먹으라고 (not 먹어라고); 짓다(ㅅ irregular) -> 지으라고 (not 지어라고); 잠그다(ㅡ) -> 잠그라고 (not 잠가라고); 자르다(르) -> 자르라고 (not 잘라고); 만들다(ㄹ) -> 만들라고 (not 만들어라고). For 가다 and a few others, the two endings happen to coincide (가다 -> 가라either way).
notes.usage: 우리 아빠는 저에게 밥을 빨리 먹으라고 했어요 'My dad told me to eat fast'; 선생님은 학생들에게 열심히 공부하라고 했어요 'The teacher told the students to study hard'; 버스 아저씨가 나한테 올라타라고 했어요 'The bus driver told me to get on (the bus)'; 애기가 배가 고파서 남편에게 밥을 먹이라고 했어요 'I told my husband to feed the baby because he was hungry'.
notes.nuance: This is a genuinely distinct ending from anything covered so far - unlike direct commands (Lesson 40), which have several formality-graded endings, there is only ONE way to quote a command, and it is built on the ~(으) pattern rather than ~아/어, which is why memorizing the irregular verb table (rather than assuming it matches ~아/어라) matters here.

pattern: N을/를 달라고 하다 (mengutip 'berikan saya N': 주다 -> 달다)
meaning: When quoting someone asking for an object to be given to THEMSELVES, 주다 is replaced by the special word 달다 - not the regular ~(으)라고 attached to 주다.

notes.formation: 달다 exists specifically as a substitute for 주다 in quoted imperative sentences where the ORIGINAL speaker asked for something for themselves - it isn't really a word worth memorizing outside this context. Attach ~라고 to 달다's stem: 달라고.
notes.usage: 밥(을) 주세요 'Give me rice' (original request) -> 밥(을) 달라고 했어요 'I said "give me rice"' (quoting it). The final speaker of the quote doesn't need to be the same person as the original requester: Person 1: 밥(을) 주세요 -> Person 3 (quoting Person 1 to someone else): 밥(을) 달라고 했어요 'He said "give me rice"'. More examples: 휴지를 달라고 했어요 'I said "please give me a tissue"'; 엄마가 숟가락과 칼을 달라고 했어 'Mom said "please give me a spoon and a knife"'; 우리 아들은 계속 용돈을 달라고 졸라요 'Our son keeps pestering for pocket money'.
notes.nuance: Contrast this with quoting 주다 using regular ~(으)라고 (Lesson 54), which is reserved for when the acting agent in the quote is being told to give something to ANOTHER (third) person: 성경에게 학생에게 펜을 주라고 했어요 'I told 성경 to give the pen to the student'. So the choice between 주라고 and 달라고 depends entirely on WHO ends up receiving the object - a third party (주라고) or the original speaker themselves (달라고).

pattern: V~아/어 달라고 하다 (mengutip 'tolong lakukan X untuk saya')
meaning: When quoting someone asking for an ACTION to be done for themselves, 달다 replaces 주다 within the already-known ~아/어 주다 construction.

notes.formation: [verb stem]~아/어 + 달라고 (replacing 주다 with 달다 inside the ~아/어 주다 construction, Lesson 41), then a predicating verb like 하다.
notes.usage: 저의 머리카락을 꼬지 말아 달라고 했어요 'I told her to please stop twisting my hair'; 학생은 선생님에게 성적을 올려 달라고 했어요 'The student said to the teacher "raise my grades"'; 비타민이 풍부하게 들어가 있는 과일만 사 달라고 했어요 'I requested to only buy fruit that is rich in vitamins'; 그들에게 조용히 해 달라고 했지만 그들은 아직 너무 시끄러워요 'I told them to "please be quiet," but they are still very loud'.

pattern: 부탁 (kebaikan/permintaan) dan 부탁하다 (meminta kebaikan)
meaning: 부탁 as a noun meaning 'favor/request', and 부탁하다 as the verb 'to ask for a favor'.

notes.formation: 부탁 functions as an ordinary noun; attaching ~하다 creates the verb 부탁하다. When the favor concerns a task/piece of work (a noun), 부탁하다 follows that noun directly, meaning to ask the listener to 'take care of' it.
notes.usage: 저는 부탁이 하나 있어요 'I have one favor/request'; 저는 더 자세한 설명을 부탁했어요 'I asked for a clearer explanation'; 남편에게 청소를 부탁했어요 'I asked my husband to take care of the cleaning (for me)'; 빨래를 아들에게 부탁하고 집에서 나왔어요 'I asked my son to take care of the laundry for me and left the house'.
notes.nuance: These sentences are often hard to translate word-for-word into natural English/Indonesian - the underlying meaning ('I handed off this task by asking you to handle it') is what matters, more than trying to force a literal one-to-one translation for every example.

pattern: V~아/어 달라고 부탁하다 / 부탁 드리다 ('meminta dengan sopan untuk...')
meaning: Combining the quoted-request ~아/어 달라고 with 부탁하다 (or its honorific form 부탁 드리다), for an action-based favor request.

notes.formation: When the favor being requested is an action rather than a plain noun, attach ~아/어 달라고 to the verb, then 부탁하다: 밥을 빨리 만들어 달라고 부탁했어요 'I asked him to make (the rice) quickly'. 부탁하다 is very commonly phrased as 부탁(을) 드리다 instead - 드리다 (Lesson 39) is normally the honorific form of 주다, reserved for when the RECEIVING person deserves high respect; here, the request itself is thought of as being 'given' to that person, which is why 드리다 fits even though the favor benefits the speaker, not the listener.
notes.usage: 밥을 빨리 만들어 달라고 부탁했어요 = 밥을 빨리 만들어 달라고 부탁 드렸어요, both meaning 'I asked him to make (the rice) quickly', with the 드리다 version simply being more formal/respectful toward the listener; 엄마에게 그것을 사 달라고 부탁 드렸어요 'I asked my mother to buy that for me' (using the honorific form when speaking respectfully about the request made to mom).
notes.nuance: This is a subtle but important exception to the general rule that 드리다 replaces 주다 only when the RECEIVER deserves respect (since here, technically, the speaker is the one whose favor is granted) - the resolution is to think of the REQUEST itself (부탁) as the thing being 'given' to the respected listener, which is a natural extension of 드리다's honorific meaning rather than a true exception to it.

pattern: V~게 하다 ('membuat/membiarkan seseorang melakukan V')
meaning: 'To make' or 'to let' someone do an action - Korean uses a single construction for both English meanings, since it doesn't distinguish 'forcing' from 'allowing'.

notes.formation: Attach ~게 to a verb stem, then 하다: 공부하다 -> 공부하게 하다. The subject 'makes/lets' the object do the action.
notes.usage: 나는 그를 공부하게 했다 can be translated either 'I made him study' or 'I let him study' - Korean doesn't distinguish between forcing and allowing; both meanings collapse into 'I did something that caused/influenced him to study'. 저는 그를 자게 할 거예요 'I will let him sleep'; 저는 학생들을 바로 준비하게 했어요 'I made the students get ready right away'. Assuming the action benefits the influenced person, ~아/어 주다 (Lesson 41) can be added on top: 제가 축제에 가게 해 주세요 'Please let me go to the festival'; 저는 학생들을 공부하게 해 주었어요 'I let the students study'.
notes.nuance: This is the same phenomenon already seen with ~아/어야 하다 translating to both 'must' and 'should' (Lesson 46): a single Korean construction sometimes maps onto multiple distinct English words, not because Korean is ambiguous, but because English draws a finer distinction than Korean grammar does - here, 'the subject causes/influences the action to occur' is the single underlying Korean meaning, regardless of whether that influence felt like force or permission.

pattern: Adj~게 하다 ('membuat seseorang menjadi Adj', misalnya 놀라게 하다 'mengejutkan')
meaning: Attaching ~게 하다 to an adjective, to say the subject causes/influences the object to BE that adjective.

notes.formation: Attach ~게 to an adjective stem, then 하다: 행복하다 -> 행복하게 하다. 놀라다 ('to be surprised') with ~게 하다 gives the natural meaning 'to surprise someone'.
notes.usage: 저는 저의 여자 친구를 행복하게 했어요 (or, with ~아/어 주다 added, 행복하게 해 주었어요) 'I made my girlfriend happy'; 제가 한국말을 할 수 있어서 저는 한국 사람들을 항상 놀라게 해요 'Because I can speak Korean, I always surprise Korean people'; 엄마가 저에게 선물을 줘서 저를 놀라게 했어요 'Because my mother gave me a present, she surprised me'. More: 저는 우리 엄마를 슬프게 했어요 'I made our mom sad'; 애기를 무섭게 하지 마세요! 'Don't make the baby scared (don't scare the baby)'; 저의 남자 친구가 저의 기분을 상하게 했어요 'My boyfriend made me feel bad'.
notes.nuance: This directly parallels the verb pattern from earlier: just as ~게 하다 with a verb means 'to make/let someone DO something', ~게 하다 with an adjective means 'to make someone BE (a certain way)' - the underlying logic (the subject influences the resulting state/action) stays the same regardless of whether a verb or adjective is being used.

pattern: N이/가 ~게 하다 + N을/를 (memengaruhi seseorang bertindak pada objek lain)
meaning: When the influenced person also acts on a further object, that person is marked with ~이/가, and the object they're acting on is marked with ~을/를.

notes.formation: [influenced person] + ~이/가 + [object they act on] + ~을/를 + [verb]~게 하다.
notes.usage: 나는 그를 공부하게 했다 'I made him study' (no further object) vs 나는 그가 한국어를 공부하게 했다 'I made him study Korean' (그 now marked ~이/가, since 한국어 is the object of his studying). 나는 학생들이 내 말을 듣게 했어 'I made the students listen to me'; 저는 남편이 결�론반지를 끼게 했어요 'I made my husband wear our wedding ring'; 저는 학생이 더 좋은 부전공을 선택하게 했어요 'I made the student select a better minor'; 저는 엄마가 저를 위해 도시락을 싸게 했어요 'I made my mom pack a lunch box for me'.
notes.nuance: This particle shift is simply a consequence of adding a second, deeper layer of action - the influenced person switches from being the sentence's direct object (~을/를, when they alone are the one 'made to do' something) to being the SUBJECT of their own embedded action (~이/가, when that action itself has an object), while the overall sentence's main subject/influencer stays the same throughout.

pattern: ~게 ('supaya/agar', tanpa 하다, diikuti klausa penyebab spesifik)
meaning: 'So that/in order to/to allow for' - placing a specific clause after ~게 instead of the generic 하다, to spell out exactly what causes the earlier action/state.

notes.formation: Attach ~게 to a verb/adjective stem as before, but instead of following it with 하다 (which leaves the 'cause' unspecified), follow it with a full clause that specifies what was done: [goal clause]~게 [specific action causing it].
notes.usage: 선생님은 제가 칠판을 보게 했어요 'The teacher did something (unspecified) that made me look at the board' vs 선생님은 제가 칠판을 보게 불을 켰어요 'The teacher turned on the light so that I could see the board' (now 불을 켰어요 replaces the generic 했어요, specifying the cause). 제가 잘 들을 수 있게 크게 말해 주세요 'Please speak loudly so that I can hear you well'; 애기가 깨지 않게 조용히 노크해 주세요 'Knock quietly so that the baby doesn't wake up'; 햇빛이 안 들어오게 커튼을 내려 주세요 'Pull the curtains down so that the sunlight doesn't come in'; 저는 학생들이 다 이해할 수 있게 설명했어요 'I explained it so that all the students could understand it'.
notes.nuance: This is structurally the exact same principle as ~게 하다 - the earlier clause is still being caused/influenced by what follows ~게 - the only difference is that here the causing action is spelled out explicitly (with its own verb) rather than left generic with 하다. As confirmed by an official TOPIK exam question referenced in the lesson, this ~게 usage means the same thing as ~도록 (a related grammar point covered in a much later lesson).

pattern: N하다-verb -> N시키다 ('membuat seseorang melakukan N', alternatif dari ~게 하다)
meaning: Replacing ~하다 with ~시키다 on the noun-form of 하다-verbs/adjectives to create the same causative meaning as ~게 하다 - the subject makes/causes ANOTHER person to do the action.

notes.formation: Replace ~하다 with ~시키다 on the noun the 하다-word is built from: 공부하다 -> 공부시키다 'to make (one) study'; 이해하다 -> 이해시키다 'to make (one) understand'; 연습하다 -> 연습시키다 'to make (one) practice'; 목욕하다 -> 목욕시키다 'to make (one) bathe'.
notes.usage: 선생님은 학생들을 방과후 수업 시간 동안 공부시켰어요 'The teacher made the students study during the after school class'; 경찰관은 남자에게 음주운전이 왜 위험한지를 이해시켰어요 'The police officer made the man understand why drunk driving is dangerous'; 저는 다람쥐를 잡고 목욕시켰어요 'I got the squirrel and gave it a bath'.
notes.nuance: The key difference between the plain 하다 form and the 시키다 form is WHO performs the action: with 하다, the sentence's subject is the one doing the action (저는 한국어를 공부했어요 'I studied Korean' - I am the studier); with 시키다, the subject makes/orders someone ELSE to do the action (선생님은 학생들을 공부시켰어요 - the teacher isn't the one studying, the students are).

pattern: Kata di mana ~하다 vs ~시키다 nyaris tidak beda makna, tapi ~시키다 terasa lebih 'kuat/memaksa'
meaning: Some 하다 words already carry a translation close to what ~시키다 would add, making the two forms hard to distinguish in English/Indonesian - the main felt difference is that ~시키다 sounds stronger, almost forceful.

notes.formation: For certain words (감동하다, 소개하다, 진정하다, 훈련하다, 흥분하다, 화해하다, and others like 교육하다/자극하다), both the ~하다 and ~시키다 forms exist and often translate to nearly the same English word, even though grammatically one is the subject performing the action and the other is the subject causing another to perform/experience it.
notes.usage: 감동하다 'to be impressed' (or 감동받다) vs 감동시키다 'to impress (someone)': 나는 감동했어 'I was impressed' vs 저는 하루 종일 열심히 일해서 엄마를 감동시켰어요 'I impressed mom because I worked hard all day'. 소개하다 'to introduce' vs 소개시키다 'to introduce': both can appear in nearly identical sentences, e.g. 저는 저의 여자 친구를 저의 부장님께 소개시켰어요 'I introduced my girlfriend to my boss'. 훈련하다/훈련시키다 both roughly translate 'to train'; 화해하다 'to reconcile' (both parties reconciling) vs 화해시키다 'to make (two people) reconcile': 저는 우리 아버지와 우리 어머니를 화해시켰어요 'I made my mother and father reconcile'.
notes.nuance: For pairs like 교육하다/교육시키다 ('to educate') or 자극하다/자극시키다 ('to irritate'), the two forms can appear in essentially identical sentences with the same English translation - the only detectable difference (confirmed through discussion with native speakers) is that the ~시키다 version sounds stronger or more forceful, as if the subject is compelling the action rather than simply doing/causing it.

pattern: 시키다 sebagai kata kerja berdiri sendiri ('membuat/menyuruh melakukan tugas')
meaning: 시키다 acting as a standalone verb (not attached to a 하다-noun), ordering/making a person do a task - essentially the same meaning as ~게 하다.

notes.formation: [influenced person]에게 + [task noun]을/를 + 시키다. It's unnatural to turn the action into a noun with ~는 것 before 시키다 (저는 학생들이 교실을 청소하는 것을 시켰어요 sounds wrong); instead, simply use the noun form of the action directly (저는 학생들에게 교실 청소를 시켰어요), or combine 시키다 with the quoted-imperative ~(으)라고 (Lesson 54) or the ~게 construction (previous lesson) to specify a full action.
notes.usage: 저는 회사원들에게 일을 시켰어요 'I made/ordered the workers to do the job'; 저는 학생들에게 교실 청소를 시켰어요 'I made the students clean the classroom' (noun form directly). Combined with ~(으)라고: 저는 학생들에게 교실을 청소하라고 시켰어요 'I made the students clean the classroom'. Combined with ~게: 저는 학생들이 교실을 청소하게 시켰어요 'I made the students clean the classroom' (all three sentences here mean the same thing). More: 저는 남편에게 쌀을 사라고 심부름을 시켰어요 'I made my husband do an errand of buying rice'; 다람쥐를 우리에 넣으라고 시켰어요 'I made him put the squirrel in the cage'.
notes.nuance: This standalone verb usage of 시키다 carries essentially the same causative meaning already established for both ~시키다 (attached to a noun) and ~게 하다 (Lesson 57) - all three constructions ultimately express 'the subject makes/orders another person to do something', just built with slightly different grammatical machinery.

pattern: N(이)나 N ('N atau N', belum diputuskan)
meaning: 'Or' between two nouns, indicating it hasn't been decided which one will be acted on (as object) or which will act (as subject).

notes.formation: ~이나 attaches after a consonant-final noun, ~나 after a vowel-final noun, placed between the two options: [noun1](이)나 [noun2].
notes.usage: 저는 빵이나 밥을 먹고 싶어요 'I want to eat bread or rice' (undecided object); 딸이나 아들을 낳고 싶어요? 'Do you want to have a daughter or a son?'. Also works on the subject: 우리 엄마나 우리 아빠가 저를 차로 거기까지 데려다 줄 거예요 'Either mom or dad will take me there by car'; 저 선수나 이 선수가 오늘 새로운 기록을 세울 것 같아요 'Either that athlete or this athlete will probably set a new record today'.
notes.nuance: The core meaning is that a choice genuinely remains undecided between the two named options - this is distinct from the standalone/'last resort' usage and the negative-sentence usage covered in separate patterns in this lesson.

pattern: N(이)나 sendirian ('yah... N sajalah', pilihan terakhir) + 아무 거나/데나/때나
meaning: ~(이)나 attached to just one noun, with nothing needing to be decided against - implying the speaker would rather do something else, but is settling for this as the best remaining option.

notes.formation: ~(이)나 attached to a single noun, with no second option following.
notes.usage: 밥이나 먹을래? '(Well...) shall we just eat rice?' (settling for rice as a last resort, e.g. too late for pizza delivery); 저는 공부나 할 거예요 '(Well...) I'm going to study'; 산책이나 할래요? '(Well...) Shall we go for a walk?'; 그냥 줄거리나 설명해 주세요 '(Well...) Just explain the plot to me'. This same principle explains the fixed words already learned in Lesson 25: 아무 거나 'anything' (literally 'no specific thing, but ANY thing would do'), 아무 데나 'anywhere', 아무 때나 'anytime' - each is 아무 ('any/some') + a noun (거/데/때) + this same ~나.
notes.nuance: There's no simple, fixed English translation for this usage - the lesson uses '(Well...)' as an imperfect stand-in, but the real meaning to internalize is 'this option isn't ideal, but it's acceptable given the circumstances', a tone of mild resignation or settling.

pattern: ~(이)나 ditempel ke kata keterangan, dan dihilangkannya partikel berulang saat ada dua pilihan
meaning: ~(이)나 can attach to a particle-carrying adverb, but when two options are given, the particle is naturally dropped from the first option.

notes.formation: When only ONE option is given, ~(이)나 can attach directly to a particle already on a noun (making it an adverb): 중간지점에나 'well, at the halfway point'. When TWO options are given, it's more natural to drop the repeated particle from the first option and let it appear only on the second: 저는 캐나다에서나 미국에서 일하고 싶어요 (grammatical but awkward) vs 저는 캐나다나 미국에서 일하고 싶어요 (natural, preferred) 'I want to work in Canada or America'.
notes.usage: 저는 버스로나 택시로 갈 거예요 (technically correct) vs 저는 버스나 택시로 갈 거예요 (natural) 'I will go by bus or by taxi'. More: 농구를 체육관이나 밖에서 하고 싶어? 'Do you want to play basketball in the gymnasium or outside?'; 주위를 살피고 저쪽으로나 이쪽으로 가세요 'Look around and then go this way or that way'.
notes.nuance: Both versions (with or without the repeated particle on the first option) are grammatically acceptable, but native speakers strongly prefer omitting it - since the particle will appear on the second option anyway, repeating it on the first is felt as redundant, even though it's not technically wrong.

pattern: V/Adj~거나 V/Adj ('melakukan V atau V', tindakan belum diputuskan)
meaning: 'Or' between two verbs/adjectives - the focus shifts from WHICH NOUN to WHICH ACTION/DESCRIPTION hasn't been decided.

notes.formation: Attach ~거나 to a verb or adjective stem: 쓰다 -> 쓰거나; 어렵다 -> 어렵거나.
notes.usage: 여자 친구를 위해 편지를 쓰거나 선물을 사 줄 거예요 'I will write a letter, or buy a present for my girlfriend' - here it isn't already decided that some action will happen (unlike ~(이)나, where the action - eating - is assumed, and only the object is undecided); the choice is between two different ACTIONS. 신발끈을 묶거나 신발을 벗으세요 'Tie your shoes or take them off'; 오래된 차를 고치거나 새로운 차를 사야 돼요 'I need to fix my old car or buy a new one'. Works with adjectives too: 이 문제가 너무 어렵거나 도움이 필요하면 교무실로 오세요 'If this question is too difficult or you need help, come to the office'.
notes.nuance: The key contrast with ~(이)나: 저는 빵이나 밥을 먹고 싶어요 already assumes eating will happen, and only WHICH FOOD is undecided; 여자 친구를 위해 편지를 쓰거나 선물을 사 줄 거예요 doesn't assume either action is fixed - WHICH ACTION itself is what's undecided.

pattern: ~거나 ~거나 (dipakai dua kali: 'terlepas dari X atau Y') + ~거나 말거나
meaning: Attaching ~거나 to BOTH options in a sentence, shifting the focus from 'one or the other will happen' to discussing the choice itself, regardless of which occurs.

notes.formation: Attach ~거나 to both verbs/adjectives, then follow with a comment about the outcome regardless of which happens: [action1]거나 [action2]거나 + [what happens either way].
notes.usage: 비가 오거나 안 오거나 중요하지 않아요 'It's not important if it rains or not' - unlike using ~거나 once (which picks between one action or the other), using it twice means the speaker is discussing what happens/how they feel REGARDLESS of which option occurs. 나머지를 먹거나 버리거나 결정해야 돼요 'You need to decide if you're going to eat the rest or throw it out'; 생선이나 고기나 모두 좋아할 거예요 'It doesn't matter if it is fish or meat, everybody will like it' (this same double-particle pattern also works with ~(이)나 on nouns). When one of the two options is simply NOT doing the action, 말다 (Lesson 40) commonly replaces the second 거나 clause: 대학교에 가거나 말거나 공부를 해야 돼요 'You need to study whether you go to university or not'; 네가 나를 사랑하거나 말거나 나는 떠날 거야 'Regardless of if you love me or not, I'm leaving'.
notes.nuance: This double ~거나 pattern is specifically suited to situations where the outcome/result genuinely doesn't depend on which option is chosen ('it doesn't matter either way') - it's not the natural choice for expressing indecision about which option you yourself will pick (that would instead use ~ㄹ/을까 말까, covered in a later lesson).

pattern: ~(이)나 / ~거나 dalam kalimat negatif ('bukan pilihan, keduanya tidak terjadi/dilarang')
meaning: When ~(이)나 or ~거나 sentences end negatively, the meaning shifts from 'choosing between two things' to 'neither of them happens/is chosen'.

notes.formation: Same ~(이)나/~거나 attachment as the earlier patterns, but the overall sentence ends in a negative form (안, ~지 않다, ~지 말다, etc.).
notes.usage: 무기나 칼이 없어요 'I don't have a weapon or a knife' - not a decision between two objects, but a statement that you have NEITHER. 저는 눕거나 앉을 수 없어요 'I can't lay down or sit down' - not a decision between two actions, but a statement that BOTH are impossible. More: 희미한 빛이나 소리도 없었어요 'There wasn't even a glimmer of light or sound' (neither existed); 기말고사를 볼 때 말을 하거나 밥을 먹어서는 안 돼요 'You shouldn't talk or eat while writing the final exam' (both actions are prohibited); 등교를 늦게 하거나 하교를 일찍 하면 안 돼요 'You shouldn't come to school late or leave school early' (both are prohibited); 저는 그 남자를 보거나 생각하지 않을 거예요 'I'm not going to look at that man or think about him' (neither will happen).
notes.nuance: This is a natural consequence of how negation interacts with 'or': in a positive sentence, ~(이)나/~거나 present a genuine choice between options, but negating the whole sentence negates BOTH options at once, turning 'A or B' into 'neither A nor B' - this mirrors how English 'I don't have a weapon or a knife' is naturally understood as 'I have neither', even though it's structurally built the same way as the positive 'choosing between' sentences.

examples.meaning: I don't have a weapon or a knife.

pattern: 어쩌면 (kata keterangan 'mungkin', dipasangkan dengan ~ㄹ/을지(도) 모르다; juga 'bagaimana mungkin...')
meaning: 'Maybe/perhaps' - a feeling-adverb (like 만약/아무리) that can be removed without changing the sentence's core meaning, typically paired with ~ㄹ/을지(도) 모르다; also used to express amazement, meaning 'how is it possible that...'.

notes.formation: Placed at the start of a sentence that ends in ~ㄹ/을지(도) 모르다 (Lesson 30, 'might/don't know if'). For the amazement usage, 어쩌면 is commonly combined with 이렇게/그렇게/저렇게 (Lesson 23).
notes.usage: 어쩌면 그녀가 올지도 몰라요 'She might come/Perhaps she will come'; 어쩌면 우리가 내일 갈 수 있을지도 몰라요 'Perhaps we will be able to go tomorrow'. Amazement usage: 어쩌면 이렇게 일찍 왔어요? 'How is it possible that you came this early?'; 어쩌면 비가 저렇게 많이 왔어요? 'How is it possible that it rained that much?'
notes.nuance: Like 만약 and 아무리 before it, 어쩌면 doesn't carry meaning independently of the construction it signals - it exists to add feeling and help the listener anticipate the kind of sentence coming. For the amazement usage, 어떻게 is actually heard more often than 어쩌면 to express the same 'how is it possible' meaning, even though both are grammatically valid here.

pattern: 아무래도 (kata keterangan 'kemungkinan besar', dipasangkan dengan 것 같다; asalnya dari 아무렇다 + ~아/어도)
meaning: 'Probably' - typically paired with 것 같다, and also derived from bending 아무러하다/아무렇다 ('to be any form of') with ~아/어도, meaning 'regardless of what happens, it will be fine'.

notes.formation: As an adverb, placed at the start of a sentence ending in 것 같다 (Lesson 35). Separately, 아무 (Lesson 25) + 러하다 forms 아무러하다 ('to be no particular form of something'), commonly contracted to 아무렇다 (following the ㅎ irregular). Attaching ~아/어도 (Lesson 48) to 아무렇다 gives 아무래도 through the same ㅎ-irregular sound change.
notes.usage: 아무래도 그녀가 우리를 만나러 안 올 것 같아요 'She probably won't come to meet us'; 아무래도 그가 벌써 떠났을 것 같아요 'He probably already left'. From the 아무렇다+아/어도 derivation: 늦게 해도 일이 아무래도 문제가 없을 거예요 'It doesn't matter if you do it late, the work won't have a problem' (regardless of what happens, things are fine).
notes.nuance: 아무 + 것 도 (Lesson 25) already meant 'anything/nothing' with negatives; 아무러하다/아무렇다 extends this same 'no particular form' idea to an adjective covering ANY quality/situation, and 아무래도 is simply what results when the already-familiar ~아/어도 ('regardless of') is layered on top.

pattern: 아무렇게나 / 아무러하게나 ('sembarangan, tanpa banyak berpikir')
meaning: An adverb formed from 아무러하다/아무렇다 by adding ~게 (to make it an adverb) then ~나 (Lesson 58), meaning an action is done hastily/carelessly.

notes.formation: 아무러하다/아무렇다 + ~게 (adjective-to-adverb) + ~나 (Lesson 58's standalone ~(이)나, 'well... whatever') = 아무러하게나/아무렇게나.

pattern: 뵈다 / 뵙다 (melihat, honorifik dari 보다, konjugasi tidak beraturan)
meaning: The honorific equivalent of 보다 ('to see'), used when the person being looked at deserves high respect - with two versions that conjugate differently.

notes.formation: 뵈다 conjugates like 되다: officially 뵈어/뵈었어, commonly merged to 봬/뵀어 (never shortened further to just 뵈 or 뵜어, which are common mistakes). 뵙다 is a separate, slightly more formal word with the same meaning, but can ONLY take additions starting with a consonant (뵙겠다, 뵙는, 뵙고) - never 뵙어 or 뵙었어.
notes.usage: 저는 어제 선생님의 할아버지를 뵈었어요 'I saw your (the teacher's) grandpa yesterday' (respect shown toward the grandpa, regardless of how formally the listener is addressed - 나는 어제 너의 할아버지를 뵈었어 is equally valid toward a casual friend). 뵙다 is commonly used with ~겠다 as a polite way to say 'see you': 내일 뵙겠습니다 'See you tomorrow'; 나중에 뵙겠습니다 'See you later'.
notes.nuance: ~(으)시 is not used here - 뵈다/뵙다 already IS the honorific substitute for 보다 (like 드시다 for 먹다, or 계시다 for 있다, Lesson 39), so it follows the same pattern of a completely separate honorific word rather than a regular ~(으)시 addition.

pattern: N 차림으로 ('mengenakan/berpakaian N')
meaning: 'Wearing' a specific type of clothing - 차림 (a noun for 'what one is wearing') follows a clothing-type word, with ~(으)로 attached to say an action is done while wearing it.

notes.formation: [clothing type] + 차림 + ~(으)로: 잠옷 차림으로 'wearing pajamas'; 교복 차림으로 'wearing a school uniform'; 정장 차림으로 'wearing a suit'; 운동복 차림으로 'wearing exercise clothes'. 옷차림 (차림 combined with 옷 'clothes') more generally refers to one's outfit.

notes.nuance: 차림 is a noun in its own right (technically meaning 'clothes'), most often seen attached after a specific clothing-type word rather than used completely alone - the resulting compound is then given the instrumental/means particle ~(으)로, the same particle used elsewhere for 'by means of'.

pattern: N(으)로 가득 차다 / 차 있다 ('penuh dengan N')
meaning: 'To be full/filled with' something - the passive counterpart of 채우다 ('to fill'), with the thing it's filled with marked by ~(으)로, and 가득 as a feeling-adverb meaning 'completely'.

notes.formation: [thing filling it]로 + (가득) + 차다/차 있다. Saying just 교실이 완전히 찼어요 without specifying what fills it sounds slightly unnatural/ambiguous - the filling agent should be marked with ~(으)로. Despite 찼다 being past tense, it describes a state that is currently true (like English 'filled'); ~아/어 있다 can also be added to 차다 for the same present-state meaning.
notes.usage: 교실이 학생들로 완전히 찼어요 = 교실이 학생들로 완전히 차 있어요 'The classroom is completely full with students'; 교실은 학생들로 가득 찼어요 'The classroom is (completely) filled with students'. This same 차다 also describes being 'full' of an emotion: 자신감에 찬 표정으로 새로운 직장에 들어갔어요 'He went into a new workplace with a face "full of" confidence'; 시험결과를 보고 저는 기쁨으로 가득 찼어요 'After looking at the exam results, I was "full of" joy'.
notes.nuance: 가득 itself carries no special translation beyond 'completely/fully' - it's mainly included for feeling alongside 차다, and 가득하다 (as a standalone adjective) is technically possible but 가득 차다 is far more natural. 차다 has several unrelated meanings in other lessons (to kick, to wear a watch, to be cold) - this pattern covers only the 'to be full' sense.

examples.meaning: The restaurant is completely full with customers.
Is the lecture hall already completely full?

pattern: 왠지 ('entah kenapa/karena suatu alasan', dari 왜 그런지)
meaning: 'For some reason/I don't know why' - a fixed adverb built from the meaning of '왜 그런지 몰라요' (Lesson 23's 그렇다 + Lesson 30's ~ㄴ/은/는/ㄹ/을지).

notes.formation: 왠지 functions as a single adverb, placed in a sentence where the speaker doesn't know why something occurs.
notes.usage: 그녀는 왠지 한국어를 배우고 싶었어요 'She wanted to learn Korean for some reason'/'I don't know why, but she wanted to learn Korean'; 나는 왠지 오늘 학교에 가기 싫어 'I don't want to go to school today for some reason'; 오늘이 일요일이지만 버스가 승객들로 왠지 가득 찼어요 'Even though today is Sunday, the bus is packed with passengers for some reason'.
notes.nuance: Rather than memorizing a fixed English translation, it helps to trace 왠지 back to its source: 왜 그런지 몰라요 ('I don't know why it is like that') - 왠지 packages that whole idea into one word, expressing an event with an unclear or unexplained cause.

pattern: 설마 ('masa sih.../tidak mungkin...', keheranan)
meaning: 'Don't tell me that.../I can't believe that...' - an adverb expressing the speaker's amazement or disbelief that something occurs (or doesn't, if negated).

notes.formation: 설마 is placed at the start of the sentence describing the astonishing fact.
notes.usage: 밥을 다 먹었어요? 'Did you eat all of the rice?' -> 설마 밥을 다 먹었어요? 'Don't tell me you ate all the rice?!/I can't believe you ate all the rice!'; 설마 그곳에 혼자 가요? 'Don't tell me you are going there by yourself?'; in the negative: 설마 밥을 아직 안 먹었어요? 'Don't tell me that you haven't eaten yet?'. 설마 can also stand entirely alone as an exclamation of disbelief, like 'No way!': in response to being told he'd probably have to pay for water at a restaurant, a father-in-law simply said 설마! 'No way! That's ridiculous!'
notes.nuance: As with other feeling-adverbs in this unit (만약, 아무리, 어쩌면), there's no single fixed English translation - the underlying feeling of astonishment/disbelief is what matters, and it can be rendered many ways ('don't tell me...', 'I can't believe...', or standing alone as 'no way!').

examples.meaning: Don't tell me you are still sick?

examples.romaja: seolma uriga naeil hakgyoe gaya dwaeyo?

pattern: 찍다 (kata kerja multi-guna: memotret, mencap, mencelup, mengetuk/scan)
meaning: A verb whose many translations ('to take a picture', 'to stamp', 'to dip', 'to dot', 'to scan') all share the underlying idea of touching two objects together.

notes.formation: Used as an ordinary transitive verb with ~을/를 marking the object involved in the 'touching'.
notes.usage: Taking a picture: 저는 사진을 찍었어요 'I took a picture'. Stamping: 저는 계약서에 도장을 찍었어요 'I stamped/sealed the contract' (도장 is the personal seal Korean people use in place of a signature). Dipping: 고기를 소스에 찍어야 돼요 'You need to dip the meat in the sauce'. Putting a period/dot: 문장이 끝날 때마다 점을 찍어야 돼요 'When a sentence is finished, you need to put a period'. Scanning a transit card: 카드를 거기에 찍어야 돼요 'You need to scan your card there'.
notes.nuance: Rather than treating each translation as an unrelated separate meaning to memorize, it's more efficient to internalize the single underlying image of 'touching one thing to another' - once that clicks, most new contexts where 찍다 appears become predictable rather than needing individual memorization.

examples.meaning: I stamped/sealed the contract.
Do you need to dip the meat in the sauce?
I did not take a picture.

options: Menyentuhkan satu benda ke benda lain

pattern: ~아/어서 다행이다 ('untunglah/syukurlah...')
meaning: 'Thankfully/fortunately...' - attaching 다행 ('fortune/luck') plus conjugated 이다 after a ~아/어서 clause to express relief or gratitude that something happened.

notes.formation: [clause]~아/어서 (Lesson 37) + 다행이다 (다행 + conjugated 이다). The adjective 다행하다 also exists to describe a fortunate event directly (아무도 안 죽은 것은 다행한 일이에요 'Nobody dying is a fortunate event'), and 다행히 works as the adverb 'fortunately'.
notes.usage: 비가 안 와서 다행이에요 'Thankfully it didn't rain'; 물이 별로 안 뜨거워서 다행이에요 'Thankfully the water isn't too hot'; 아직 사람이 별로 없어서 다행이에요 'Thankfully there aren't that many people yet'; 돈을 안 줘서 다행이에요 'Thankfully I didn't give (him) any money'.
notes.nuance: This simply reuses the already-known ~아/어서 ('because') construction with the noun 다행 ('fortune') and 이다 predicating it, giving a natural, everyday way to express thankfulness or relief - grammatically no different from any other ~아/어서 + noun + 이다 sentence.

examples.meaning: Thankfully you took many pictures.
Thankfully it's not too expensive?
It wasn't fortunate that I didn't give (him) any money. (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: 다행이다 dibangun dari gabungan apa?
quiz.explanation: 다행이다 is 다행 (a noun, 'fortune') with 이다 conjugated after it.

pattern: N월달 ('suatu waktu di bulan N', saat tanggal pasti tidak diketahui)
meaning: Attaching 달 ('month') to a month name when the exact day isn't known or specified.

notes.formation: [month]달, e.g. 5월달 'sometime in May'; 6월달 'sometime in June' - compare to a specific date like 8월 15일 ('August 15th', Lesson 11), which names an exact day.
notes.usage: 저는 5월달에 한국에 갈 거예요 'I'm going to Korea sometime in May'; 저는 6월달에 시험을 볼 거예요 'I'm going to take an exam sometime in June'.
notes.nuance: This directly contrasts with the exact-date construction from Lesson 11 (month + day, e.g. 1월 2일 'January 2nd') - attaching 달 instead of a specific day number signals that only the month is known/relevant, not the precise date within it.

examples.meaning: I'm going to Korea sometime in May.
Am I going to take an exam sometime in June?

pattern: N을/를 바라다 ('berharap N', umum di ucapan selamat tertulis)
meaning: 'To hope for' a noun - most naturally seen in formal written greetings/well-wishes, hard to translate directly, with a notable spoken/written pronunciation split.

notes.formation: [noun]을/를 바라다. Since 바라다's stem ends in ㅏ, the official rule says ~아/어 additions should stay as 아 rather than merge further, giving 바라/바라요 as the technically correct forms.
notes.usage: 행복을 바랍니다 (roughly 'wishing you happiness'); 건강을 바랍니다 ('wishing you health'); 행운을 바랍니다 ('wishing you good luck') - these are rarely spoken aloud outside formal/fabricated speech, and are far more common in written greeting cards or formal messages. 바라다 can also be used in full sentences to mean wanting to 'possess/gain' something: 그 회사가 일본통화만 바라요 'That company only wants Japanese currency'.
notes.nuance: Despite 바라/바라요 being the officially correct pronunciation, Korean speakers overwhelmingly say (and often write, even in songs) 바래/바래요 instead - the lesson author's own Korean wife could not bring herself to record the 'correct' 바라/바라요 forms. Because of this, learners are advised to simply say 바래/바래요 in speech to sound natural, while knowing 바라/바라요 is the prescriptively correct form.

examples.meaning: Wishing you good luck.
Does that company only want Japanese currency?
That company does not want Japanese currency.

quiz.question: Bentuk mana yang secara resmi/preskriptif benar untuk 바라다 + ~아/어?
quiz.explanation: Officially, since 바라다's stem ends in ㅏ, it should stay 바라, even though 바래 is far more common in speech.

pattern: V/Adj~기(를) 바라다 ('berharap...')
meaning: Attaching ~기(를) (Lesson 29's nominalizer) to a verb/adjective clause before 바라다, to hope that an entire clause/situation occurs.

notes.formation: [clause]~기(를) + 바라다 (commonly pronounced/written 바래 in casual speech, per the previous pattern).
notes.usage: 저는 그 일을 잘 하기를 바라요 'I hope I do that job well'; 숙제가 많지 않기를 바라요 'I hope there isn't a lot of homework'; 그가 나에게 돈을 많이 주기를 바라 'I hope he gives me a lot of money'; 지금 만날 여자가 예쁘기를 바라요 'I hope the girl I am meeting now is pretty'.
notes.nuance: There's no need to force the English word 'hope' into every translation - depending on context, these sentences can equally be understood as a request the speaker is making of the listener (많은 사람들이 오시기를 바랍니다, said to a group before a party, works as both 'I hope many of you come' and 'Please come'). This dual reading (wish vs. polite request) is explored further in the next pattern.

examples.meaning: I hope that swan can swim again.
Do you hope the government amends that policy?
I hope you don't wear your shoes indoors.

quiz.question: Apa yang ditempel ke klausa kata kerja/sifat sebelum 바라다?
quiz.explanation: ~기(를) (Lesson 29's nominalizer) is attached to the clause before 바라다.

pattern: V~기 바랍니다 sebagai perintah/permintaan formal (dengan ~아/어 주(시)기 untuk melunakkan)
meaning: Using bare ~기 바랍니다 gives an authoritative command feel; adding ~아/어 주다 (and its honorific ~아/어 주시다) softens it into a formal, polite request, commonly heard in public announcements.

notes.formation: Bare command feel: [verb]~기 바랍니다. Softened: [verb]~아/어 주기 바랍니다. Softened and honorific/very formal: [verb]~아/어 주시기 바랍니다.
notes.usage: 그 일을 하기 바랍니다 (said by a boss to workers) carries an authoritative tone, implying the work should/must be done, as though ordering it. Adding ~아/어 주다 removes that authoritative feel: 그 일을 해 주기 바랍니다. Adding ~(으)시 makes it maximally formal, most often heard in loudspeaker announcements to crowds: 공항철도나 KTX를 타시고 싶은 승객은 이 역에서 갈아타시기 바랍니다 'Riders wanting to take the Airport Railroad or the KTX, please transfer at this station'; 실내에서 운동을 하지 말아 주시기 바랍니다 'Please don't exercise indoors'; 모든 학생들이 딱 12시에 도착해 주시기 바랍니다 'All students please arrive at exactly 12:00'.
notes.nuance: This forms a politeness ladder for giving the same basic instruction: 지금 나가 (bare informal) < 지금 나가라 < 지금 나가세요 < 지금 나가기 바랍니다 (authoritative) < 지금 나가 주기 바랍니다 (softened) < 지금 나가십시오 < 지금 나가 주시기 바랍니다 (most formal/softened) - all roughly translate to 'please go now', but sit at very different levels of formality and command-feel.

pattern: V/Adj~았/었으면 좋겠다 ('semoga/andai saja...')
meaning: 'I hope/I wish' - attaching the past-tense ~(으)면 (Lesson 43) plus future-conjugated 좋다 ('to be good'), best treated as one inseparable unit meaning 'wish/hope', regardless of the actual timing of what's hoped for.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective]~았/었으면 + 좋겠다 (좋다 + ~겠다). Despite mixing a past-tense marker (~았/었) and a future-looking marker (~겠다), the whole construction expresses a present hope/wish, whether about the present or future situation.
notes.usage: 비가 안 왔으면 좋겠어요 'I hope it doesn't rain'; 양이 많았으면 좋겠어요 'I hope there is a lot'; 내일 일이 없었으면 좋�지어요 'I wish I didn't have work tomorrow'; 나를 무조건 사랑했으면 좋겠어 'I wish you loved me unconditionally'; 엄마가 저를 데리러 왔으면 좋겠어요 'I wish mom would come to pick me up'. 하다 or 바라다 (from this same lesson) can substitute for 좋다: 우리가 곧 만났으면 해 = 우리가 곧 만났으면 바래요 'I wish we could meet soon'.
notes.nuance: This is deliberately best learned as one fixed chunk rather than analyzed piece-by-piece - the author suggests ~았/었으면 좋겠다 as a whole conveys 'wish', distinct from separately interpreting ~(으)면 ('if/when') plus 좋겠다 ('it would be good') as individually meaningful parts, even though native speakers say both readings end up expressing the same thing.

examples.meaning: I hope the house will be clean when I go home.

pattern: V~(으)면서 ('sambil...', dua tindakan terjadi bersamaan)
meaning: 'While/as' - placing two clauses in one sentence to show they occur at the same time.

notes.formation: ~면서 attaches to a vowel-final stem (or one ending in ㄹ); ~으면서 attaches to a consonant-final stem (except ㄹ). Irregulars follow their usual rules: 듣다 (ㄷ irregular) -> 들으면서.
notes.usage: 저는 밥을 먹으면서 공부했어요 'I ate (rice) while studying'; 저는 영화를 보면서 콜라를 마셨어요 'I drank cola while watching a movie'; 학업을 진행하면서 직장도 다녀요 'As I progress my studies, I also go to work'; 눈이 길에 계속 쌓이면서 길이 점점 미끄러워져요 'As snow piles up on the road, it gets more and more slippery'.
notes.nuance: The two actions must genuinely occur simultaneously/continuously - this differs sharply from ~아/어서 (Lesson 17), which links a position/state to a following action in sequence (저는 앉아서 공부했어요 'I sat down and (then) studied'). Using ~(으)면서 with 앉다 instead (저는 앉으면서 공부했어요) would literally mean 'I studied while transitioning from standing to sitting', which is almost never the intended meaning - so ~(으)면서 fits ongoing simultaneous actions, not a state entered before another action begins.

pattern: Adj/이다~(으)면서 ('sekaligus...', memiliki dua sifat/identitas)
meaning: Attaching ~(으)면서 to adjectives or 이다 - since these don't 'occur' the way verbs do, the meaning shifts to 'having both properties/identities at once'.

notes.formation: Same ~(으)면서 attachment rule applies to adjective stems and to 이다.
notes.usage: 이 음식은 매우면서 짜요 'This food is spicy and salty (at once)'; 그 기념비가 아름다우면서 흥미로워요 'That monument is beautiful and interesting'. With 이다: 그 사람은 저의 부장이면서 친구예요 'That person is my boss and (also) my friend'; 요즘 핸드폰은 전화기이면서 컴퓨터예요 'Cell phones these days are phones and (also) computers'.
notes.nuance: These sentences are close in meaning to the simpler ~고 (Lesson 17: 이 음식은 맵고 짜요), and the difference doesn't need to be sharply distinguished - but ~(으)면서 gives a feeling that the two descriptions are more tightly interrelated/connected as a single characterization, while ~고 simply lists two separate descriptions side by side.

examples.meaning: The weather today is cloudy and chilly.

pattern: V~(으)면서 (pemakaian lain: dua klausa yang BERLAWANAN, 'padahal...')
meaning: A distinct usage where the subject does both clauses, but the two clauses contradict each other - typically used complaining about someone's hypocrisy or contradictory behavior.

notes.formation: Same ~(으)면서 attachment, but the two clauses describe contradictory facts about the same subject.
notes.usage: 그 여자가 식당을 열고 싶다고 하면서 요리를 못해요 'That girl says she wants to open up a restaurant, but she doesn't know how to cook'; 저의 와이프가 외국 브랜드를 좋아하면서 한국에서 만들어진 제품만 사요 'My wife likes foreign brands, but only buys products made in Korea'; 그 사람이 한국에서 살면서 한국어를 할 수 없어요 'That person lives in Korea, but he can't speak Korean'; 그가 저에게 기념품을 사 준다고 하면서 아무 것도 안 샀어요 'He said he would buy me a souvenir, but didn't buy anything'.
notes.nuance: This usage is typically colored by a tone of complaint or exasperation ('Ugh, he does this, but then does that!') - the same grammatical form as the simultaneous-action usage, but context (contradictory rather than compatible clauses) signals this different meaning. ~도 can be added to ~(으)면서 for extra emphasis on the contradiction (covered in a much later lesson).
