pattern: N에 의한 (bentuk atributif, menerangkan kata benda berikutnya)
meaning: Attaching ~ㄴ to ~에 의하다 to describe an upcoming noun, following the same principle already seen with 대하다/관하다/관련하다 (Lesson 34).

notes.formation: [cause noun]에 의한 + [noun], mirroring 환경에 대한 것/환경에 관한 것/환경에 관련한 것 from Lesson 34.
notes.usage: 담배에 의한 사망은 증가하고 있어요 'Deaths due to smoking are increasing'; 매년 인종차별에 의한 사망자가 늘고 있어요 'Every year, the number of deaths due to racism is increasing'; 날씨에 의한 피해는 예방할 수 없는 문제예요 'Damage due to weather is a problem that we can't prevent'; 모르는 사람과 같은 집에서 살면 오해에 의한 싸움이 자주 생겨요 'If you live with a person you don't know, fights due to misunderstandings often occur'.
notes.nuance: This is a direct application of the attributive principle already learned for similar 'about/regarding' words (대하다, 관하다, 관련하다) - ~에 의하다 simply joins that same family of words that can attach ~ㄴ to describe an upcoming noun.

examples.meaning: Deaths due to smoking are increasing.

pattern: N(으)로 인해/인한 ('karena/akibat N', pengganti ~에 의해 kecuali untuk 의하면)
meaning: 'Due to/as a result of' - can substitute for ~에 의해 (both the active-sentence and attributive uses) with essentially no difference in meaning, but CANNOT replace ~에 의하면 ('according to').

notes.formation: [noun](으)로 인해 (active sentence use, replacing ~에 의해) or [noun](으)로 인한 (attributive use, replacing ~에 의한).
notes.usage: 안개로 인해 비행기가 못 떴어요 = 안개에 의해 비행기가 못 떴어요 'The plane couldn't take off due to the fog'; 그 사람은 사고로 인해 목숨을 잃었어요 'That person died as a result of a car accident'; 야외결혼식이 비로 인해 취소되었어요 'The outdoor wedding was cancelled due to the rain'. Attributive: 담배로 인한 사망 = 담배에 의한 사망 'deaths due to smoking'; 호우로 인한 홍수 'a flood due to heavy rain'; 지진으로 인한 피해 'damage due to an earthquake'. NOT possible: 신문으로 인하면... (incorrect - only ~에 의하면 works for 'according to').
notes.nuance: If a distinct English translation is needed to tell them apart, ~(으)로 인하다 can be rendered 'as a result of' while ~에 의하다 stays 'due to' - but Korean speakers themselves consider the sentences built with either construction to be identical in meaning, with the one clear restriction being that ~(으)로 인하다 has no equivalent to the 'according to' (~에 의하면) usage of ~에 의하다.

examples.meaning: The concert was cancelled due to the weather.

pattern: V~는/ㄴ/은 대로 ('sesuai/seperti yang...') + 그대로/마음대로
meaning: 'As/according to' - 대로 described by a verb clause (usually past-tense, since it refers to something already known/observed), plus the fixed adverbs 그대로 ('as it was') and 마음대로 ('as one's heart desires').

notes.formation: [verb clause, usually past]~ㄴ/은 대로, or present ~는 대로 when the situation is still ongoing. 그 (referring to a known situation) + 대로 = 그대로. 마음 (heart) + 대로 = 마음대로.
notes.usage: 제가 예상한 대로 재미있었어요 'As I expected, it was fun'; 제가 들은 대로 이 지역 호박은 진짜 맛있어요 'As I heard, the pumpkins here are delicious'. Present tense (ongoing): 내가 시키는 대로 해 줘 'Please do it as I ask'. 그대로: 이 상황을 그대로 그냥 인정하세요 'Just accept the situation as it is'. 마음대로: 먹고 싶은 것을 마음대로 고르세요 'Choose whatever food you want'.
notes.nuance: 대로 in the past tense reflects something already known/experienced (what I expected, heard, saw); in the present tense, it implies the situation is still unfolding. 알다 and 시키다 are especially common present-tense partners for 대로.

pattern: 인기 dengan berbagai kata kerja ('populer', naik/turunnya popularitas)
meaning: 인기 ('popularity') is a simple noun, but pairs with several different verbs depending on the nuance: 많다 (having a lot), 끌다 (attracting/gaining), 얻다 (gaining), 떨어지다 (dropping), 있다/없다 (having/not having).

notes.formation: [person/thing]에게/한테/께 인기가 많다; 인기를 끌다 (with ~고 있다/~는 중이다 for ongoing popularity, since 끌다 is a verb taking ~를); 인기를 얻다 (gaining); 인기가 떨어지다 (dropping); 인기가 있다/없다 (simple existence).
notes.usage: 그 만화책은 성인들에게 인기가 많아요 'That comic book is popular among adults'; 그 모자는 색깔이 예뻐서 인기를 끌고 있어요 'That hat is getting popular because the color is pretty'; 그 물품이 영화에 나와서 인기를 얻었어요 'That product was in a movie, so it got popular'; 아이폰 인기는 이제 떨어지고 있어요 'The iPhone's popularity is dropping now'; 그 영화는 인기가 없어요 'That movie isn't popular'.
notes.nuance: The group something is popular WITH is marked with ~한테/에게/께ㅤ(많다), while 끌다 uses ~를/을 since it's an active verb. Each verb adds a slightly different flavor: 많다 states a static amount, 끌다/얻다 emphasize gaining popularity, 떨어지다 emphasizes losing it.

examples.hangul: 그 선생님은 키가 커서 학생들한테 인기가 많아요
examples.romaja: geu seonsaengnimeun kiga keoseo haksaengdeulhante ingiga manhayo

pattern: 당연하다/당연히 ('tentu saja/wajar/jelas')
meaning: 'Obvious/of course' - best translated as 'obvious' rather than the dictionary's 'natural', used both as an adverb (당연히) and adjective (당연하다), including the response '당연하지!' and joking substitute '당근'.

notes.formation: Adverb: 당연히. Adjective (attributive: 당연한): describes an obvious situation. Response to a question: 당연해요!/당연하지! (~지/죠, previewed here, adds emphasis without changing meaning). Joking substitute: 당근 ('carrot', a pun on the sound of 당연 + often 당근이지!).
notes.usage: 그는 당연히 왔어요 'He obviously came' (Of course he came!); Person 1: 내일 갈 거예요? -> Person 2: 당연해요! 'Of course!' As adjective: 그가 그 여자를 사랑하는 것은 당연해요 'It's obvious that he loves that girl'. Rhetorical question form: 그가 그 여자를 사랑하는 것은 당연한 게 아니에요? 'Isn't it obvious that he loves that girl?'
notes.nuance: 당연하다's core meaning is 'obvious', a shade more specific than the dictionary's 'natural/correct'. Younger speakers substitute 당근 ('carrot') as a pun/joke for 당연 - saying this to a Korean will reliably make them laugh.

pattern: 알맞다/어울리다 ('cocok/serasi')
meaning: 'Appropriate/suitable' - 알맞다 for things matching well (appearance, taste, smell); 어울리다 for the same, plus also for people getting along well.

notes.formation: [thing1]은/는 [thing2]에 알맞다/어울리다.

pattern: N 전체 ('seluruh N')
meaning: 'The whole' - a noun placed after another noun to refer to its entirety, from Hanja 全 (all) + 體 (body/thing).

notes.formation: [noun] 전체, placed directly after the noun it refers to.
notes.usage: 학교 전체 'the whole school'; 도시 전체 'the whole city'; 학교 전체가 닫혀 있어요 'The whole school is closed'; 우리는 도시 전체를 걸어 다녔어요 'We walked around the whole city'; 부장님이 회사원 몇 명을 해고할 거라고 해서 회사 전체가 긴장했어요 'The whole company was nervous because the boss said he will fire some workers'.
notes.nuance: 전체 functions as an ordinary noun attached directly after another noun, similar in structural pattern to other noun-combining words seen throughout the course.

pattern: N은/는 바로 그 때문이다 ('itulah alasannya...')
meaning: 'That is why...' - referring to an already-discussed situation with 그 ('that'), stressed by 바로 ('precisely'), followed by 때문이다 ('is the reason'), with the resulting action nominalized via ~는 것.

notes.formation: [action]~는 것은 바로 그 때문이에요. 그 refers to a previously known situation; 바로 emphasizes 'precisely'; 때문 + 이다 states 'is the reason'.
notes.usage: 제가 가고 싶은 것은 바로 그 때문이에요 'That is why I want to go'; 제가 그녀를 좋아하는 것은 바로 그 때문이에요 'That is why I like her'; 제가 한국어를 배우고 있는 것은 바로 그 때문이에요 'That is why I am learning Korean'.
notes.nuance: A simpler alternative is to just use 그래서 (Lesson 37, referring back to a previous reason) before the action: 그래서 가고 싶어요 'That is why I want to go' - both express the same idea, but 바로 그 때문이다 is more explicit/emphatic about pinpointing 'that' specific reason.

examples.hangul: 제가 한국어를 배우고 있는 것은 바로 그 때문이에요

pattern: V~아/어서는 안 되다 ('seharusnya tidak boleh...', bereaksi ke tindakan yang baru terjadi)
meaning: 'One should not' - attaching ~아/어서 (Lesson 37) then 안 되다 to indicate a problem WILL occur if the action is completed - the opposite of ~아/어도 되다 ('may/can', Lesson 51).

notes.formation: [verb]~아/어서는 안 되다, mirroring the earlier ~아/어도 되다 structure but with 안 되다 instead of 되다.
notes.usage: 밥을 많이 먹어서는 안 돼요 'You shouldn't eat a lot'; 선생님을 무시해서는 안 돼요 'You shouldn't ignore your teacher'; 그렇게 빨리 뛰어서는 안 돼요 'You shouldn't run that fast'; 사람을 겉모습으로 평가해선 안 돼요 'You shouldn't judge somebody on their looks' (해서는 contracted to 해선).
notes.nuance: Even though stated in the present tense, these sentences usually refer to something that just happened - 그렇게 빨리 뛰어서는 안 돼요 is typically said right after observing someone running too fast, not as a purely abstract, general statement.

pattern: V~(으)면 안 되다 ('tidak boleh...', sedikit lebih kuat) + bentuk pertanyaan sebagai permintaan sopan
meaning: 'One must not' - similar to ~아/어서는 안 되다 but slightly stronger, and very commonly used as a polite question ('can't you...?'/'is it okay if...?'), including double-negative forms and combination with ~아/어 주다.

notes.formation: [verb]~(으)면 안 되다. As a question: [verb]~(으)면 안 돼요?. Double negative: [verb, negated]~지 않으면/안 [verb]으면 안 돼요? (asking if it's okay NOT to do something). Combined with ~아/어 주다: [verb]~아/어 주면 안 돼요? (a polite request).
notes.usage: 그렇게 하면 안 돼요 'You must not do it like that'; 이 차에 디젤을 넣으면 안 됩니다 'You must not put diesel fuel in this car'. As a question: 이렇게 하면 안 돼요? 'Can't you do it like this?/Is it okay if you do it like this?'; 조금 더 주면 안 돼요? 'Can't you give me a little bit more?'. Double negative: 밥을 지금 안 먹으면 안 돼요? 'Can we not eat now?/Is it okay if we don't eat now?'; 이번에 여행할 때 수천 장의 사진을 찍지 않으면 안 돼요? 'Can you not take thousands of pictures this time when we travel?'. With ~아/어 주다: 밥을 사 주시면 안 돼요? 'Are you able to buy me rice?'; 교통카드를 충전해 주면 안 돼요? 'Are you able to charge my subway card?'.
notes.nuance: The question form is a genuinely polite way to make a request, and pairs very naturally with ~아/어 주다. When the answer is 'no', it's typically expressed simply as 안 돼요 ('No, it can't be done'). The negation-inside-negation structure (a negated verb + 안 되다) can feel like a double negative in English, but simply asks whether NOT doing something is acceptable.

examples.meaning: You must not omit that information.
Are you able to charge my subway card?

examples.hangul: 그 대회를 참여하지 않으면 안 돼요?

pattern: V~(으)면 되다 ('cukup...saja/seharusnya', saran lembut)
meaning: Attaching plain 되다 (without 안) to ~(으)면 creates a meaning similar to ~아/어야 하다 ('must/should', Lesson 46), but framed as a soft, gentle suggestion rather than a firm obligation.

notes.formation: [verb]~(으)면 되다, literally 'everything will be okay if you [verb]'.
notes.usage: 서울역에서 내려야 돼요 'You must get off at Seoul station' (~아/어야 되다, firm obligation) vs 서울역에서 내리면 됩니다 'You should get off at Seoul station' (~(으)면 되다, gentler suggestion). Often used when giving advice: 다음 역에서 내리면 돼요 'You can/should get off at the next station'. Frequently translates more naturally as 'one can': 조금만 넣으면 돼요 'Just put a little bit in'; 조금 더 올라가면 돼요 'Just keep going up a little bit further'; 코피를 휴지로 막으면 돼요 'You can block the nosebleed with a tissue'; 애기가 피곤하면 업어 주면 돼요 'If the baby is tired, you can carry him on your back'.
notes.nuance: The core feeling is 'everything will be fine/okay if you do this' - a much gentler framing than the firmer ~아/어야 하다 obligation. This softness is exactly why it's so common when someone is asked for advice or directions, offering a suggestion rather than issuing a command.

examples.meaning: You can block the nosebleed with a tissue.
How much more salt should I put in?
It's fine if you don't put a little bit in. (used to show the pattern)

quiz.explanation: ~(으)면 되다 frames the same idea as a gentle suggestion, while ~아/어야 되다 feels like a firmer obligation.

pattern: V/Adj~(으)니까 ('karena...', mirip ~아/어서 tapi sering sebagai dalih)
meaning: 'Because/so' - similar to ~아/어서 (Lesson 37), but commonly used when the first clause is an excuse for why the second clause happens (often why something can't be done), sometimes with a hint of annoyance; unlike ~아/어서, the clause before ~(으)니까 CAN be conjugated into the past.

notes.formation: ~니까 attaches to a vowel-final stem (or ㄹ/ㅎ-irregular stem, both drop their final letter, e.g. 살다 -> 사니까, 그렇다 -> 그러니까); ~으니까 attaches to a consonant-final stem. ㅅ/ㄷ/ㅂ irregulars follow their usual rules; ㅡ/르 are unaffected (just add ~니까). The clause can be conjugated to the past first: ~았/었으니까.
notes.usage: 학교에 가야 되니까 지금 못 만나요 'I need to go to school, so I won't be able to meet'; 옆방이 아주 시끄러우니까 저는 잠을 못 잤어요 'The room next to us is very loud, so I couldn't sleep'. Past tense: 어제 너무 바빴으니까 못 갔어요 'I couldn't go yesterday because I was so busy'; 너를 좋아하지 않았으니까 헤어졌어 'I broke up with you because I didn't like you'.
notes.nuance: While ~(으)니까 often carries a feeling of excuse/mild annoyance, this isn't a strict rule - it's also used for simple cause-and-effect without any negative undertone, as shown in later patterns in this lesson.

examples.hangul: 그 셔츠를 사고 싶은데 돈이 없으니까 살 수 없어요

pattern: Mengakhiri kalimat dengan ~(으)니까(요) ('karena...', jawaban)
meaning: Ending a sentence with ~(으)니까(요), leaving the rest implied - commonly used to answer a question starting with 'because...', similar to how ~는데 (Lesson 77) can end a sentence.

notes.formation: [clause]~(으)니까(요), left unfinished at the sentence's end, with ~요 optional for formality.
notes.usage: Person 1: 지금 만날 수 있어요? 'Can you meet now?' -> Person 2: 아니요~ 못 만나요. 학교에 가야 되니까요 'No, because I have to go to school'; Person 1: 나랑 왜 헤어졌어? 'Why did you break up with me?' -> Person 2: 너를 좋아하지 않았으니까 '…Because I didn't like you'.
notes.nuance: Just like ending a sentence with ~는데 (Lesson 77), this can come across as a little rude, carrying a slight feeling of talking back - even with ~요 attached, though it always depends on context and tone.

examples.meaning: No, I can't buy it. Because I have no money.

pattern: ~(으)니까 untuk saran ('Ayo..., karena...')
meaning: ~(으)니까 is also commonly used when making a suggestion, still carrying the 'because' meaning without any negative/excuse undertone.

notes.formation: [reason clause]~(으)니까 + [suggestion, often with ~자 or ~ㄹ래요].
notes.usage: 버스가 복잡하니까 택시를 타자! 'Let's take a taxi because the bus is so crowded!'; 너무 더우니까 시원한 것을 먹을래요? 'Let's eat something cool because it is so hot'; 밥이 없으니까 라면 먹자! 'Let's eat Ramen because there is no rice'.
notes.nuance: This shows ~(으)니까's excuse/annoyance feeling isn't a fixed rule - in suggestion sentences like these, it's simply a neutral, practical reason for a proposed action, with no negative undertone at all.

examples.meaning: Let's take a taxi because the bus is so crowded!
Shall we eat something cool because it is so hot?
I don't want to eat Ramen even though there is no rice. (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: Apa yang ditunjukkan penggunaan ~(으)니까 dalam kalimat saran seperti '버스가 복잡하니까 택시를 타자!'?
options: ~(으)니까 tidak selalu membawa nada dalih/kesal - bisa jadi alasan netral
quiz.explanation: In suggestion sentences, ~(으)니까 conveys a neutral reason without any excuse/annoyance feeling.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: Let's eat Ramen because there is no rice! -> 밥이 [BLANK] 라면 먹자!

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'Let's take a taxi because the bus is so crowded!'

pattern: ~(으)니 (versi singkat dari ~(으)니까, mengatur latar dengan nuansa 'karena') + ~았/었으니 ('sekarang setelah...')
meaning: Dropping ~까 from ~(으)니까 gives ~(으)니 - functioning much like ~는데 (setting up context for the next clause), but with a slight 'because' feeling instead of 'even though'; in the past tense, often best translated 'now that...'.

notes.formation: Same irregular-attachment rules as ~(으)니까, just without the final ~까. Unlike ~(으)니까, ~(으)니 typically isn't used at the very end of a sentence.
notes.usage: 밥이 없으니 라면 먹자! 'Let's eat Ramen because there is no rice!'; 제가 배가 안 고프니 더 먹기 싫어요 'I don't want to eat anymore because I am full'. More common in writing than ~(으)니까, which is more common in speech. In the past tense, 'now that...' fits naturally: 밥이 다 됐으니 많이 드세요! 'Now that the rice is ready, eat a lot!'; 빨래를 다 했으니 지금 자도 돼요 'Now that I have finished the laundry, I can go to bed'; 충치를 치료했으니 치아가 이제 안 아파요 'Now that I treated my cavity, my teeth don't hurt'.
notes.nuance: There are two closely related, hard-to-separate meanings: (1) a plain 'because', identical to ~(으)니까, and (2) simply setting up background information for the next clause (like ~는데, but with a 'because' flavor instead of 'even though'). The author's own advice: don't worry about strictly separating these two meanings - if a direct causal link between the clauses is clear, read it as 'because'; if the link is less obvious, read it as background-setting, similar in spirit to ~는데.

pattern: Adj/이다~구나/군/군요 ('oh, saya tidak sadar...', kata sifat/이다, dengan pengecualian 있다/없다)
meaning: 'Oh! I didn't realize that...' - attached directly to an adjective/이다 stem, expressing the speaker's surprise at newly realized information, mostly felt as talking to oneself; ~구나/~군 informal, ~군요 formal.

notes.formation: Attach ~구나/~군/~군요 directly to the adjective stem (or to 이 for 이다). EXCEPTION: 있다/없다 (despite being adjectives) still take this form directly on their stem as if adjectives here (unlike some other grammar points where they behave like verbs).
notes.usage: 낚싯줄이 이렇게 비싸구나 'I didn't know that fishing line is this expensive'; 네가 매우 똑똑하구나 'I didn't realize that you are so smart'; 미국에서 비만이 아주 큰 문제이구나 'I didn't realize that obesity was such a big problem in America'; 이 전철에 가방을 올려놓을 수 있는 선반이 없군 'I didn't realize there was no shelf to put your bag onto on the subway'. 그렇다 + this ending gives 그렇구나, commonly used alone to mean 'Oh...(I didn't realize that)' after hearing new information.
notes.nuance: ~이/가 (not ~은/는) naturally marks the subject in these sentences, since Lesson 17 established ~이/가 for subjects the speaker is just now noticing/realizing - exactly the situation these endings describe. ~구나 is far more common in speech than ~군, though younger people commonly use ~군 while chatting online.

pattern: ~았/었구나/군/군요 (waktu lampau) dan ~겠구나/군/군요 (dugaan masa depan)
meaning: Attaching ~구나/군/군요 to the past-tense ~았/었 for realizing something already happened, or to ~겠다 for guessing something will be the case in the future.

notes.formation: [stem]~았/었 + 구나/군/군요 (past, applies to verbs, adjectives, and 이다 alike). [stem]~겠 + 구나/군/군요 (future guess, ~겠다 preferred over ~ㄹ/을 것이다 since these realizations of future events are typically guesses).
notes.usage: Past: 벌써 먹었구나 'Oh, I didn't realize that you already ate'; 어제 생일이었구나 'Oh, I didn't realize that yesterday was your birthday'; 둥지가 나무에서 떨어졌구나 'Oh, I didn't realize that the nest fell from the tree'. Future guess: 돈이 없겠구나 'Oh, we will probably not have money'; 당황스럽겠구나 'Oh, you will probably be embarrassed'.
notes.nuance: The realization itself always happens in the present moment - what varies is the TIMING of the fact being realized (past event, or future guess). Since future realizations are inherently guesses rather than certainties, ~겠다 (not the more definite ~ㄹ/을 것이다) is the natural choice here.

pattern: V/Adj/이다~네(요) ('wah, ternyata...', kekaguman/keterkejutan, lebih ditujukan ke pendengar)
meaning: Similar in meaning to ~구나/군/군요 (Lesson 84), expressing surprise at newly realized information - but felt less like pure self-talk (roughly 60% self/40% to the listener, vs. ~구나's 90/10), and more likely used when the speaker is genuinely IMPRESSED rather than just noting a mundane fact.

notes.formation: Attach ~네(요) directly to a verb/adjective/이다 stem, no tense-based ~는/은 split needed (unlike ~구나/군/군요's verb/adjective distinction).
notes.usage: 아들이 귀엽네요 'Oh, I didn't realize that your son is so cute'; 이 음식점은 음식이 정말 맛있네요 'Wow, this restaurant's food is really delicious'; 선생님! 영어를 너무 잘하시네요! 'Teacher! pattern: V~자마자 ('segera setelah...')
meaning: 'As soon as' - attaching ~자마자 directly to a verb stem (never conjugated to past/future itself; the overall sentence's tense is read from the second clause).

notes.formation: [verb stem]자마자, with no tense marker attached to it directly - the following clause's own conjugation shows whether the whole event is past, present, or future.
notes.usage: 집에 도착하자마자 밥을 먹어야 돼요 'As soon as we arrive at home, I need to eat' (future); 버스가 출발하자마자 사람들은 움직였어요 'As soon as the bus moved, people started moving' (past); 경찰관들은 범죄자를 찾자마자 기소할 거예요 'As soon as the police find the criminal, they will prosecute him' (future); 제가 가르치기 시작하자마자 학생들이 조용해졌어요 'As soon as I started teaching, the students got quiet' (past).
notes.nuance: Like many other Korean connectors already learned (~기 때문에, ~는데, etc.), the clause before ~자마자 stays in its plain, unconjugated form - only the following clause carries the sentence's actual timing.

pattern: V~는 대로 ('segera setelah...', alternatif dari ~자마자, jarang di percakapan)
meaning: Reusing 대로 (Lesson 79's 'as/according to' noun) described by a present-tense ~는 clause, to mean the same 'as soon as' - understood as identical to ~자마자, but far less common in everyday speech.

notes.formation: [verb]~는 대로, always present tense in the first clause regardless of the overall sentence's timing.

pattern: V~자 (1: 'segera setelah...', hanya untuk tindakan yang sudah terjadi; 2: sebab-akibat)
meaning: ~자 can substitute for ~자마자 for 'as soon as', but ONLY when the action has already occurred - it cannot be used for future/not-yet-happened actions. ~자 can also show a cause-and-effect relationship, though ~아/어서/때문에 are more common for that meaning.

notes.formation: [verb stem]자, restricted to already-occurred actions for the 'as soon as' meaning; for cause-and-effect, no such restriction applies.
notes.usage: 'As soon as' (already happened): 버스가 출발하자 사람들은 움직였어요 'As soon as the bus moved, people started moving' (acceptable, since it already happened) - but 경찰관들은 범죄자를 찾자 기소할 거예요 would be UNNATURAL (replacing ~자마자 in a not-yet-happened, future context). Cause-and-effect: 바람이 불자 그 집이 쓰러질 것 같아요 'The house might fall down because of the wind blowing'; 엄마가 소리를 지르자 아기가 깜짝 놀랐어요 'The baby was surprised because the mother raised her voice' (this same sentence is genuinely ambiguous between 'because' and 'as soon as' - and native speakers say the distinction rarely needs to be pinned down, since the practical result is the same either way).
notes.nuance: This restriction (~자 only for completed actions) is the key limitation separating it from ~자마자, which works for both completed and not-yet-completed actions. For cause-and-effect, ~아/어서 and ~기 때문에/때문에 (Lessons 37-38) remain more common than ~자.

pattern: N이다+~자 ('sekaligus juga N', dua kata benda pada satu hal) + 처음이자 마지막
meaning: Attaching ~자 to 이다 indicates one noun is inherently two things at once - commonly seen in the fixed expression 처음이자 마지막 ('the first and last').

notes.formation: [noun1]이자 [noun2] + 이다.
notes.usage: 저는 선생님이자 학생이에요 'I am a teacher and a student'; 이 식사는 우리 점심이자 저녁이에요 'This meal is our lunch and dinner'; 요즘 핸드폰은 전화기이자 컴퓨터예요 'Cell phones these days are phones and computers'; 저의 남편은 저의 제일 친한 친구이자 제가 제일 사랑하는 사람이에요 'My husband is my best friend and the person who I love the most'. Fixed idiom: 이것은 처음이자 마지막 기회예요 'This is the first and last chance'; 그 사람은 우리 나라의 처음이자 마지막 왕이었어요 'That person was our country's first and last king'.
notes.nuance: This is a distinct, third meaning of ~자 (alongside 'as soon as' and cause-and-effect) - specifically for 이다, expressing that a single noun holds two identities/roles simultaneously, not sequential or causal at all.

pattern: V/Adj/이다~는/ㄴ/은/ㄹ/을 줄 알았다 ('kupikir...', ternyata salah karena kelalaian menilai)
meaning: 'I thought...' - describing 줄 (in past, present, or future tense as appropriate) with 알았다, specifically implying the speaker had a lapse in judgment and mistakenly believed something that turned out to be false.

notes.formation: [clause, tense matching when the mistaken belief was about]~는/ㄴ/은/ㄹ/을 줄 알았다.
notes.usage: 천원만 준 줄 알았어요 'I thought you only gave me 1,000 won' (past); 학생인 줄 알았어요 'I thought you were a student' (present, 이다); 아빠가 저에게 돈을 줄 줄 알았어요 'I thought that dad will give me money' (future). Comparing with quoted-opinion ~다고 생각하다: 그녀가 예쁘다고 생각했어요 'I thought she was pretty' (a genuine, still-held opinion) vs 그녀가 예쁜 줄 알았어요 '(Oh,) I thought she was pretty' (implies you were WRONG - you've since learned she isn't).
notes.nuance: The key distinguishing feature from ~다고 생각했어요 is that ~는/ㄴ/은/ㄹ/을 줄 알았다 specifically implies the belief was mistaken due to some lapse in judgment (e.g. seeing something from far away, misunderstanding a situation) - the speaker has since realized the truth was different from what they originally believed.

meaning: Using 모르다 instead of 알다 flips the meaning: the speaker originally believed something was NOT true, but has since realized it actually IS true.

notes.usage: 그녀가 예쁜 줄 몰랐어요 'I didn't know she was pretty' (originally thought she WASN'T pretty, now realizes she is); 거기가 비싼 줄 몰랐어요 'I didn't know it was expensive there' (originally thought it wasn't expensive, now knows it is); 그 핸드폰이 좋은 줄 몰랐어요 'I didn't know that cell-phone was good' (originally thought it wasn't good, now knows it is).

pattern: ~다시피 ('seperti yang kau tahu/lihat...', merujuk ke persepsi pendengar)
meaning: Referring to the listener's own knowledge or perception - most commonly attached to 알다 ('as you know') and 보다 ('as you can see'), with the '다' being part of the grammar itself, not the verb's stem.

notes.formation: 알다시피/보다시피, often with ~도 attached to the person ('you ALSO know/see'), and ~(으)시 for a highly respected listener: 아시다시피/보시다시피.
notes.usage: 너도 알다시피… 'As you know…'; 선생님도 아시다시피… 'As you (teacher) know…'; 너도 보다시피… 'As you (can) see…'; 부장님도 보시다시피… 'As you (boss) (can) see…'. In full sentences: 부장님도 아시다시피 저는 내일 출장을 가야 돼요 'As you know, I have to go on a business trip tomorrow'; 너도 보다시피 우리 집 상황이 매우 안 좋아 'As you can see, the situation of our house is really not good'.
notes.nuance: ~도 emphasizes that the listener, in addition to the speaker, is already aware of/perceiving the fact - it's specifically about referencing shared or already-known information, not introducing something new.

pattern: N이/가 아니라 ('bukan N, melainkan...')
meaning: Replacing 다 with 라 on 아니다 (giving 아니라) to contrast two clauses - the first noun is NOT something, and the second IS.

notes.formation: [noun1]이/가 아니라 [noun2](이다). 아니라 itself is never conjugated to past/future - the final clause carries the sentence's actual tense.
notes.usage: 그 사람은 학생이 아니라 선생님이에요 'That person is not a student, he is a teacher'; 저것은 사람이 아니라 눈사람이에요 'That is not a person, it is a snowman'; 제가 선생님이 아니라 학생을 도와주는 사람이었어요 'I wasn't a teacher, I was a student helper' (past tense carried by the final clause).
notes.nuance: Be careful not to confuse this with attaching ~라(서) to 아니다 to give a REASON (Lesson 37): 저는 선생님이 아니라(서) 그것을 잘 몰라요 'I don't know that because I'm not a teacher' - a different meaning built from a similar-looking form.

pattern: V/Adj~는 게 아니라 ('bukan..., melainkan...', negasi klausa)
meaning: Describing 것 (usually shortened to 게) with a verb/adjective clause before 아니라, to contrast two entire CLAUSES instead of just two nouns.

notes.formation: [clause]~는 것이 아니라 (usually contracted to ~는 게 아니라) + [contrasting clause].
notes.usage: 저는 밥을 먹는 게 아니라 공부하고 있어요 'I'm not eating, I'm studying'; 그 여자는 예쁜 게 아니라 못생겼어요 'That girl isn't pretty, she is ugly'; 저는 인색한 게 아니라 그냥 돈이 없어요 'I'm not cheap, I just don't have any money'; 길이 울퉁불퉁한 게 아니라 네가 운전을 못하는 거야 'It is not that the road is bumpy, it is that you can't drive well'.
notes.nuance: 위하다 ('for the sake of', already adjective-conjugated like 대하다/관하다/의하다/인하다) can combine with this pattern for nuanced sentences: 제가 한국말을 배우고 있는 이유는 저의 여자 친구를 위한 게 아니라 그녀의 부모님을 위한 것이에요 'The reason I am learning Korean is not for my girlfriend, but for her parents' - built from ~는 것, 위하다's attributive 위한, and ~는 게 아니라 together.

pattern: 그게 아니라 ('bukan itu maksudnya') dan 다름이 아니라 ('mari kita bahas yang serius')
meaning: 그것이 (contracted 그게) + 아니라 refers back to a prior situation to mean 'it's not that...'; 다름이 아니라 is a formal phrase used to shift from small talk into real business.

notes.formation: 그게 아니라 [correction], placed at the start of a response to something just said. 다름이 아니라 (literally something like 'it's not a difference'), used as a fixed formal transition phrase.
notes.usage: 그게 아니라 나는 너를 그냥 보고 싶어 'It's not that, I just want to see you'; 그게 아니라 저는 돈을 벌어야 돼요 'It's not that, I just need to earn money' (both require prior context to make sense). 다름이 아니라 functions like the English 'alright, let's get to business here' - commonly used by a speaker to shift from personal small talk (with a coworker, client, or boss) into the actual matter at hand.
notes.nuance: 그게 아니라 always needs surrounding context to be understood, since it's directly correcting some assumption or statement the listener just made. 다름이 아니라 is specifically reserved for formal situations, marking a clear pivot point in a conversation.

pattern: V~기로 하다 ('memutuskan untuk...')
meaning: 'To decide to' - nominalizing a verb clause with ~기 (Lesson 29), attaching ~(으)로, then predicating with 하다 - the verb before ~기로 always stays in the present tense, while 하다 itself is usually conjugated to the past (since the decision already happened).

notes.formation: [verb]~기로 하다/했다. The verb before ~기로 is always present tense, even describing something decided for the past or future.
notes.usage: 제가 친구를 공원에서 만나기로 했어요 'I decided to meet my friend in the park'; 우리가 내일 만나기로 했어요 'We decided to meet tomorrow'; 우리가 어제 만나기로 했어요 'We decided to meet yesterday' (만나 stays present-tense in both). Can be negated: 지금부터 그 친구를 신용하지 않기로 했어요 'From now on I decided to not trust that friend'.
notes.nuance: This is treated almost like a fixed idiom due to its simple, consistent translation - the key thing to remember is that the verb before ~기로 never changes tense; only 하다 (typically in the past, since the decision itself already occurred) carries the sentence's timing.

pattern: ~기로 결정하다 (substitusi 결정하다 untuk 하다) + digabung dengan ~는데 untuk alasan
meaning: 결정하다 ('to decide') can substitute for plain 하다 with the same meaning; ~는데 (Lessons 76-77) is commonly used before ~기로 하다 to give the background/reason for the decision.

notes.formation: [verb]~기로 결정하다 (substitute for 하다). [reason clause]~는데 + [verb]~기로 했다 (giving context for the decision).
notes.usage: 서울에 지하철로 가기로 결정했어요 'We decided that we would take the subway to Seoul'. With ~는데: 어제 먹어 봤는데 너무 싱거워서 소금을 조금 넣기로 했어요 'I tried it yesterday, and it was too bland so I decided to put a bit of salt into it'; 저는 어제 학생들에게 설명했는데 내용이 조금 애매해서 다시 하기로 했어요 'I explained it to the students yesterday, but the content is a little ambiguous so I decided to explain it again'.
notes.nuance: 결정하다 is simply a more explicit synonym for 하다 in this construction, with identical meaning. Using ~는데 beforehand is a natural, common way to set up WHY a decision was made, connecting the reasoning clause smoothly into the decision clause.

meaning: When a decision was originally made but ultimately didn't happen, ~기로 했는데 (with 원래, 'originally') is often best translated 'supposed to do'.

notes.formation: 원래 [verb]~기로 했는데 [what actually happened instead].

pattern: V/Adj~다가 (waktu sekarang: tindakan terhenti/terputus oleh peristiwa berikutnya)
meaning: 'While' - when the verb/adjective before ~다가 is in the present tense, it indicates that action was halted/cut short, and the following clause states what caused the interruption (not the completed result of the first action).

notes.formation: [verb/adjective stem]다가 + [interrupting event].
notes.usage: 학생은 열심히 공부하다가 잠이 들었어요 'The student studied hard and then fell asleep' (studying was cut short by falling asleep); 요리를 하다가 주방에서 불이 나서 급하게 가스레인지를 껐어요 'I was cooking, and then a fire started in the kitchen so I urgently turned off the stove'; 날씨가 춥다가 갑자기 더워졌어요 'The weather was cold, and then suddenly became hot' (adjective example).
notes.nuance: It would be INCORRECT to use ~다가 when the first action finishes as planned (재료를 다 섞다가 드세요 is wrong; use ~고/~아/어서 instead: 재료를 다 섞고/섞어서 드세요) - ~다가 specifically requires an unanticipated interruption, not a normal completion. The interrupting action is usually something the SAME subject does, and this is typically included explicitly unless clear from context.

examples.meaning: While sleeping in the bedroom, he suddenly passed away.

quiz.explanation: ~다가 requires an unanticipated interruption, not a normal planned completion.

pattern: V/Adj~았/었다가 (waktu lampau: tindakan selesai sebelum tindakan berikutnya dimulai)
meaning: Adding ~았/었 before ~다가 shows the first action was COMPLETED before the second action started - unlike bare ~다가, the end result of the completed action is what appears in the following clause.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective stem]~았/었다가 + [resulting action, after completion].
notes.usage: 요리를 했다가 먹을 사람이 없어서 다 버렸어요 'I cooked, and because there was nobody to eat the food, I threw it all away' (cooking finished, then the food was thrown away). Compare 가다: 저는 학교에 가다가 친구 집에 갔어요 'While going to school, I was interrupted and went to a friend's house instead' (never arrived at school) vs 저는 학교에 갔다가 친구 집에 갔어요 'I went to school, and then went to my friend's house' (arrived at school first, then went on). 해물을 먹었다가 토했어요 'I ate seafood and then threw up'; 저는 그녀한테 데이트를 하자고 했다가 거절당했어요 'I asked her out, and then I was rejected'.
notes.nuance: This is the crucial past-tense contrast with plain ~다가: with ~다가, the first action never finishes (interrupted); with ~았/었다가, the first action DOES finish, and the second clause is simply the next thing that happened as a RESULT, not an interruption.

pattern: 있다가 ('nanti/sebentar lagi', dan N + 있다가 untuk jangka waktu)
meaning: ~다가 attached to 있다 gives 있다가, almost synonymous with 'later' (literally 'after being here/after this') - can stand alone, or be preceded by a time duration to say 'X later'.

notes.formation: 있다가 alone, or [time duration] 있다가.
notes.usage: Person 1: 언제 가고 싶어요? 'When do you want to go?' -> Person 2: 있다가 'Later'. 저는 조금 있다가 해산물을 먹으러 갈 거예요 'I will go eat seafood a little bit later'. With time: 10분 있다가 나가자! 'Let's leave in 10 minutes!'; 우리는 아마 1년 있다가 결혼할 것 같아요 'We will probably get married in a year'.
notes.nuance: 조금 is commonly placed before 있다가 to specifically mean 'just a little bit later', while a specific time duration (10분, 1년, etc.) placed before it indicates exactly how much later something will happen.

pattern: ~다가 untuk sebab-akibat (kausalitas tersirat, tidak langsung seperti ~아/어서)
meaning: ~다가 can also mean 'because', but unlike ~아/어서/~기 때문에/~(으)니까, there's usually no DIRECT causal link stated - instead, it's implied that something ABOUT doing the first action led to the second.

notes.formation: [verb]다가 + [resulting event], with a looser causal connection than ~아/어서.
notes.usage: 제가 빨리 걷다가 발가락을 부딪혔어요 'I was walking fast and then (something about walking fast) stubbed my toe' vs the more direct 제가 빨리 걸어서 발가락을 부딪혔어요 'Because I was walking fast I stubbed my toe' (a clear, sole cause). More: 눈길을 걷다가 넘어졌어요 'I was walking on a snowy road, and something about that caused me to fall'; 친구만 믿다가 결국 가족을 잃었어요 'I only trusted my friend, and something about that eventually caused me to lose my family'.
notes.nuance: 학생은 열심히 공부하다가 잠이 들었어요 is genuinely ambiguous between 'the student studied hard, then (something about that) caused him to fall asleep' (cause-effect) and 'while studying hard, he fell asleep' (interruption) - but as the author notes, in practice this distinction rarely matters, since both readings convey essentially the same underlying event sequence, and context resolves any real ambiguity.

pattern: N에다가 (menekankan tempat, ~다가 ditempel ke ~에)
meaning: Attaching ~다가 to the location particle ~에 for extra emphasis, with no meaning change from ~에 alone.

notes.formation: [place noun]에다가, freely interchangeable with plain ~에.
notes.usage: 밥을 냉장고에 넣어 = 밥을 냉장고에다가 넣어 'Put the rice in the fridge'; 유리에 붙여 주세요 = 유리에다가 붙여 주세요 'Please stick it on the glass'; 재료를 그릇에 섞어 = 재료를 그릇에다가 섞어 'Mix the ingredients in the bowl'.
notes.nuance: This is a purely stylistic addition with no functional difference from plain ~에 - it's simply a more emphatic-sounding way of marking the same location.

pattern: N와/과 비교하다 ('membandingkan N', kata kerja, berbeda dari ~보다)
meaning: 'To compare' - unlike ~보다 (Lesson 19, a particle attached directly to a noun), 비교하다 is a real verb conjugated at a clause's end, with the compared noun marked ~와/과/랑/이랑/하고.

notes.formation: 저를 [noun]와/과 비교하다. Combined with ~(으)면 (Lesson 43): [noun]와/과 비교하면, 'if you compare to...'.
notes.usage: 저를 그 사람과 비교하지 마세요 'Don't compare me with that person'; 저의 시어머니가 저를 자기 딸과 항상 비교해요 'My mother-in-law always compares me to her daughter'. With ~(으)면: 저는 그 사람과 비교하면 더 똑똑해 보여요 'If you compare me to that person, I look smarter' (≈ 저는 그 사람보다 더 똑똑해 보여요 using ~보다).
notes.nuance: 비교하다 comes from the Hanja 比 ('to compare') - the same character appears in the related word 비하다, covered in the next pattern.

pattern: N에 비해(서) ('dibandingkan dengan N')
meaning: 비하다 (from the same Hanja 比 as 비교하다) functions like 대하다/위하다/관하다 - attach ~에 to a noun, then 비해(서), to compare that noun with something else.

notes.formation: [noun]에 비해(서) + [comparison].
notes.usage: 우리 아들은 또래에 비해 훨씬 똑똑해요 'Our son is much smarter compared to his peers'; 한국어는 영어에 비해 모음이 더 많아요 'There are more vowels in Korean compared to English'; 동물의 어금니가 앞니에 비해 더 강해요 'The molars of animals are stronger compared to their front teeth'.
notes.nuance: 비하다 belongs to the same family of Hanja-based comparison/reference words as 대하다 (Lesson 13), 위하다 (Lesson 13), and 관하다 (Lesson 34) - all attach ~에 to a noun before their own specific meaning-adding word.

pattern: Angka + 배 ('kali lipat', urutan besaran)
meaning: 배 acts as a counter for orders of magnitude ('times'), using pure Korean numbers like any other counter.

notes.formation: [pure Korean number] 배 + 더 [adjective]: 두 배 더 강하다 'twice as strong'. ~(으)로 can optionally be added with no meaning change: 두 배로 더.
notes.usage: 저는 저의 남동생보다 두 배 더 강해요 'I am twice as strong as my younger brother'; 이 자판기가 편의점보다 식품을 세 배 더 비싸게 팔아요 'This vending machine sells food for three times the price of a convenience store'. The comparison target can be omitted when comparing to an implied original situation: 그 동안 집값은 열 배 비싸졌어요 'During that time the price of houses went up ten fold'. Decimals use 점 ('point'): 그 주식 가격은 2.5배로 올랐어요 'That stock's price went up 2.5 fold'.
notes.nuance: Since 배 counts something (orders of magnitude), the preceding number must be the native Korean counting number (두, 세, 네...), not the Sino-Korean number, following the same rule as all other Korean counters.

examples.hangul: 우리 학교 강당은 제가 다녔던 중학교 강당에 비해 두 배 더 넓어요

pattern: Pecahan Korea (N분의 M, penyebut disebut lebih dulu)
meaning: Korean fractions are said denominator-first (with 분의 in between), counter-intuitively for English speakers - as either the object or subject of a sentence, using Sino-Korean numbers.

notes.formation: [denominator]분의 [numerator]: 2분의 1 'one half'; 4분의 1 'one quarter'; 5분의 2 'two fifths'. 분 comes from Hanja 分 ('part/division'), so 4분의 1 literally means 'one part of four'. Sino-Korean numbers are used (일, 이, 삼...). ~의 is pronounced 에 here.
notes.usage: As object: 저는 그 영화의 3분의 1을 봤어요 'I watched one third of that movie'; 화가가 전체 그림의 4분의 1을 벽에 그렸어요 'The painter painted one quarter of the whole painting on the wall'. As subject: 우유의 성분의 1/5은 물이에요 'One fifth of the components of milk is water'; 요즘에 학생의 3분의 1은 그 필통을 가지고 있어요 'These days, one third of students have that pencil case'.
notes.nuance: When referring to a fraction OF a noun, the fraction is usually placed after the noun with ~의 attached to the noun (사람의 2분의 1 'one half of people'); it's also grammatically possible to place the fraction first with ~의 attached to it instead (2분의 1의 사람), though this is less common.

pattern: Pecahan + ~만큼 ('sebesar pecahan...', membandingkan besaran)
meaning: Describing a fraction with the thing being compared to (using ~의), then attaching ~만큼 (Lesson 72) to express a comparison by that fractional amount.

notes.formation: [comparison target]의 [fraction]만큼.
notes.usage: 저는 제 친구 용돈의 1/2만큼 받아요 'I get half the amount of allowance as my friend' (though 반 'half' would be more natural than the fraction for exactly one-half). Equivalent restated: 제가 받는 용돈은 제 친구가 받는 용돈의 2분의 1이에요 'The allowance I receive is half of what my friend receives'; or with 배: 저의 친구는 저보다 용돈을 두 배 더 받아요 'My friend gets twice the allowance that I get'. notes.nuance: Careful with the math: '4분의 1만큼 싸다' means 25% CHEAPER (a quarter less in price), which is mathematically equivalent to saying the price IS '4분의 3' (three-quarters) of the comparison price - these two fractions describe the same relationship from different angles, which can be confusing but is worth double-checking in context.

pattern: V/Adj/이다~잖아(요) ('kau tahu kan.../jangan lupa...', menegaskan fakta yang seharusnya sudah diketahui pendengar)
meaning: Attached to the end of a sentence, ~잖아(요) asserts that the listener already knows (or should already know) the fact being stated - loosely 'as you know/don't forget that...', used when talking to someone who shares or should share this knowledge.

notes.formation: Attached directly to a verb/adjective/이다 stem at the very end of a sentence - no further grammar can be added after ~잖아(요).
notes.usage: 맞잖아요! 'I told you it was correct! You should have known!' (said after winning a debate, e.g. about Canada's capital being Ottawa); 내일은 토요일이잖아요! 'You should know that tomorrow is Saturday!' (reminding a friend of shared context before making a plan); 나는 돈이 없잖아! 'Don't forget that I don't have any money!' (after having already told the listener this earlier); 그거를 거기다가 버리지 마! 플라스틱을 재활용해야 되잖아 'Don't throw that there! You should know that we have to recycle plastics' (reminding a child of something taught many times before).
notes.nuance: The key requirement is that the listener already possesses (or should possess) the stated knowledge - ~잖아(요) is used to remind/assert this shared fact, often as background before telling a longer story, or as a pointed reminder. It's also commonly attached to 맞다 to assert 'I told you so' after being proven right in a disagreement.

pattern: ~잖아(요) bisa terkesan kasar ke yang dihormati (gunakan ~알다시피 sebagai gantinya)
meaning: Because ~잖아(요) asserts that the listener should already know something, it can come across as rude or confrontational ('I TOLD you so!') when used with elders or highly-respected people - ~알다시피 (Lesson 88) is a safer, more polite alternative in those situations.

notes.formation: Compare: [statement]~잖아요 (can sound assertive/rude to a superior) vs [superior]도 아시다시피 [statement] (polite, Lesson 88's honorific 'as you know').
notes.usage: 제가 어제 아팠잖아요! 'Don't forget/You should know that I was sick yesterday!' (potentially rude if said to a boss) vs 부장님도 아시다시피 저는 어제 아파서 회사에 늦게 왔어요 'As you know, I was sick yesterday, so I was late' (much more polite, safer with a boss).
notes.nuance: Despite this caution, ~잖아(요) is heard constantly in everyday speech without sounding angry or rude in most contexts - the concern specifically applies to speaking with elders or people deserving high respect, where its inherently assertive undertone ('I'm telling you that you should already know this') can land poorly.

pattern: 있잖아(요) ('begini...', pembuka kalimat tetap saat mencari kata-kata)
meaning: ~잖아(요) attached to 있다 forms a fixed unit (not the separate meanings of 있다 + 잖아요 combined), commonly used at the start of a sentence when someone is gathering their thoughts or signaling they have something to say.

notes.formation: 있잖아/있잖아요, treated as a single fixed conversational opener.
notes.usage: 있잖아… 오늘은 재활용을 해야 되는 날이야 'So, you know,… Today is the day to do recycling'.
notes.nuance: Unlike the literal-meaning combinations seen elsewhere in Korean, 있잖아(요) should not be parsed as '있다 (to have/exist) + 잖아(요) (you should know)' - it functions as its own fixed phrase, roughly equivalent to English conversational fillers like 'so, you know...' or 'um, so...'.

pattern: V/Adj/이다~거든(요) ('karena...', memberi tahu pendengar informasi yang belum diketahuinya)
meaning: 'Because' - similar to ~아/어서, but specifically used when the sentence is providing NEW information the listener doesn't already know - essentially the opposite function of ~잖아(요) (Lesson 93). Easy to attach since ~ㄱ triggers no irregulars.

notes.formation: [stem]거든(요), for present-tense reasons. Past: [stem]~았/었거든(요). Future: [stem]~ㄹ/을 것이거든(요) (often contracted to ~거거든요, since 것 shortens to 거 and 이 can drop).
notes.usage: 마카다미아를 왜 이렇게 많이 가져왔어? 'Why did you take so many macadamia nuts?' -> 마카다미아를 좋아하거든! 'Because I like macadamia nuts!'; 바닥이 춥거든 'Because the floor is cold'. Past: 물속에 안 들어갔어. 너무 무서웠거든 'I didn't go into the water. Because it was too scary'. Future: 내일 못 가겠어. 친구를 만나러 서울에 갈 거거든 'Tomorrow I won't be able to go. Because I'm meeting a friend in Seoul'.
notes.nuance: This is the mirror opposite of ~잖아(요): while ~잖아(요) asserts the listener ALREADY knows a fact, ~거든(요) is used to TEACH the listener something they don't yet know - the reason being given is genuinely new information to them.

pattern: ~거든(요) sebagai pembuka kalimat berikutnya ('begini,..., jadi...')
meaning: Since ~거든(요) inherently signals new information for the listener, a sentence ending in it commonly sets up context for what's said next - the following statement now makes sense because of the newly-provided reason.

notes.formation: [reason clause]~거든(요). [following statement that now makes sense].
notes.usage: 제가 캐나다 사람이거든요. 그래서 프랑스어도 할 수 있어요 'I'm Canadian. So, I can speak French as well' (without the first sentence, the listener wouldn't know why you can speak French); 어제 일을 다 했거든요. 그래서 오늘 할 일이 없어요 'I finished all of my work yesterday. Therefore, I have nothing to do today'; 오늘 친구를 만나러 서울 갈 거거든요. 혹시 같이 갈래요? 'I'm going to Seoul to meet a friend tonight. Would you like to go together?'
notes.nuance: The overall feeling combines 'providing new information' with a slight 'because' meaning that sets up the following sentence - there's no perfect English translation, but the core function is giving the listener a fact they need in order for the next statement to make sense.

pattern: ~거든 ('kalau/saat...', jarang, dengan klausa kedua perintah/saran) dan 아니거든! ('bukan begitu!')
meaning: A less common usage where ~거든 means 'if/when' (similar to ~(으)면), typically when the second clause is an imperative or suggestion; also, ~거든 commonly attaches to 아니다 to express disagreement, especially among younger speakers.

notes.formation: [condition]거든 + [imperative/suggestion]. Disagreement: 아니거든!
notes.usage: 바지가 너무 크면 교환해! = 바지가 너무 크거든 교환해! 'If the pants are too big, change them!'; 숙제를 다 하면 알려 줘! = 숙제를 다 하거든 알려줘! 'Let me know when you are done your homework!' Disagreement: Person 1: 그 남자가 너무 잘생겼어 'That man is so handsome' -> Person 2: 아니거든! 'No he's not!'
notes.nuance: This conditional usage of ~거든 is not very common but does appear occasionally (including on the TOPIK test, as an alternative to ~(으)면 in imperative-ending sentences). The 아니거든! disagreement usage is distinctly a younger-generation habit, typically used to assertively push back on something just said.

pattern: V/Adj~도록 ('supaya/agar...', satu makna dasar dengan 5 terjemahan berbeda)
meaning: ~도록 has a single underlying Korean meaning - 'causing a situation to occur' - that gets rendered into several different English translations depending on context; the first and most basic is 'so that/in order to', functionally identical to ~게 (Lesson 59) but more formal/written.

notes.formation: [clause]~도록 + [main action that causes it].
notes.usage: 아침에 일찍 일어나도록 어젯밤에 일찍 잤어요 'I went to bed early last night in order to get up early in the morning'; 버스를 놓치지 않도록 정류장으로 뛰어 갔어요 'I ran to the bus stop so that I would not miss the bus'; 학생들이 알아들을 수 있도록 천천히 말했어요 'I spoke slowly so that the students could understand me'. This meaning is very commonly seen on Korean signs: 다른 승객들이 불편하지 않도록 신문을 읽지 마세요 'Please don't read a newspaper on the train so that other passengers are not uncomfortable'.
notes.nuance: ~도록 can be swapped for ~게 in all these sentences with no meaning change, but ~도록 is favored in formal writing and signage, while ~게 is more natural in everyday speech. All five 'translations' of ~도록 in this lesson share the same core Korean function: a clause is being 'caused to occur' by the main action.

pattern: V~도록 하겠습니다/할게요 ('saya akan pastikan...') + V~도록 하세요 (perintah)
meaning: When ~도록 attaches to a verb followed by 하다 in the future tense, it indicates the speaker will make sure that action happens (formal, workplace-appropriate); the same construction as a command tells a listener to make sure something is done.

notes.formation: Statement of intent: [verb]~도록 하겠습니다/할게요/할 거예요. Command: [verb]~도록 하세요.
notes.usage: 내일까지 하도록 하겠습니다 'I will (be sure to) do it by tomorrow'; 제가 지금부터 열심히 일하도록 할게요 'I will (be sure to) work hard from now on'. As a command: 쿠키를 사각형 모양이 되도록 만들어 주세요 'Be sure to make the cookies into a square shape'; 기한 내에 서류를 갖춰서 학과에 내도록 하세요 'Be sure to prepare the documents within the timeframe and submit them to the department'; 소득세를 기한 안에 내지 않으면 벌금이 부과되기 때문에 꼭 3월 31일까지 내도록 하세요 'If you don't pay your taxes in time, a fine will be imposed, so be sure to pay by March 31st'.
notes.nuance: Both the intent and command versions still fit the same core ~도록 idea: the clause before ~도록 is being 'caused to occur' - by the speaker's own future effort in the intent version, or by the listener's compliance in the command version. This carries a formal, workplace-appropriate 'I will be sure to' feeling rather than a blunt future statement.

examples.meaning: I will (be sure to) prepare the documents and give them to you in the afternoon.

pattern: ~도록 하다/시키다 (masa lalu: 'membuat/memaksa') + ~도록 (sampai titik/tingkat)
meaning: ~도록 attached to a verb, followed by a past-tense causative verb (하다 or 시키다), refers to a command that was already given ('made/forced someone to do'); ~도록 can also express doing an action to a certain extent ('to the point of').

notes.formation: Causative/command reference: [verb]~도록 했다/시켰다. Extent: [verb]~도록 + [main action].
notes.usage: 부장님은 모든 직원들이 회의에 참석하도록 했어요 'The boss made all of the workers come to the meeting'; 부모님은 제가 대학교에 진학하도록 강요하셨어요 'My parents forced me to go to University'; 선생님이 학생들을 동그라미 모양으로 서도록 했어요 'The teacher made the students stand in a circle'. Extent: 선수는 숨을 못 쉬도록 빨리 뛰었어요 'The athlete ran fast to the extent that he couldn't breathe'; 제가 김치를 질리도록 먹었어요 'I ate kimchi to the extent that I was sick of it'; 우리는 발이 아프도록 걸어 다녔어요 'We walked around to the point that our feet hurt'.
notes.nuance: Even these seemingly different translations still fit the same core ~도록 principle: the clause before ~도록 is 'caused to occur' - by a command from a superior (make/force), or as an extreme end-result of doing the main action (to the point of). The same sentence can sometimes carry BOTH translations validly (e.g. a mask 'making' victims unable to recognize someone can be read as either 'so that' or 'to make'), reinforcing that the underlying Korean meaning is unified even when English needs different words.

examples.hangul: 선생님이 학생들을 동그라미 모양으로 서도록 했어요
examples.romaja: seonsaengnimi haksaengdeureul donggeurami moyangeuro seodorok haesseoyo

pattern: V/Adj~지/죠 ('...kan?', mengubah pernyataan jadi pertanyaan penegasan)
meaning: Attached to a verb/adjective stem, ~지 (informal) or ~죠 (formal) turns a statement into a tag question, similar to Canadian English 'eh?' or 'isn't it?' - implying the speaker already suspects/knows the answer and is reconfirming.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective stem]지/죠? Past: [stem]~았/었지/죠?. Future: [stem]~ㄹ/을 거지/죠? No irregulars occur since ~ㅈ triggers none.
notes.usage: 날씨가 추워요? 'Is it cold?' (genuinely doesn't know) vs 날씨가 춥죠? 'It is cold, isn't it?' (reconfirming a belief). More: 선생님! 바쁘죠? 'Teacher! You are busy, aren't you?'; 어제 학교에 안 갔죠? 'You didn't go to school yesterday, did you?' (past); 선생님도 갈 거죠? 'Teacher, you are going too, right?' (future).
notes.nuance: This also works with question-word questions (카드를 어디에 두었죠? 'Where did you put the card, again?'), where the English 'isn't it' translation becomes illogical, but the same underlying feeling remains: the speaker suspects they once knew the answer (or half-remembers it) and is softly reconfirming, rather than asking a completely fresh question.

examples.meaning: That person's family has a lot of wealth, right?
You speak Korean well now, don't you?
You still haven't decided yet, have you?

quiz.question: Perbedaan antara '날씨가 추워요?' dan '날씨가 춥죠?' adalah...

Yang kedua hanya untuk waktu lampau
quiz.explanation: ~죠?/지? implies the speaker already suspects/knows the answer and is reconfirming, unlike a genuine question.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: You didn't go to school yesterday, did you? -> 어제 학교에 [BLANK]

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'Teacher, you are going too, right?'

pattern: ~지 dengan kata tanya, bertanya ke diri sendiri ('...ya?/apa ya?')
meaning: ~지 naturally works for asking oneself a question when a question word is present (e.g. 'what should I eat again?'), but sounds illogical asking oneself WITHOUT a question word - the latter only makes sense directed at someone else.

notes.formation: [question word] + [verb/adjective]지?, self-directed.
notes.usage: 내가 뭐 먹었지? 'What did I eat again?'; 선생님이 어디 갔지? 'Where did the teacher go?'; 그 사람이 누구였지? 'Who was that person?'; 뭐 하지? 'What should I do?'; 어디 가지? 'Where should I go?'. WITHOUT a question word, self-directed use is illogical: 밥을 먹지? ('I am eating, right?' - makes no sense asking yourself) is only natural when directed at someone else.
notes.nuance: This mirrors ~ㄹ/을까 (Lesson 63): both can express asking oneself a question, but ~지 without a question word inherently implies asking ANOTHER person to confirm something, which is illogical when directed at oneself - only the question-word version makes sense as genuine self-talk.

examples.meaning: What is the difference between a verb and adjective?
How should/can I change the wheel?
Who should I not meet? (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: Kenapa '밥을 먹지?' tidak logis ditujukan ke diri sendiri?
options: Karena tidak ada kata tanya, jadi seolah bertanya ke orang lain untuk konfirmasi
Karena 먹다 tidak bisa dipakai dengan ~지
quiz.explanation: Without a question word, ~지 inherently implies asking someone else to confirm, illogical when self-directed.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: Ah, where did I put my card again? -> 아~ 카드를 어디 [BLANK]

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate, asking yourself: 'Who should I meet?'

pattern: ~지/죠! ('tentu saja!', jawaban)
meaning: Attached to a verb/adjective/이다 as a response to a question, ~지/~죠 gives a feeling of 'of course!' - typically restating the verb/adjective just used in the question.

notes.formation: [same verb/adjective/이다 as the question]지/죠!
notes.usage: 내일 갈 거야!? 'Are you going tomorrow?' -> 갈 거지 'Yeah, of course I'm going' (지 attached to 이다/것이다's future form); 배고파? 'Are you hungry?' -> 배고프지! 'Of course I'm hungry!'; 소득세를 안 내? 'You don't pay income tax?' -> 내지! 'Of course I pay it!'. Also commonly used with 당연하다 (Lesson 79) instead of restating the question's verb: 배고파요? -> 당연하지!! 'Of course!!'
notes.nuance: When used this way, ~지 is much more common than ~죠, since this usage is inherently informal, and it wouldn't make sense to pair an informal function with the formal ~죠. Context and rising/falling tone of voice distinguish this 'of course!' usage from the earlier tag-question usage.

examples.meaning: Are you hungry? Of course I'm hungry!

examples.hangul: 내년에 내가 인터넷고등학교로 갈 거야. 거기서 직접 수업을 안 해요? 하지!

pattern: ~지/죠 menggantikan 하다/되다 setelah ~아/어야 ('harus...!', informal)
meaning: ~지 (or less commonly ~죠) can substitute for 하다/되다 entirely within ~아/어야 하다/되다 (Lesson 46's 'must'), giving a colloquial way of insisting something must be done.

notes.formation: [verb]~아/어야지/죠! (replacing 하다/되다 entirely).
notes.usage: 저는 지금 가야 돼요 'I must go now' (standard) -> 나는 지금 가야지! 'I must go now!' (colloquial); 열심히 공부를 해야지! 'You need to study hard!'; 사람들이 크리스마스에 크리스마스트리를 만들어야지! 'People need to put up a Christmas tree for Christmas!'
notes.nuance: This replacement is fairly colloquial; ~지 is much more common in this role than ~죠, which is only really used with someone you're very close to but who is older, when you want slightly more formality than bare ~지 without going all the way to a fully formal register.

examples.meaning: You need to study hard!

quiz.explanation: ~죠 is rarely used here, mainly with someone close but older, for slightly more formality than ~지.

pattern: V~게 되다 ('akhirnya jadi...', di luar kendali, terasa rendah hati)
meaning: 'To end up' - combining ~게 ('to be made to happen', Lesson 56) with 되다 ('to become') to indicate a situation was 'made to become' a certain way, happening out of one's control, almost by chance or fate.

notes.formation: [verb]~게 되다/되었다.
notes.usage: 저는 그 회사에 취직했어요 'I got a job at that company' (sounds like boasting about one's own achievement) vs 저는 그 회사에 취직하게 되었어요 'I ended up getting a job at that company' (sounds more humble, implying it happened without much personal influence). More: 막차를 타게 되었어요 'I ended up taking the last train'; 동생이 죽은 후에 제가 우울증을 겪게 되었어요 'After my brother died I ended up suffering from depression'; 무슨 요일에 갈지 결정을 못해서 그냥 토요일에 가게 됐어요 'We couldn't decide what day to go on, so we just ended up going on Saturday'.
notes.nuance: The key feeling ~게 되다 adds is that the outcome happened without the subject having much control or influence over it - this is why it can make a sentence sound more humble compared to a plain, direct statement of the same fact, since the speaker isn't taking full credit/responsibility for what happened.

~게 되다 hanya dipakai untuk kalimat negatif

pattern: ~게 되다 tidak alami dengan kata sifat (pakai ~아/어지다) + 어쩌다 (kata perasaan)
meaning: While ~게 되다 can grammatically attach to adjectives, it sounds unnatural there - ~아/어지다 (Lesson 18) conveys the same meaning much more naturally; 어쩌다 ('by chance') is a near-meaningless feeling-word commonly paired with ~게 되다 sentences.

notes.formation: Adjective + ~게 되다 (unnatural) vs adjective + ~아/어지다 (natural). 어쩌다 placed early in a sentence ending in ~게 되다.
notes.usage: 날씨가 춥게 되었어요 (unnatural) vs 날씨가 추워졌어요 'The weather got cold' (natural); 그 여자가 뚱뚱하게 되었어요 (unnatural) vs 그 여자가 뚱뚱해졌어요 'That girl got fat' (natural). With 어쩌다: 어쩌다 그녀를 버스에서 보게 되었어요 'I ended up seeing her on the bus'; 어쩌다 시험을 합격하게 되었어요 'I ended up passing the exam'.
notes.nuance: 어쩌다 belongs to the same family of feeling-adverbs as 만약 (Lesson 43) and 어쩌면 (Lesson 59) - its dictionary meaning ('accidentally/by chance') has little independent force outside sentences like these, where it simply reinforces the 'out of one's control' feeling already carried by ~게 되다.

pattern: N뿐(이다) ('hanya N', tidak ada apa-apa lagi selain N) + N뿐만 아니라 ('bukan hanya N, tapi juga...')
meaning: 뿐 attached directly to a noun (as a particle) means 'nothing other than' that noun - 'only/just'; adding ~만 아니라 extends this to 'not only N, but also...'.

notes.formation: [noun]뿐(이다). Extended: [noun]뿐만 아니라 [other noun]도.
notes.usage: 내가 원하는 유일한 것은 너뿐이야 'The only thing I want is you'; 그 창고에 있는 것은 짝퉁뿐이에요 'The only thing in that warehouse is fakes'. With ~만 아니라: 너뿐만 아니라 나도 경기에서 패했어 'Not only you, but I also lost the match'; 커피뿐만 아니라 간식도 샀어요 'Not only did I buy coffee, but I also bought snacks'; 가족뿐만 아니라 친구들도 사랑해야 돼요 'Not only family, but you also need to love your friends too'.
notes.nuance: In this usage, 뿐 functions purely as a particle attached to a noun (not a standalone word) - this is distinct from the pseudo-noun usage covered in the next pattern, where 뿐 is described by a verb/adjective/이다 clause and carries a different nuance.

quiz.explanation: Attached to a noun, 뿐 functions as a particle meaning 'only/nothing other than'.

pattern: V/Adj/이다~ㄹ/을 뿐(이다) ('hanya sekadar...', tidak ada yang istimewa/khusus)
meaning: Describing the pseudo-noun 뿐 with a verb/adjective/이다 clause (via ~ㄹ/을) creates a different nuance than N뿐 - not 'literally nothing else exists', but 'there's nothing special/particular about this'.

notes.formation: [clause]~ㄹ/을 뿐(이다). Past clause: ~았/었을 뿐(이다).
notes.usage: 집에 있는 음식을 다 먹어서 이제 먹을 수 있는 게 라면뿐이에요 'I ate everything in the house, so the only thing left is just ramen' (literally nothing else remains, N뿐). vs 물을 조금 넣었다고 화를 이렇게 많이 내? 그냥 라면일 뿐이야 'I just put a little bit of water in it, why are you so mad? It's just ramen' (nothing special about it, ~ㄹ 뿐). More: 그것은 농담일 뿐이에요 'It's just a joke'; 그것을 사는 것은 돈 낭비일 뿐이에요 'Buying that is just a waste of money'; 저는 그냥 모든 일에 최선을 다 할 뿐이에요 'I just do my best in everything I do'. Past: 저는 하늘을 봤을 뿐이에요 'I was just looking at the sky'; 네가 시키는 대로 했을 뿐이야 'I was just doing as you ordered'.
notes.nuance: The N뿐 and ~ㄹ/을 뿐 versions can both translate as 'just X', but N뿐 asserts nothing else literally exists (a factual state of scarcity), while ~ㄹ/을 뿐 asserts nothing special or significant is going on (a dismissive/minimizing tone), often used to calm someone down or downplay a situation.

examples.hangul: 제가 배우가 되는 것은 꿈일 뿐이에요
examples.romaja: jega baeuga doeneun geoseun kkumil ppunieyo

pattern: ~ㄹ/을 뿐 di tengah kalimat (mendeskripsikan suatu keadaan, tanpa konjugasi lebih lanjut)
meaning: 뿐 can also appear mid-sentence (not just at the end), where it isn't conjugated further and the whole construction describes the state in which a following action is done.

notes.formation: [clause]~ㄹ/을 뿐 + [second clause describing what the subject was NOT doing, or the limited state they remained in].
notes.usage: 그녀는 저를 쳐다봤을 뿐 그냥 앉아 있었어요 'She just sat there staring at me'; 강아지가 저를 쳐다봤을 뿐 도망가지 않았어요 'The dog just sat there staring at me, not running away'; 그 노예가 창문 밖을 봤을 뿐 아무 말도 하지 않았어요 'That slave just looked outside and didn't say anything'; 그 남자는 손톱을 물어뜯을 뿐 전화를 받지 않았어요 'The man didn't answer his phone, and was just biting his fingernails'.
notes.nuance: This mid-sentence use of 뿐 conveys the sense of 'only doing X (and nothing more)' as a way to characterize an ongoing state - typically used to emphasize the limited nature of what the subject was doing, often contrasted with something more significant they were NOT doing.

pattern: V/Adj~ㄹ/을 뿐만 아니라 ('tidak hanya..., tapi juga...')
meaning: Extending the N뿐만 아니라 pattern to verbs/adjectives by attaching ~ㄹ/을 뿐만 아니라, to say 'not only X, but also Y' about an action or description rather than a noun.

notes.formation: [clause]~ㄹ/을 뿐만 아니라 [second clause]도.
notes.usage: 그는 가난할 뿐만 아니라 못생겼어요 'He is not only poor, but ugly'; 그 학생이 친구를 괴롭힐 뿐만 아니라 돈도 뺏어요 'That student doesn't just harass his friend, but he also takes his money'; 이 회사는 집을 제공할 뿐만 아니라 차도 제공해요 'Not only does this company provide housing, but it also provides a car'; 음식이 없을 뿐만 아니라 음식을 살 수 있는 돈도 없어요 'Not only do we not have any food, but we also don't have any money to buy food either'.
notes.nuance: This directly parallels N뿐만 아니라, just applied to a full verb/adjective clause via the ~ㄹ/을 attributive-style attachment already familiar from the pseudo-noun pattern earlier in this lesson - both express 'not only A, but B' at the level of clauses instead of single nouns.

pattern: V~(으)려면 ('kalau bermaksud/ingin...', gabungan ~(으)려고 + ~(으)면)
meaning: 'If one intends to/if one wants to' - a contraction combining ~(으)려고 ('with the intent of', Lesson 32) and ~(으)면 ('if/when', Lesson 43), as if saying '~하려고 하면...'.

notes.formation: [verb]~(으)려면 [second clause, typically ending in ~아/어야 하다, ~이/가 필요하다, or an imperative].
notes.usage: 그렇게 비싼 것을 사려면 돈이 많이 필요해요 'If you intend to buy something that expensive, you need a lot of money'; 서울에 가려면 지하철을 타세요! 'If you intend to go to Seoul, then take the subway!'; 주소를 바꾸려면 직접 와야 돼요 'If you intend to change your address, you should come in person'; 뒷맛을 없애려면 새콤한 것을 먹어야 돼요 'If you want to get rid of that aftertaste, you need to eat something sour'.
notes.nuance: Korean grammatical principles frequently combine and contract like this - ~(으)려면 is a clean example of two already-known pieces fusing into one. Sentences with ~(으)려면 characteristically pair with a second clause expressing necessity or obligation (~아/어야 하다, ~이/가 필요하다) or a direct command, since the natural continuation of 'if you intend to do X' is 'here's what you need to do'.

pattern: 갖다 (singkatan dari 가지다, 'memiliki') + aturan tambahan gramatika yang aneh
meaning: 갖다 is a shortened form of 가지다 ('to have/possess', usually paired with 있다), but because it's an abbreviation with a consonant-final stem (unlike 가지다's vowel-final stem), it can ONLY take grammatical additions that would attach identically to both forms.

notes.formation: 갖다 can take: ~고, ~는, ~지 (consonant-only additions with no vowel-choice ambiguity) -> 갖고, 갖는, 갖지. It CANNOT take: ~아/어, ~았/었다, ~(으)면, ~ㄴ/은 (additions that would differ between 가지다's vowel-final rule and 갖다's consonant-final rule).
notes.usage: 그 나라의 국민들은 다 여권을 갖고 있어야 돼요 'That country's people all need to have a passport' (= 가지고 있어야); 용기를 갖고 힘내세요! 'Get some courage, and good luck!' (= 가지고); 이 문법 현상에 관심을 갖는 사람이 없어요 'There is nobody interested in this grammatical phenomenon' (= 가지는). NEVER 갖아/갖어 or 갖으면/갖면 - these would need 가지다/가지면 instead.
notes.nuance: The rule exists because there's genuine ambiguity about which conjugation rule to follow (갖다's own consonant-final rule, or the original 가지다's vowel-final rule) whenever a vowel is involved - so Korean simply restricts 갖다 to only the additions where both forms would produce the identical result, sidestepping the ambiguity entirely.

pattern: 갖다 + ~다(가) ('ambilkan/bawakan...') dibanding 갔다 (dari 가다)
meaning: ~다(가) (Lesson 91) commonly attaches to 갖다 to mean 'to possess something and then do something with it' - often translated 'give/bring/throw out' - easily confused in pronunciation with 갔다 ('went and came back', from 가다 + past + 다가).

notes.formation: 갖다 주세요 ('please get and give me'); 갖다 버리세요 ('please take and throw out'); 갖다 드릴까요? ('shall I get and give you'). Contrast: 갔다 오다 ('to go and come back', 갔다 = 가다's past stem + ~다가).
notes.usage: 휴지를 갖다 주세요 'Give me a tissue, please' (literally: get a tissue, then give it to me); 쓰레기를 갖다 버리세요 'Throw out the garbage' (take the garbage, then throw it out); 커피를 갖다 드릴까요? 'Would you like some coffee?' (would you like it if I got coffee and gave it to you?). Contrast: 지금 갔다 올게요 'I will go and come back' vs 지금 갖다 줄게요 'I will get it and give it to you'.
notes.nuance: 갖다 (possess-and-act) and 갔다 (go-and-return) sound nearly identical and are frequently confused - the distinguishing factor is meaning: 갔다 always involves the verb 가다 ('to go'), while 갖다 always involves possessing an object and doing something with it.

examples.meaning: Give me a pen, please.
Would you like some coffee?

pattern: V/Adj/이다~아/어 가지고 ('karena...', colloquial)
meaning: 가지다 has another use as a grammar point meaning 'because', by attaching ~아/어 가지고 to the end of the reason clause - very colloquial and common in speech, but rare in writing.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective/이다]~아/어 가지고 + [resulting clause].
notes.usage: 어제 늦게 끝나 가지고 집에 못 갔어요 'Because I finished late yesterday, I couldn't go home'; 우리가 너무 일찍 와 가지고 오랫동안 기다렸어요 'Because we came so early, we had to wait for a long time'; 오늘 날씨가 너무 더워 가지고 약속을 취소했어요 'Because the weather is so hot today, I cancelled my plans'.

pattern: 머무르다(머물다), 서두르다(서둘다), 서투르다(서툴다): singkatan yang tidak bisa memakai tambahan-hanya-vokal
meaning: These shortened verb forms behave like ordinary ㄹ-final verbs (like 팔다) for most additions, but CANNOT take any addition that would force a vowel-only conjugation, since 머무르다 already has its own 르-irregular vowel form.

notes.formation: 머무르다 (full form, follows 르-irregular) has shortened 머물다 (behaves like ㄹ-final 팔다). Consonant-only additions work fine: 머물자, 머물고, 머물겠다, 머물지 않다. Vowel-or-consonant-choice additions also work: 머물면, 머물면서. ㄹ-irregular additions work as expected: 머물 (~ㄹ/을), 머물래, 무무시다, 머무세요. BUT vowel-only additions (~아/어, ~았/었) are INCORRECT: 머물어(요)/머물었어(요) are wrong.
notes.usage: 우리는 부산 중심에 있는 호텔에서 머물렀어요 'We stayed in a hotel in the center of Busan' (using full 머무르다 with 르-irregular ~렀 for past tense, since 머물다 can't take ~았/었 directly); 부산에서 3일 동안 머무르고 서울로 가는 게 어때요? 'What do you think about staying in Busan for three days and then going to Seoul?' The same rule applies to 서두르다(서둘다, 'to hurry') and 서투르다(서툴다, 'to not be good at something').
notes.nuance: The reason for this restriction mirrors 갖다's situation: since 머물다 lacks its own vowel-final way to attach ~아/어 (there's genuine ambiguity about whether to follow the 르-irregular rule of the full form 머무르다, or some other rule for 머물다), Korean simply forbids that combination entirely, forcing speakers to fall back on the full form 머무르다 whenever a vowel-only addition (like past or present tense conjugation) is needed.

quiz.question: Kenapa '머물었어요' salah?
options: Karena tambahan hanya-vokal (~았/었) tidak bisa dipakai pada 머물다 - harus pakai bentuk penuh 머무르다
Karena 머물다 hanya dipakai di masa depan
quiz.explanation: Vowel-only additions like ~았/었 cannot attach to 머물다 - the full form 머무르다 must be used instead.

pattern: V~는/ㄴ/은 척하다 ('berpura-pura melakukan...', 보조동사)
meaning: 'To pretend to' - 척하다 is a 보조동사 ('helping verb', like 있다 in ~고 있다, 보다 in ~아/어 보다, 주다 in ~아/어 주다), attaching after the present-tense ~는 or past-tense ~ㄴ/은 attributive on a verb.

notes.formation: Present: [verb]~는 척하다. Past: [verb]~ㄴ/은 척하다.
notes.usage: 엄마가 오자 저는 설거지하는 척했어요 'As soon as my mom came I pretended to do the dishes' (present attributive, describing an ongoing pretend action); 아이는 엄마 말을 들은 척했어요 'The child pretended he listened to his mother' (past attributive, the listening itself is framed as a completed/past act being pretended). More: 고양이가 야생 개를 보고 누워서 죽은 척했어요 'The cat saw the wild dog and then lay down and pretended to be dead'; 그 이벤트가 마음에 들지 않았지만 감동한 척했어요 'I didn't like that event, but I pretended that it impressed me'.
notes.nuance: This fits the same pattern as other 보조동사 already learned - 척하다 by itself has no standalone use and only functions attached after the attributive form of another verb, adding the specific 'pretending' meaning to that main action.

examples.meaning: He pretended to study when the teacher looked at him.

examples.hangul: 학생이 그 문단을 읽는 척하고 수업 시간 동안 그냥 앉아 있었어요?

examples.romaja: muri heureuneun sorireul an mot deureun cheokhago geunyang jasseoyo
examples.meaning: I did not pretend that I couldn't hear the water flowing and just slept. (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: 척하다 termasuk kategori kata kerja apa?

pattern: Adj/이다~ㄴ/은 척하다 ('berpura-pura menjadi/bersikap...')
meaning: When 척하다 follows an adjective or 이다, it always uses the ~ㄴ/은 attributive (never ~는), since adjectives/이다 follow their own attributive rule, distinct from verbs.

notes.formation: [adjective/이다]~ㄴ/은 척하다.
notes.usage: 여자는 자기 남자 친구한테 귀여운 척했어요 'The girl pretended to be cute to her boyfriend'; 원하는 것을 받으려고 남자는 슬픈 척했어요 'The man pretended to be sad to get what he wanted'; 그 사람이 부자인 척하고 항상 돈의 중요성을 강조했어요 'That person pretended to be rich and always emphasized the importance of money' (이다 example); 저는 파티에서 행복한 척했는데 사실 요즘에 진짜 슬퍼요 'I pretended to be happy at the party, but I am actually really sad these days'.
notes.nuance: This is a direct application of the standard verb/adjective attributive split (already familiar from ~는 것 and throughout the course) to 척하다 - the previous pattern's ~는/~ㄴ/은 tense split only applies to verbs, while adjectives/이다 simply always use ~ㄴ/은 regardless of the overall sentence's tense.

pattern: 아는/모르는 척하다 (idiom), 잘난 척하다 ('sombong') dan 체하다 (alternatif)
meaning: 알다/모르다 commonly pair with 척하다 to mean 'pretend to know/not know'; 잘나다 ('to be great/superior') paired with 척하다 idiomatically means 'to brag'; 체하다 is a common, near-identical alternative to 척하다.

notes.formation: 아는 척하다/모르는 척하다 (알다/모르다's present attributive + 척하다). 잘난 척하다 (fixed idiom for bragging). Alternative: [same attributive]체하다.
notes.usage: 그는 정답을 아는 척했어요 'He pretended that he knew the answer'; 어제 외식했을 때 식당에서 아는 친구를 봤지만 모르는 척했어요 'Yesterday when I went out to eat, I saw a friend I know at the restaurant, but I pretended I don't know him'. Bragging: 그녀는 시험을 잘 보고 친구들한테 잘난 척했어요 'She bragged to her friends after doing well on the exam'; 그 선생님이 서울대를 졸업하셔서 항상 잘난 척하셔요 'That teacher always brags because he graduated from Seoul National University'. Alternative word: 식당에서 교수님은 저를 모른 체했어요 'The professor pretended to not know me in the restaurant'.
notes.nuance: 잘난 척하다 is a fixed idiomatic pairing worth memorizing as a unit, since 잘나다 ('great/superior') combined with 'pretending' naturally produces the sense of 'showing off/bragging'. 체하다 can substitute for 척하다 in essentially all of its uses with no meaningful difference.

pattern: V/Adj~더라도 ('meski/kalaupun...', lebih tegas daripada ~아/어도)
meaning: 'Even if' - a more emphatic alternative to ~아/어도 (Lesson 48's 'regardless of'), specifically stressing that no matter what happens in the first clause, the second clause absolutely still occurs.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective stem]더라도 + [clause that happens regardless].
notes.usage: 날씨가 춥더라도 꼭 오세요 'Even if it is cold, make sure that you come'; 시험을 잘 보더라도 입학하지 못할 것 같아요 'Even if I do well on the exam, I won't be able to get into University'; 그 여자가 오더라도 그녀랑 얘기를 안 할 거예요 'Even if that girl comes, I'm not going to talk to her'; 이 술집은 인기가 많아서 일찍 가더라도 입장할 수 없을지도 몰라요 'That bar is really popular, so even if we go early, I don't know if we will get in'.
notes.nuance: Compared to plain ~아/어도, ~더라도 carries added emphasis/stress on the certainty of the second clause happening no matter what - it's the stronger, more insistent version of the same underlying 'regardless of' idea.

pattern: ~았/었더라도 (waktu lampau: 'meski dulu sudah...', hipotesis lampau)
meaning: Attaching ~더라도 to the past-tense ~았/었 shows that even if something HAD occurred in the past, it wouldn't have changed the outcome - these sentences are hypothetical and typically paired with the ~았/었을 것이다 ending.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective]~았/었더라도 + [hypothetical result]~았/었을 것이다.
notes.usage: 열심히 공부를 했더라도 시험에 떨어졌을 거예요 'Even if I studied really hard for the exam, I would have failed'; 돈이 있었더라도 그 컴퓨터를 사지 않았을 거예요 'Even if I had money, I wouldn't have bought that computer'.
notes.nuance: As already established in Lesson 48 with ~아/어도, sentences using this past-tense hypothetical structure naturally pair with the ~았/었을 것이다 ending, since they're describing an imagined alternate past that didn't actually happen.

pattern: ~았/었더라면/더라도 ~았/었을 텐데(요) ('seandainya..., pasti akan...', hipotesis dengan nuansa penyesalan)
meaning: 텐데 (from the pseudo-noun 터 + 이다 + ~ㄴ데) can substitute for 것이다 in hypothetical ~더라면/~더라도 sentences (Lessons 43, 99), adding a subtle feeling of regret, annoyance, or 'too bad' that plain 것이다 lacks.

notes.formation: ~ㄹ/을 + 터 + 이다 + ~ㄴ데 = ~ㄹ/을 텐데. Replaces 것이다 in: [hypothetical clause]~더라면/더라도 [result]~았/었을 텐데(요).
notes.usage: 날씨가 좋았더라면 저는 공원에 갔을 거예요 = 날씨가 좋았더라면 저는 공원에 갔을 텐데요 'If it were nice out, I would have gone' (텐데 adds a feeling of regret); 날씨가 좋았더라도 저는 공원에 안 갔을 텐데요 'Even if it were nice out, I still wouldn't have gone' (텐데 here feels closer to annoyance). Present tense also works when the second clause is a supposition dependent on the first: 음식이 더 있으면 좋을 텐데 'It would be good if there was more food' (implying 'too bad there isn't more').
notes.nuance: 텐데's meaning is genuinely hard to pin down in words - it's a blend of regret, annoyance, and 'that's too bad', with the specific flavor depending on context. A sentence WITHOUT any natural sense of regret/annoyance (뛰다가 조심하지 않았다면 넘어졌을 거예요 'If I wasn't careful running, I would have fallen') would sound strange with 텐데요 added, since there's nothing to regret about a hypothetical fall that didn't happen.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을 텐데(요) di akhir kalimat ('sepertinya akan...', dugaan dengan nuansa khawatir/kesal)
meaning: Attached at a sentence's end, ~ㄹ/을 텐데(요) expresses a supposition ('I suppose/expect that...'), typically about something the speaker is NOT the acting agent of - compared to ~ㄹ/을 것 같다, it's slightly more confident and carries a subtle worried/annoyed/'too bad' undertone.

notes.formation: [clause]~ㄹ/을 텐데(요).
notes.usage: 비가 올 텐데 'It will probably rain (I suppose that it will rain)'; 날씨가 추울 텐데 'The weather will probably be cold...' (implying mild worry/annoyance about the cold); 그 식당이 이미 닫았을 텐데 'The restaurant is probably already closed' (implying 'too bad, it's probably already closed'); 퇴근시간이라서 길이 막힐 텐데 'The roads will probably be jammed because it is rush hour'.
notes.nuance: Compared to 비가 올 것 같아 ('It will probably rain', Lesson 35), ~ㄹ/을 텐데 conveys slightly MORE certainty (like the difference between 'I might go' and 'I will probably go'), plus a subtle feeling of being worried, annoyed, or thinking 'that's too bad' - depending on context, the same sentence could be read as concern, irritation, or resignation.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을 텐데 / ~ㄹ/을 테니까 di tengah kalimat ('kemungkinan besar..., jadi...')
meaning: ~ㄹ/을 텐데 can also connect two clauses mid-sentence, meaning 'it is probable that... so...' - the second clause is often a suggestion. ~(으)니까 can substitute for the ~ㄴ/은/는데-derived ending to give ~ㄹ/을 테니까, with very similar meaning.

notes.formation: [probable clause]~ㄹ/을 텐데 [suggestion/consequence]. Alternative: [probable clause]~ㄹ/을 테니까 [suggestion/consequence].
notes.usage: 그 식당이 이미 닫았을 텐데 가지 말자 'The restaurant will probably already be closed, so let's not go'; 길이 막힐 텐데 지하철로 가자 = 길이 막힐 테니까 지하철로 가자 'The roads will probably be jammed, so let's take the subway'; 우유가 없을 텐데 하나만 사세요 'We probably don't have any milk, so buy one'. Not always a suggestion: 부장님이 없었을 텐데 그래도 부장님을 만나러 회사에 갔어요? 'The boss probably wasn't there, regardless, did you go to work to meet him?'
notes.nuance: This construction is functionally very similar to combining ~ㄹ/을 것 같다 (Lesson 35) with ~아/어서 (Lesson 36) - 길이 막힐 텐데 지하철로 가자 and 길이 막힐 것 같아서 지하철로 가자 convey essentially the same meaning through different grammatical routes.

pattern: ~ㄹ/을 테니까 ('saya akan..., jadi...', menyatakan niat)
meaning: ~ㄹ/을 텐데 or ~ㄹ/을 테니까 can also express the speaker's own intention to do something, with the second clause reflecting that intent - the author notes ~ㄹ/을 테니까 is more natural and common for this specific usage than ~ㄹ/을 텐데.

notes.formation: [speaker's intended action]~ㄹ/을 테니까 [related second clause].
notes.usage: 지금 갈 테니까 조금 더 기다려 주세요 'I'm going to leave now, so wait just a little bit longer'; 제가 돈을 많이 벌 테니까 걱정하지 마세요 'I am going to earn a lot of money, so don't worry'; 내가 다양한 야채를 살 테니까 야채로 맛있는 것을 만들어 먹자 'I will buy a variety of vegetables, so let's make something delicious with them'. Can also end a sentence incomplete, like ~아/어서: 걱정 마. 내가 돈을 많이 벌 테니까… 'Don't worry. Because I'm going to earn a lot of money…'
notes.nuance: While sources may say both ~ㄹ/을 텐데 and ~ㄹ/을 테니까 are acceptable for expressing intention, the author's personal experience is that ~ㄹ/을 테니까 sounds significantly more natural for this specific purpose - when the acting agent of the sentence is the speaker themselves expressing what they intend to do.
