pattern: Singkatan partikel: 난/넌/날/널, 걸/건 (dan penghilangan partikel sepenuhnya)
meaning: In speech (and writing that mimics speech, like texting or quoted dialogue), ~는/~를 commonly abbreviate to just ~ㄴ/~ㄹ attached to a vowel-final noun - most often seen with 나/너 and 것/거 - and particles can also be dropped entirely when they can be assumed from context.

notes.formation: 나를 -> 날; 너를 -> 널; 나는 -> 난; 너는 -> 넌 (저는 -> 전 also possible but sounds informal). 것/거 + ~를/는 -> 걸/건. Any vowel-final noun could technically abbreviate this way, but it's most common with these words.
notes.usage: 난 어렸을 때 해병이었어 'When I was younger I was a marine'; 넌 누구를 기다리고 있니? 'Who are you waiting for?'; 이건 얼마예요? 'How much is this?'; 그걸 하지 마세요 'Don't do that please!'. Particles can also be dropped entirely: 나는 밥을 먹고 싶어 -> 나 밥 먹고 싶어 'I want to eat (rice)'; 나 이 손목시계 늘 차고 있어 'I always wear a watch'.
notes.nuance: This reflects the broader Korean principle that anything assumable from context doesn't need to be explicitly stated - if the listener can infer the particle is there, omitting or abbreviating it is natural. This is most common in speech, internet messaging (Facebook, Kakao), and literary dialogue meant to mimic real speech - not in standard formal writing.

pattern: 그러니까 ('itu masalahnya!'/'benar sekali!', berdiri sendiri, dan 'itulah kenapa...' terhubung ke klausa)
meaning: 그러니까 (from 그렇다 + ~(으)니까) is best used alone after someone states an opinion/fact, meaning 'That's the thing!'/'I know, right?!' - it can also connect to a following clause to mean 'that is why...', similar to 그래서.

notes.formation: 그러니까! (standalone agreement). 그러니까 [clause] (connected, meaning 'that's why').
notes.usage: Person 1: 그 러시아에서 온 선수가 많이 넘어졌는데 어떻게 이길 수 있어? 'That skater from Russia fell so many times, how could she win?' -> Person 2: 그러니까! 'That's the thing!' Connected: 그러니까 에너지를 절약해야지! 'That's why we need to save energy!'; 그러니까 학생들이 반의 목표를 위해 각자의 역할을 잘 해야 돼요 'That's why students in the class each need to do their role well in order to achieve the class goal'.
notes.nuance: Internet/casual speakers (especially teenage/20-something girls) sometimes further contract 그러니까 to 그니깡 - the author advises against adopting this specific variant unless that demographic fits. The standalone usage is genuinely hard to pin down with a fixed translation, since it expresses enthusiastic agreement rather than a literal 'because' meaning.

pattern: 그치/그쵸 ('...kan?', singkatan dari 그렇지/그렇죠)
meaning: 그치 (informal, from 그렇지) and 그쵸 (formal, from 그렇죠) are used after a statement to ask the listener to agree, functionally similar to ~지/죠 (Lesson 93); they can also stand alone to show agreement with what was just said.

notes.formation: [statement], 그치?/그쵸? (tag question). 그치!/그쵸! (standalone agreement).
notes.usage: 날씨가 너무 더워, 그치? 'The weather is very hot, isn't it!?' (= 날씨가 너무 덥지?); 어젯밤에 안개가 많이 꼈어요, 그쵸? 'There was a lot of fog last night, wasn't there?' (= 어젯밤에 안개가 많이 꼈죠?). Standalone agreement: 한국피자가 제일 맛있다! 'Korean pizza is the most delicious pizza!' -> 그치! '(I agree!)'
notes.nuance: 그치/그쵸 are almost exclusively reserved for speech - you'd only see them written where dialogue is trying to mimic real spoken conversation (texting, quoted speech in stories). When used standalone, their meaning is very close to 그러니까's standalone usage, both expressing agreement, though 그치/그쵸's core connection is to the tag-question function of ~지/죠.

pattern: 얘/걔/쟤 (singkatan dari 이 아이/그 아이/저 아이) + singkatan internet umum
meaning: 얘, 걔, and 쟤 abbreviate 이 아이, 그 아이, and 저 아이 respectively ('this/that/that [child]') - commonly used among friends referring to each other, not just literal children; plus a rundown of common internet/texting abbreviations.

notes.formation: 이 아이 -> 얘; 그 아이 -> 걔; 저 아이 -> 쟤. Common internet abbreviations: ㅋㅋ ('lol', from the sound of chuckling); ㅠㅠ (crying eyes, sadness); 넘 (abbreviation of 너무); 낼 (abbreviation of 내일); 꺼 (abbreviation of 것/거, often after 내: 내꺼 'mine'); ~ㅇ ending (cute suffix added to a conjugated verb/adjective or after 요/습니다, e.g. 먹었어 -> 먹었엉).
notes.usage: 쟤가 누구야? 'Who is that?'; 얘가 내가 전에 말한 친구야 'This is the friend that I was talking about'; 걔가 코로나에 걸린 사람과 접촉해서 걔도 걸렸어요 'That kid was a close-contact with a person who caught COVID, so he caught COVID too'. Internet speech: 난 넘넘 배고파! 'I'm sooooo hungry!'; 넌 내꺼야! 'You're mine!'; 내일 맛있는 걸 사 줘용! 'Buy me something delicious tomorrow, please!' (cute ~ㅇ ending).
notes.nuance: 아이 itself is abbreviated to 애 and used for referring to children roughly 12 and under (or students, from a teacher's perspective) - 얘/걔/쟤 extend this same abbreviation pattern to the demonstrative-marked versions. The ~ㅇ ending is considered cute and is mainly used by young women; an older person using it (over ~30) is typically doing so jokingly.

examples.meaning: This is the friend that I was talking about.

pattern: V/Adj~ㄴ/는다고 해요 -> ~ㄴ/는대(요) (kontraksi kutipan)
meaning: ~다고 해(요) (Lesson 52's quoting construction) commonly contracts to ~대(요) in speech - usable regardless of the quoted clause's own tense (stem, ~ㄴ/는-, ~았/었-, or ~겠-), and only for relaying what someone ELSE said, never one's own present thought.

notes.formation: ~하다고 해요 -> 하대요; ~한다고 해요 -> 한대요; ~했다고 해요 -> 했대요; ~하겠다고 해요 -> 하겠대요.
notes.usage: 아들은 미역국을 좋아한대요 'Our son says that he likes seaweed soup' (= 좋아한다고 해요); 저의 친구들은 저의 글씨가 예쁘대요 'My friends say that my handwriting is pretty' (adjective); 감자를 아직 안 삶았대요 'He says that he hasn't yet boiled the potatoes' (past); 선생님이 오늘 조퇴하겠대요 'The teacher says he will leave early today' (future).
notes.nuance: This abbreviation is ONLY natural for relaying another person's quote - saying 나는 배고프대 (about oneself) is unnatural. Even when the present-tense contraction ~대(요) is used, context makes clear the quote was actually SPOKEN in the past (since you had to have heard it already) - ~댔어요 (attaching further past tense to ~대) exists to explicitly mark the speaking act itself as past, but in practice ~대(요) alone is usually sufficient and more common. Pronunciation can be confused with ~는데 (Lessons 76-77) by an untrained ear.

pattern: N이다 kutipan -> (이)래(요), termasuk waktu depan 거래요
meaning: ~(이)라고 해(요) (Lesson 52's 이다-quoting construction) contracts to ~(이)래(요) - including when the quoted clause is future tense (~ㄹ/을 것이다, contracted to 거래요).

notes.formation: 너무 어려운 문제라고 해요 -> 너무 어려운 문제래(요). 그 사람은 선생님이라고 해요 -> 그 사람은 선생님이래요. Future: 슬기가 내일 학교에 갈 거라고 했어요 -> 슬기가 내일 학교에 갈 거래요.
notes.usage: 그 노인이 예순 아홉 살이래요 'That old man says he is sixty years old'; 그 커플이 오늘 결혼기념일이래요 'That couple says it is their anniversary today'. Future: 그 가게가 물건 가격을 다 인상할 거래요 'That store says they will continue to raise the prices of goods'; 정부가 그 세금을 내일부터 징수할 거래요 'The government says that it will collect that tax starting from tomorrow'.
notes.nuance: Just as with ~대(요), even when the original quote was spoken in the past, the present-tense contraction ~(이)래(요) remains common and is understood from context to refer to a past utterance - ~(이)랬어요 (with explicit past tense added) exists but isn't strictly necessary.

pattern: Perintah kutipan -(으)라고 해요 -> -(으)래(요)
meaning: ~(으)라고 해(요) (Lesson 54's quoted-imperative construction) contracts to ~(으)래(요), following the same contraction pattern as the 이다-quoting abbreviation.

notes.formation: 엄마가 빨리 오라고 했어요 -> 엄마가 빨리 오래요. 엄마가 천천히 먹으라고 했어요 -> 엄마가 천천히 먹으래요.
notes.usage: 엄마가 빨리 오래요 'Mom says/said "come quick!"'; 엄마가 천천히 먹으래요 'Mom says/said "eat slowly"'; 여자 친구는 반지 혹은 목걸이 사래 'My girlfriend says/said "buy a ring or necklace"'.
notes.nuance: Because ~(으)라고 해요 and ~(이)라고 해요 (the 이다-quote from the previous pattern) share a very similar structure, their abbreviated forms (~(으)래요 and ~(이)래요) look nearly identical - context and the underlying meaning (a command vs. a description) distinguish them.

pattern: ~자고 해요 -> ~재(요) (ajakan kutipan) dan ~(느)냐고/~(으)냐고 물어보다 -> ~냬 (pertanyaan kutipan)
meaning: ~자고 해(요) (Lesson 53's quoted-suggestion construction) contracts to ~재(요); ~(느)냐고/~(으)냐고 물어보다/하다 (Lesson 53's quoted-question construction) contracts to ~냬.

notes.formation: 아빠가 밥을 먹자고 했어 -> 아빠가 밥을 먹재요. 그 여자가 예쁘냐고 물어봤어요 -> 그는 여자가 예쁘냬.
notes.usage: Suggestion: 아빠가 밥을 먹재요 'Dad says/said "Let's eat"'; 여자 친구가 야시장에 가재 'My girlfriend says/said "let's go to the night market"'; 갑자기 남자 친구가 헤어지재서 여자가 붙잡을 거래요 'All of a sudden the boyfriend said "let's break up," so the girl says she will try to get him back' (note 재 combining with ~아/어서 for a reason clause). Question: 그는 여자가 예쁘냬 'He asked "Is the girl pretty?"'; 삶은 감자를 꺼내도 되냬 'She asked if it is okay to take out the boiled potato'.
notes.nuance: This completes the set of quoting contractions covered across this lesson: ~대(요) for plain statements, ~(이)래(요) for 이다/future, ~(으)래(요) for commands, ~재(요) for suggestions, and ~냬 for questions - each mirrors the full form's meaning while compressing the pronunciation, and all are common in speech but rare in formal writing (except when representing direct dialogue).

pattern: 한 dan 약 (memperkirakan angka/jumlah, mirip ~쯤)
meaning: 'About/approximately' - 한 is placed before the number being estimated (very common in speech, rare in writing except direct quotes), while 약 does the same job but is significantly less common than 한 or ~쯤 (Lesson 22).

notes.formation: 한 [number]. 약 [number]. Both can be combined with the already-known ~쯤 for extra emphasis on approximation.
notes.usage: 그 차의 속도가 한 150킬로였어요 'The speed of that car was about 150 km/h'; 우리가 내일 한 2시에 도착할 거예요 'We will arrive tomorrow at about two o'clock'; 우리 등산 동호회에 회원이 한 100명 있어요 'There are about 100 members in our hiking club'. With ~쯤: 어제 가게에 사람 한 스무 명쯤 왔어요 'Yesterday, about 20 people came to the store'. With 약: 캐나다 인구는 약 35,000,000 명이에요 = 캐나다 인구는 한 35,000,000 명이에요 = 캐나다 인구는 35,000,000 명쯤이에요, all meaning 'Canada's population is about 35 million'.
notes.nuance: Unlike ~쯤 sentences, it's uncommon to use 한 to ask a question about an approximate amount - 한 mainly appears in statements. All three forms (한, 약, ~쯤) can convey the same approximation meaning, but differ in how common they are: 한 and ~쯤 are frequent, 약 is comparatively rare.

pattern: V/Adj~(으)므로 ('karena/oleh sebab itu', tulisan formal) + 그러므로
meaning: Another way to say 'because/therefore' (alongside ~아/어서, ~기 때문에, ~(으)니까) by connecting two clauses with ~(으)므로 - more common in formal writing than in speech; combined with 그렇다 to give 그러므로, a formal alternative to 그래서.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective]~(으)므로 + [result clause], conjugatable to past or present tense like ~기 때문에. 그렇다 + ~(으)므로 = 그러므로.
notes.usage: 이불을 강한 햇빛에 말리므로 더 빨리 말랐어요 'I dried the blanket in the strong sun so it dried quickly'; 성적이 낮았으므로 그 학생은 좋은 대학교에 못 갔어요 'That student couldn't go to a good university because of his low grades'; 그 사람이 대통령을 암살했으므로 징역 100년이 선고되었어요 'That person was sentenced to 100 years in prison because he assassinated the president'. 그러므로: 동양 문명이 서양 문명보다 농업을 먼저 시작했어요. 그러므로 발달이 더 빨랐습니다 'Eastern civilization started farming before Western civilization. Therefore, their development was faster.'
notes.nuance: ~(으)므로 behaves grammatically like ~기 때문에 (attachable to past or present-tense stems), but its formal, written register sets it apart from the more casual ~아/어서/~(으)니까 - it's the kind of connector you'd expect in academic writing, official documents, or news reports rather than casual conversation.

pattern: N 전반 ('secara umum/menyeluruh', berbeda dari 보통/일반적으로)
meaning: While 보통/일반적으로 translate to 'generally/usually', 전반 means something different: 'across the board, in a general sense, among all parts of' a noun.

notes.formation: [noun] 전반(에), placed after the noun it refers to comprehensively.
notes.usage: 저는 한국 역사 전반에 관심이 있어요 'I am interested in Korean history in general' (all parts of Korean history) vs 저는 한국 역사를 보통 좋아해요 'I generally/usually like Korean history' (a different, habitual-liking meaning). More: 서울시는 영어 원어민에 관한 예산 전반을 줄이고 있어요 'The City of Seoul is lowering the budget for native English speakers in general (across the board)'; 미국 통화가 요즘에 비싸지고 있어서 물품 값이 전반적으로 올라가고 있어요 'The price of goods in general (across the board) is increasing because the US dollar is increasing'.
notes.nuance: The key distinction: 보통/일반적으로 describe HOW OFTEN or TYPICALLY something happens (a habit/frequency sense), while 전반 describes the SCOPE of something - that it applies comprehensively across every part of a category, not just typically/usually.

pattern: N을/를 당하다 (kata kerja/akhiran pasif untuk hasil negatif)
meaning: 당하다 functions as a verb (or attaches to nouns to form new verbs), indicating one receives or experiences a NEGATIVE outcome - a passive-feeling construction reserved specifically for people on the receiving end of something bad.

notes.formation: As a standalone verb: [negative-outcome noun]을/를 당하다. Attached to a verb-forming noun: [noun]당하다 (e.g. 거절하다 'to reject' -> 거절당하다 'to be rejected').
notes.usage: 교통사고에서 사람 다섯 명은 부상을 당했어요 'Five people were injured in the car accident'; 집에 가는 동안 사고를 당했어요 'I got into an accident on my way home'; 그 왕따 학생은 다른 학생들한테 괴롭힘을 당했어요 'That outcast was humiliated by other students'. Attached to nouns: 그는 그 여자한테 데이트를 하자고 했는데 거절당했어요 'He asked that girl on a date, but got rejected'; 그녀는 밤에 낯선 남자들한테 공격당했어요 'She was attacked by unknown men at night'; 제가 2년 전에 사기당해서 요즘에 돈을 엄청 아껴 써요 'I was scammed two years ago, so I really need to be careful with my money these days'.
notes.nuance: ~당하다 is specifically for when a PERSON is on the losing end of a situation; when a non-person (like a budget or proposal) is the one being rejected/affected, the ordinary passive 되다 is used instead - compare 새로운 예산이 사장한테 거절되었어요 'The new budget was rejected by the CEO' (되다, non-person) with 거절당했어요 (당하다, when a person is rejected).

pattern: ~에/에서 + 는/은 ('di N (dibanding tempat/waktu lain)...')
meaning: Attaching ~는/은 to the particles ~에 or ~에서 adds the comparison function of ~는/은 (Lessons 1, 2, 17, 22, 24) - implying the statement is true here/now/in this specific case, as opposed to some other situation (stated or implied).

notes.formation: [place/time noun]에는/에서는.
notes.usage: 한국에서는 사람들이 김치를 많이 먹어요 'In Korea, people eat a lot of Kimchi' (implying elsewhere, they might not); 이 가방에는 귀중품이 없어요 'There are no valuables in this bag' (implying another bag might have some); 그 가방에는 귀중품이 있는데 이 가방에는 귀중품이 없어요 'There are valuables in this bag, but not in this bag' (comparison stated explicitly in the same sentence). More: 놀이동산에 여름에는 사람이 많아요 'There are many people at the amusement park in the summer' (vs other seasons); 몇 달 전에 서른 살이 되어서 우울했는데 이제는 전혀 우울하지 않아요 'A few months ago I was depressed about turning thirty, but now I'm not depressed at all'.
notes.nuance: The 'something else' being compared against doesn't need to be explicitly stated - it can be implied from context, or the two sides of the comparison can both appear within the same sentence, connected by another clause.

pattern: ~는/은 ditempel ke pseudo-kata benda (수, 적, 필요, 줄) dan partikel lain (~부터, ~까지, ~(으)로, ~(으)면)
meaning: The comparison function of ~는/은 can attach to pseudo-nouns like 수 (Lesson 45), 적, 필요, 줄, and to other particles/connectors like ~부터, ~까지, ~(으)로, ~(으)면, adding the same implied contrast with an unstated alternative.

notes.formation: 수는/적은/필요는/줄은. Particles: ~(로)부터는, ~까지는, ~(으)로는, ~(으)면은.
notes.usage: 밥을 먹을 수는 있어요 'I can eat rice (but not something else)'; 에어컨을 틀 수는 없지만 선풍기를 틀 수는 있어요 'You can't turn the air conditioner on, but you can turn the fan on'; 망가진 컴퓨터를 고치려고 컴퓨터 전문가에 맡긴 적은 없어요 'I haven't yet taken my broken computer to a specialist'; 이력서를 작성을 했는데 온라인으로 제출을 할 줄은 몰라요 'I wrote up a resume, but I don't know how to apply online'. With particles: 시험 전 날까지는 밤을 샜는데 당일에는 일찍 잤어요 'I stayed up all night until the day of the test, but on the day of the test I went to sleep early'; 운동을 그렇게 하면은 몸을 다칠 수 있어요 'You can hurt yourself if you exercise like that (compared to other ways)'.
notes.nuance: This shows the sheer versatility of ~는/은's comparison function - because it can layer onto virtually any noun or particle, learners encounter it constantly in unfamiliar-looking combinations that all share the same underlying 'this, as opposed to something else' logic.

pattern: ~지는 않다 / ~진 않다 ('tidak..., berlawanan dengan ekspektasi')
meaning: Adding ~는/은 after ~지 in ~지 않다 signals that the situation differs from what the listener might expect - 'despite what you expect, it's not the case that...'. ~지는 almost always contracts to ~진.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective]~지는/진 않다.
notes.usage: 시간이 오래 걸리지 않을 것이에요 (plain) -> 시간이 오래 걸리지는 않을 것이에요 'It won't take a long time' (despite the listener's expectation that it will); 저는 요리를 잘 하진 않습니다 '(Despite what you'd expect, being in a cooking class,) I am not good at cooking'. More: 그런 사람이 많진 않아요 '(Despite what you'd expect,) there aren't that many people'; 그 가수가 인기가 많은데 티켓이 아직 매진되진 않았어요 'That singer is very popular but the tickets still haven't sold out'.
notes.nuance: This usage is genuinely hard to grasp without many examples - the ~는/은 here signals a contrast with the LISTENER's assumed expectation, not a comparison between two explicit things in the sentence. Context (what was implied or assumed just before the sentence was said) is essential for recognizing why ~지는/진 was chosen over plain ~지 않다.

pattern: V/Adj~긴 하다 ('meremehkan suatu fakta', ~기 + ~는 hasil)
meaning: Attaching ~는 to ~기 after a verb/adjective creates a way of downplaying the stated fact - the speaker might feel modest, shy, or want to soften the claim; ~기는 almost always contracts to ~긴.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective]~기는/긴 하다 (or the same verb/adjective repeated instead of 하다): 있긴 있어/있긴 해.
notes.usage: 생각이 있긴 있어 = 생각이 있긴 해 'I have an idea' (but downplaying it, e.g. thinking it isn't very good); 날씨가 춥긴 추워요 = 날씨가 춥긴 해요 'It's cold (but not that cold, just a little)'; 공부를 열심히 하긴 했어 'I studied hard (but not that hard)'. Commonly paired with ~지만 for the resulting contrast: 돈이 있긴 하지만 조금 부족해요 'I have money, but just not enough'; 계획이 있긴 있었지만 갑자기 취소되었어요 'I had plans, but they got cancelled'; 우리 학교 애들이 똑똑하긴 한데 노력을 안 해요 'The kids at our school are smart, but they don't try hard'.
notes.nuance: The specific way the fact is 'downplayed' depends entirely on context - it can express modesty, mild embarrassment, an admission with a caveat, or simply softening an otherwise blunt statement. This nuance took the author years to fully grasp and is best absorbed through many examples rather than a single fixed rule.

pattern: ~는/은 dipakai dua kali (membandingkan dua hal) + 'Bagaimana dengan X?' (N은/는?)
meaning: ~는/은 attached to two different nouns in the same sentence highlights how they differ from each other; standing alone after just a noun, ~는/은 asks for clarification/information about that specific thing ('what about...?').

notes.formation: [noun1]는/은 [clause1], [noun2]는/은 [clause2]. Standalone: [noun]은/는(요)?
notes.usage: Double comparison: 사과는 맛있고 바나나는 맛이 없어요 'The apples are delicious, but the bananas are not'; 오늘은 비가 오고 내일은 비가 안 와요 'Today it is raining, but tomorrow it won't'. Standalone 'what about': Person 1: 집에 도착했어요 'I arrived home' -> Person 2: 밥은? 'Have you eaten yet? (What about food?)'; Person 1: 저는 내일 엄마와 오빠랑 같이 밥을 먹을 거예요 'Tomorrow, I am going to eat with my mom and brother' -> Person 2: 아빠는? 'What about your dad?'
notes.nuance: The standalone 'what about X?' usage is a natural, compact way to ask the listener to say more about a specific topic - a student answering a teacher's question could naturally turn the question back with just 선생님은? ('And you, teacher?'), relying on context to fill in the rest.

pattern: ~아/어지다 vs ~아/어뜨리다 (pasangan intransitif/transitif: 'terjadi dengan sendirinya' vs 'menyebabkan terjadi')
meaning: Many word pairs share a root, with ~아/어지다 forming an intransitive verb (something happens, no stated cause) and ~아/어뜨리다 forming the transitive equivalent (a subject actively causes it to happen to an object) - not to be confused with the ~아/어지다 grammar point attached to adjectives.

notes.formation: 떨어지다 (intransitive, 'to fall') / 떨어뜨리다 (transitive, 'to drop'); 쓰러지다/쓰러뜨리다 ('to collapse/topple'); 무너지다/무너뜨리다 ('to collapse'); 헝클어지다/헝클어뜨리다 ('to be/get tangled'); 부서지다/부서뜨리다 ('to be smashed/to smash'); 부러지다/부러뜨리다 ('to be broken/to break'); 흐트러지다/흐트러뜨리다 ('to be messy/to make messy'); 구부러지다/구부러뜨리다 ('to be bent/to bend'); 누그러지다/누그러뜨리다 ('for one's heart to soften/to soften someone's heart'); 터지다/터뜨리다 ('to explode/to make explode').
notes.usage: 병이 탁자에서 떨어졌다 'The bottle fell from the table' (no stated cause) vs 나는 병을 떨어뜨렸다 'I dropped the bottle' (I am the cause); 건물이 쓰러졌다 'The building was knocked down' vs 바람은 건물을 쓰러뜨렸다 'The wind knocked down the building'; 줄이 완전히 헝클어졌어요 'The string is completely tangled' vs 애기가 케이블을 헝클어뜨렸어요 'The baby tangled up the cable'.
notes.nuance: 쓰러지다 and 무너지다 both mean roughly 'to collapse', but differ subtly: 쓰러지다 is for something toppling OVER (like a wind-blown tree), while 무너지다 is for something collapsing INTO itself without toppling (like a controlled building implosion) - the end result is similar, but the process differs.

pattern: ~화 (化) ('-isasi/pen-...-an', perubahan)
meaning: 화 is a Hanja character meaning 'change', attached after the noun form of a ~하다 verb to indicate a transformation - most naturally translated with the English suffix '-ification/-ization'.

notes.formation: 국제 (international) + 화 = 국제화 (internationalization/globalization). ~화 + 하다 forms a verb: 국제화하다 ('to globalize').
notes.usage: 운동은 피의 순환을 활성화해요 'Exercise vitalizes blood flow'; 산업화는 경제 성장을 가속화할 수 있어요 'Industrialization can accelerate the development of the economy'; 우버는 택시 서비스를 상업화해서 성공했어요 'Uber succeeded in commercializing the service of getting a taxi'; 요즘에 오래된 도시를 현대화하는 곳이 많아요 'These days there are a lot of old cities that are modernizing themselves'.
notes.nuance: This pattern is very productive - many other ~화하다 words follow the same structure: 일반화하다 (to generalize), 합리화하다 (to rationalize), 차별화하다 (to differentiate), 서구화하다 (to westernize), 다양화하다 (to diversify), 대중화하다 (to popularize), 평준화하다 (to standardize), 간소화하다 (to simplify).

pattern: Menambahkan 이 ke nama yang berakhiran konsonan (menghindari ambiguitas pengucapan)
meaning: When a Korean name ends in a consonant (받침), 이 is commonly inserted between the name and particles like ~는/은, ~이/가, ~를/을 - purely to avoid pronunciation ambiguity, and considered colloquial.

notes.formation: [name ending in 받침]이 + 는/이/를, etc. Only done with the specific consonants ㄱ, ㅁ, ㄴ, ㅇ, ㄹ, ㅂ (the only ones commonly seen as a name's final consonant); never with vowel-final names, since there's no ambiguity there.
notes.usage: 희영은 pronounced without 이 sounds ambiguous (could be heard as '희여는'), so 희영이는 is used instead: 희영이는 이빨을 부러뜨렸어요 'Heeyoung broke her tooth'. More: 은혁이가 시험준비를 하고 있어요 '은혁 is preparing for the exam'; 기범이는 희영이를 만나러 어제 학교에 갔어요 '기범 went to school yesterday to meet 희영'.
notes.nuance: Omitting 이 is grammatically fine and both versions are used - Korean speakers describe leaving it out (in casual daily speech) as sounding slightly '느끼해' (greasy/cheesy, the same word used for overly rich food or corny romantic language) compared to including it, though this feeling is admittedly hard to pin down precisely.

examples.meaning: 은혁 is preparing for the exam.

pattern: ~아/어하다 ditambahkan ke kata sifat (mendeskripsikan perasaan orang LAIN)
meaning: Adjectives describing an internal feeling (부끄럽다, 슬프다, 기쁘다, 부럽다, 싶다, etc.) commonly attach ~아/어하다 when the sentence describes what ANOTHER person is feeling, since the speaker can't directly know another's internal state.

notes.formation: [feeling adjective]~아/어하다, used when the subject is someone other than the speaker.
notes.usage: 그는 너무 부끄러워했어요 'He was very shy' (natural, describing another's feeling); 희영이는 밥을 먹고 싶어해 'Heeyoung wants to eat' (싶다 + ~아/어하다). Without an object, 제가 너무 부끄러워했어요 (about oneself) is typically incorrect - BUT it becomes acceptable with an object: 제가 가난을 너무 부끄러워했어요 'I am shy about my poorness'; 제가 친구의 성공을 너무 기뻐했어요 'I am very glad about my friend's success'; 제가 친구의 죽음을 너무 슬퍼했어요 'I am sad about my friend's death'; 제가 남의 성공을 너무 부러워했어요 'I am envious of others' success'.
notes.nuance: It would technically be possible (though unusual) to describe another person's feeling without ~아/어하다 (그는 너무 부끄러웠어요) - this might appear in novels, where the author has full, certain knowledge of a fictional character's inner state, unlike in real-life conversation about real people. This mirrors the earlier-learned 좋다 -> 좋아하다 / 싫다 -> 싫어하다 pattern (Lesson 12), where an object is what licenses using these adjectives about a person's active preference rather than a bare, opinion-only statement.

pattern: ~께서(는) (penanda subjek formal untuk orang yang sangat dihormati)
meaning: ~께서 marks the subject of a sentence when that subject is a person deserving high respect - more common in writing and very formal speech than in everyday conversation; ~는 can be added (~께서는) for its usual comparison nuance.

notes.formation: [highly respected subject]께서(는) + [honorific-conjugated predicate].
notes.usage: 아버님께서 밥을 드셨습니다 'The father ate'; 할아버지께서 옛날에 런던에서 사셨어요 'Our grandfather lived in London a long time ago'; 지금 교장선생님께서 잠깐 말씀을 하시겠습니다 'Now, the principal will speak for a moment'. With ~는 added: 아버님께서는 밥을 드셨습니다 'The father ate (but someone else, maybe the mother, didn't)' - the same comparison nuance as ordinary ~는/은.
notes.nuance: Using ~께서 is optional and reserved for very formal situations (like a vice principal formally introducing a principal to 100 parents) - most people wouldn't notice or mind if it were omitted, unlike failing to use honorific speech levels (~요/~ㅂ/습니다) which would be a much more serious breach of respect.

pattern: V/Adj/이다~든지 (간에) ('entah A atau B..., tidak masalah')
meaning: 'Whether A or B/it doesn't matter if A or B' - attaching ~든지 to multiple possibilities, indicating none of them is being singled out (unlike ~중에, 'among'), since either could occur or be true; 간에 ('between', from Hanja 間) is often added at the end, sometimes adding a slight negative undertone.

notes.formation: [possibility1]든지 [possibility2]든지 (간에) + [outcome that applies regardless]. ~든지 attaches to verb/adjective stems or to 이다 (merging with a vowel-final noun: 밥이든지).
notes.usage: 포크를 사용하든지 젓가락을 사용하든지 더 편한 것을 사용하세요 'Whether you use a fork or chopsticks, use the one that is more comfortable'; 경기에서 이기든지 지든지 열심히 해야 됩니다 'It doesn't matter if you win or lose the game, you should try hard'; 밥이든지 피자든지 빨리 골라! 'It doesn't matter if it is rice or pizza, but choose quickly!' With 간에: 우리가 내일 가든지 내일모레 가든지 간에 어차피 가야 돼요 'It doesn't matter if we go tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, anyways, we have to go'.
notes.nuance: 간에 can technically be added to any ~든지 sentence, but doing so sometimes adds a slight negative connotation (though not always, since language nuance is complex) - it's a bit more common to see 간에 specifically when the speaker is expressing indifference/not caring about the outcome, rather than in a neutral instructional sentence.

pattern: ~든지 말든지 ('entah...atau tidak', tindakan vs tidak-melakukan)
meaning: When the two possibilities are simply 'doing an action' or 'not doing it', ~든지 말든지 (with 말다, the negative-command word) is commonly used instead of repeating the verb negated.

notes.formation: [verb]든지 말든지 + [outcome regardless of the choice].
notes.usage: 우리가 가든지 말든지 나는 신경을 안 써 'I don't care if we go or not'; 시험이 있든지 말든지 간에 학교에 가야 돼요 'It doesn't matter if there is an exam or not, you have to go to school'; 쓰레기를 분리하든지 말든지 재활용 차가 와서 수거해 갈 거에요 'It doesn't matter if we separate the garbage or not, the recycling truck is going to come and take it away'.
notes.nuance: This is simply a more compact alternative to repeating the full verb negated (가든지 안 가든지 -> 가든지 말든지) - since one of the two options is inherently just 'not doing X', using 말다 (already familiar as the negative-imperative word) is a natural shortcut.

pattern: 뭐/누구/언제/어디 + 든지 ('apa/siapa/kapan/di mana saja')
meaning: ~든지 commonly attaches directly to the question words 뭐, 누구, 언제, and 어디 to mean 'whatever/whoever/whenever/wherever' - some learners memorize these as fixed vocabulary words rather than analyzing the ~든지 connection, though the result is the same.

notes.formation: 뭐든지 = whatever; 누구든지 = whoever; 언제든지 = whenever; 어디든지 = wherever.
notes.usage: 한 달 동안 뭐든지 먹어도 돼요 'For one month, you are allowed to eat whatever you want'; 누구든지 사람들이 믿을 수 있는 친구가 필요해요 'Everybody needs a friend they can trust' (literally 'it doesn't matter who, people need...'); 우리 집에 언제든지 오세요 'Come to our house anytime!'; 어디든지 앉아도 돼요 'Sit anywhere!'
notes.nuance: These four combinations are extremely common in everyday speech, functioning almost like standalone vocabulary items even though they're built from the same ~든지 principle covered throughout this lesson - recognizing the underlying pattern helps make sense of why they carry an 'it doesn't matter which one' meaning.

pattern: 무슨 일이 벌어지든지 (간에) ('terlepas dari apa yang terjadi')
meaning: 벌어지다 (already meaning 'to have a gap/space' or, like 생기다/일어나다, 'for something to arise/happen') commonly combines with ~든지 after 무슨 일이 to mean 'whatever happens/regardless of what happens'.

notes.formation: 무슨 일이 벌어지든지 (간에) + [clause that holds true regardless].
notes.usage: 어떤 일이 벌어졌어요? 'What came up?'; 중동에서 전쟁이 벌어졌어요 'A war started in the Middle East' (벌어지다's 'to arise/happen' meaning). Combined with ~든지: 무슨 일이 벌어지든지 간에 그녀랑 결혼할 거예요 'Regardless of what happens, I'm marrying her'; 무슨 일이 벌어지든지 간에 이 문제를 객관적으로 해결해야 돼요 'Regardless of what happens, we need to solve this problem objectively'.
notes.nuance: This is a fixed, idiomatic-feeling combination worth recognizing as a whole, since 벌어지다 itself has multiple meanings (a physical gap, and something arising/happening) - but paired specifically with 무슨 일이 and ~든지, it reliably conveys 'whatever happens'.

pattern: N까지(도) ('bahkan sampai...', menekankan sejauh mana sesuatu terjadi)
meaning: A separate usage of ~까지 (distinct from 'until', Lesson 12) that expresses the extent to which something happened - 'even X' - implying many other things also happened/were done, and X was an extreme extra. ~도 can be added for even more emphasis.

notes.formation: [noun]까지 (or 까지도 for extra emphasis).
notes.usage: 친구가 문어까지 먹었어요 'My friend even ate octopus' (implying he ate many other things, and octopus was the extreme extra) - compare to 친구가 문어도 먹었어요 'My friend ate octopus as well' (simply an additional item, without stressing how many other things were eaten). 나는 숙제까지 다 했어 'I even finished my homework' (implying many other tasks were also done); 할머니까지 오셨어요 'Even grandma came' (implying grandma usually doesn't come). With ~도: 제가 책상뿐만 아니라 장롱까지도 옮겼어요 'I didn't just move the desk, but also the wardrobe'.
notes.nuance: The key contrast with plain ~도 ('also/too'): ~까지 stresses that the item mentioned is an extreme, surprising addition to a longer list of things, while ~도 is a neutral 'in addition to' with no such implication of surprise or extent.

examples.meaning: I even finished my homework.
Did even grandma come too?
My friend did not even eat octopus.

quiz.explanation: ~까지 stresses an extreme, surprising extra item; ~도 is a neutral 'in addition to'.

pattern: ~는지도 몰라요 ('bahkan tidak tahu...', dibanding dugaan tidak pasti dari Lesson 30)
meaning: Adding ~도 to ~는지 can add emphasis that the uncertain fact is just ONE of several other things also unknown ('don't even know...') - distinct from Lesson 30's use of ~도 for a hedged guess ('might'); context distinguishes the two meanings.

notes.formation: [embedded question clause]~는지도 몰라요/모르겠어요.
notes.usage: 이것이 무엇인지 몰라요 'I don't know what this is' vs 이것이 무엇인지도 몰라요 'I don't EVEN know what this is' (emphasis: this is just one of many things not known). In future tense, ambiguous between two meanings: 엄마가 올지도 모르겠어요 could mean 'I don't know if mom will come' (Lesson 30's hedge) OR 'I don't even know if mom will come' (this lesson's emphasis) - context clarifies which. More: 문을 어떻게 열지도 모르잖아! 'You don't even know how to open the door!'; 설거지를 어떻게 제대로 하는지도 몰라요 'I don't even know how to do the dishes properly'.
notes.nuance: This is a genuinely ambiguous construction in the future tense specifically, since both Lesson 30's guess-softening ~도 and this lesson's 'not even' emphasis-~도 produce the identical form ~ㄹ/을지도 모르다/몰라요 - only the surrounding context (is the speaker hedging a guess, or emphasizing total ignorance of multiple things?) resolves which meaning is intended.

pattern: ~는데도 ('meski/walaupun...', lebih kuat daripada ~는데, dekat ~지만)
meaning: Adding ~도 to ~는데 (Lessons 76-77) intensifies its already-present 'even though' feeling, making it closer in strength to ~지만 - commonly translated 'in spite of/despite/although'.

notes.formation: [clause]~는데도 (or ~(으)ㄴ데도 for adjectives/이다, ~았/었는데도 for past).
notes.usage: 열심히 공부했는데도 시험에 떨어졌어요 'Despite studying very hard, I failed the exam'; 날씨가 추웠는데도 우리는 야외공연을 보러 갔어요 'Despite the cold weather, we went to see an outdoor performance'; 할아버지가 지팡이가 없었는데도 일어나셔서 전등을 켰어요 'Even though grandpa didn't have his cane, he got up and turned on the light'; 제가 자꾸 그만하라고 했는데도 친구가 말을 계속 했어요 'Even though I kept telling him to stop, my friend kept talking'.
notes.nuance: ~는데 alone already carries a mild 'even though' shade, but ~는데도 pushes that feeling to nearly the strength of ~지만 - useful when the contrast between the two clauses deserves more emphasis than plain ~는데 conveys.

pattern: ~다가도 ('bahkan sambil/saat...', situasi muncul selama tindakan tertentu, di antara yang lain)
meaning: Adding ~도 to ~다가 (Lesson 91) shows that a situation arises during one particular action, in addition to arising during other actions too - 'even while doing...'.

notes.formation: [verb]다가도 + [situation that also arises during other actions].
notes.usage: 공부를 하다가도 그녀에 대한 생각이 났어요 'Even while I was studying, I thought about her' (implying he thinks of her during many other activities too, not just studying); 제가 울다가도 가끔 웃음이 나요 'Even when I cry I laugh sometimes'; 피자를 먹다가도 김치를 먹고 싶었어요 'Even while I was eating pizza, I wanted to eat kimchi'.
notes.nuance: Attaching ~도 to ~다가's OTHER meaning (one action being interrupted/followed by another, e.g. 학교에 갔다가 친구 집에 갔어요) does NOT work - 학교에 갔다가도 친구 집에 갔어요 is nonsensical. However, when a sentence is already ambiguous between 'while' and 'interrupted-then' readings (like 학생은 열심히 공부하다가 잠이 들었어요), adding ~도 IS acceptable and pushes the reading toward 'even while' (학생은 열심히 공부하다가도 잠이 들었어요 'Even while studying hard, the student fell asleep - among many other situations where he also fell asleep').

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 수도 있다/없다 ('mungkin saja.../bahkan tidak bisa...')
meaning: Attaching ~도 to 수 (Lesson 45) doesn't mean 'can do X too' - instead, it indicates that the possibility/situation in the clause is ALSO possible, best translated 'it is possible that...'; with 없다 instead of 있다, it emphasizes an inability, best translated with 'even' ('can't even...').

notes.formation: [clause]~ㄹ/을 수도 있다 ('it is possible that...'). [clause]~ㄹ/을 수도 없다 ('can't even...').
notes.usage: 나는 축구를 할 수도 있다 does NOT mean 'I can play soccer too' (that would be 나는 축구도 할 수 있다) - instead: 비가 올 수도 있다 'It is possible that it will/might rain'; 계획이 변할 수도 있어요 'It's possible that the plans can change'; 친구가 올 수도 있어요 'It's possible that my friend can come'. With 없다: 나는 축구를 할 수도 없어 'I can't even play soccer'; 방이 너무 지저분해서 움직일 수도 없어요 'You can't even move because her room is so messy'; 선생님이 되지 않은 것을 생각할 수도 없어요 'I can't even think about not being a teacher'; 아내랑 이혼하는 것을 상상할 수도 없어요 'I can't even imagine divorcing my wife'.
notes.nuance: This is a genuinely distinct meaning from simply 'can do X too', which requires ~도 to attach directly to the object noun instead (축구도 할 수 있다). Once attached to 수 specifically, ~도 signals possibility (with 있다) or emphasized inability (with 없다) - two related but different nuances depending on which final word is used.

pattern: ~았/었었다 ('dulu pernah..., tapi sekarang tidak lagi', past perfect)
meaning: Adding an extra ~었~ to an already past-tense conjugation removes the ambiguity of whether the action/state continues into the present - it explicitly states the situation happened in the past and has since ENDED, similar to English's 'past perfect' or 'used to'.

notes.formation: [stem]~았/었었다, adding a second ~었 after the regular past-tense ~았/었.
notes.usage: 제가 고등학교 때 불꽃놀이를 아주 좋아했어요 'When I was in high school I really liked fireworks' (ambiguous - might still like them now) vs 제가 고등학교 때 불꽃놀이를 아주 좋아했었어요 'When I was in high school I had liked fireworks' (explicitly no longer the case). More: 어렸을 때 멸치를 아예 안 먹었었어요 'When I was young I didn't eat anchovies at all (but now I do)'; 사람들이 그 시장이 나쁘다고 했었어요 'People used to say that mayor was bad'; 옛날에 그 도시에는 사기꾼이 엄청 많았었어요 'A long time ago in that city, there used to be a lot of scammers'.
notes.nuance: The regular past tense (~았/었다) is ambiguous about whether the situation continues to the present - it COULD still be true now, but the sentence doesn't say either way. ~았/었었다 removes that ambiguity, explicitly marking the situation as finished and no longer applicable.

pattern: 갔다 vs 갔었다 (perbedaan lebih terasa saat subjeknya BUKAN pembicara)
meaning: ~었었다 is especially common with 가다 ('to go') to specify someone went somewhere and has since returned - when the speaker themselves is the subject, the difference is barely noticeable (since 'I went' already implies I'm not still there), but when the subject is someone else, the added ~었 makes a clearer difference.

notes.formation: [went somewhere]갔다 vs [went somewhere]갔었다.
notes.usage: When the speaker is the subject, both versions feel nearly the same: 저는 붓을 사러 서울에 갔어요 'I went to Seoul to buy paint brushes' (assumed you're no longer there) vs 저는 붓을 사러 서울에 갔었어요 (explicitly stated you're no longer there) - little practical difference. When the subject is someone else, the contrast is clearer: 아빠가 풍경을 보러 제주에 갔어요 'Dad went to Jeju to see the landscape' (ambiguous whether he's still there) vs 아빠가 풍경을 보러 제주에 갔었어요 'Dad went to Jeju to see the landscape' (and has come back - no longer there).
notes.nuance: This illustrates why ~었었다's usefulness becomes more apparent with third-person subjects - when talking about yourself, the fact that you're currently speaking already implies you've left wherever you went, so the extra ~었 adds little new information; but for someone else, whether they're 'still there' or 'have returned' is genuinely unclear without it.

pattern: ~ㄴ가/은가/는가/나 보다 ('sepertinya...', dugaan berdasarkan bukti langsung)
meaning: 'I guess/it looks like' - attached to the end of a sentence, this indicates a guess the speaker believes is true, specifically based on DIRECT evidence/experience just witnessed - unlike ~ㄹ/을 것 같다 (Lesson 35), which is more of an intuition-based guess without immediate supporting evidence.

notes.formation: ~ㄴ가 보다: 이다 and vowel-final adjective stems (여기가 휴게실인가 봐요). ~은가 보다: consonant-final adjective stems (그 사람이 싫은가 봐요). ~는가 보다: all verbs, 있다/없다 (온수가 잘 안 나오는가 봐요). ~나 보다: can substitute for any of the above (이다, adjectives, or verbs) - in practice, ~ㄴ/은가 보다 is more natural with adjectives/이다, and ~나 보다 is more natural with verbs, though technically all combinations are grammatical. 보다 here is an adjective, so a sentence can correctly end in 보다 but not 본다.
notes.usage: 시험이 어려울 것 같아요 'The exam is/will probably be hard' (intuition, no direct evidence) vs 시험이 어려운가 봐요 'I guess the exam is hard' (said while proctoring and seeing students sighing/giving up - direct evidence). 그 외국인이 김치를 좋아하는가 봐요 'I guess that foreigner likes kimchi' (watching him eat kimchi with every bite) vs 그 외국인이 김치를 좋아할 것 같아요 'That foreigner probably likes kimchi' (just assuming, e.g. because kimchi is popular). More: 사과가 너무 비싼가 봐요 'I guess the apples are too expensive' (evidence: nobody is buying them).
notes.nuance: The core distinction from ~ㄹ/을 것 같다 is the SOURCE of the guess: ~ㄴ가/은가/는가/나 보다 requires something directly observed/experienced right then, while ~ㄹ/을 것 같다 can be a more free-floating intuition without any specific supporting evidence.

pattern: ~았/었나 보다 / ~겠나 보다 (waktu lampau/depan, ~나 보다 lebih umum dari ~는가 보다)
meaning: Attach ~나 보다 (or, less commonly, ~는가 보다) directly to the past ~았/었 or future ~겠 marker, regardless of whether the base word is a verb, adjective, 이다, 있다, or 없다 - in the past tense, ~나 보다 is significantly more natural than ~는가 보다.

notes.formation: [stem]~았/었나 보다 (past, more natural) or ~았/었는가 보다 (past, less natural). [stem]~겠나 보다 (future guess).
notes.usage: 빨래를 아직 안 헹궜나 봐요 'I guess the laundry hasn't rinsed yet'; 수신이 안 됐는가 봐요 = 수신이 안 됐나 봐요 'I guess there is no reception' (~나 봐요 more natural); 아기가 접시를 깨뜨렸나 봐요 'I guess the baby broke the plate'; 급하게 가다가 접시를 바닥에 엎어서 다시 요리해야 되겠나 봐요 'I was walking too fast and dropped my plate, so it looks like I'll have to cook again' (future/necessity guess).
notes.nuance: While technically both ~았/었는가 보다 and ~았/었나 보다 are grammatical for any word type, native usage strongly favors ~나 보다 in the past tense regardless of whether the underlying word is a verb, adjective, or 이다 - making ~나 보다 the practical default to reach for once you're conjugating into the past.

pattern: ~나/ㄴ가 보네(요) (menggabungkan dugaan-berbukti dengan keterkejutan ~네(요))
meaning: Since sentences with ~ㄴ가/은가/는가/나 보다 already describe a guess made from freshly noticed evidence, it's common to further attach ~네(요) (Lesson 83's surprise/realization ending) to 보다.

pattern: 어쩔 수 없다 ('tidak ada yang bisa dilakukan', 어쩌다 + ~ㄹ 수 없다)
meaning: A fixed combination of the verb form of 어쩌다 (unrelated to the adverb 어쩌다 from Lesson 94) with ~ㄹ 수 없다 (Lesson 45), best treated as a single unit meaning 'there's nothing that can be done about this situation'.

notes.formation: 어쩔 수 없다/없어요, standing alone or preceded by a reason clause.
notes.usage: 어쩔 수 없어요 'There's nothing I/we/you can do…' (standalone). With a preceding clause: 흔적이 없어서 어쩔 수 없어요 'There is no evidence, so there is nothing we can do'; 애기가 삐져서 어쩔 수 없어요 'The baby is upset, there is nothing we can do'; 상황이 조금 안타깝지만 어쩔 수 없어요 'The situation is unfortunate, but there is nothing we can do about it'.
notes.nuance: Despite superficially looking like just another instance of ~ㄹ/을 수 없다 attached to a verb, 어쩌다 (verb form) has no independent, standalone meaning outside this fixed expression - so 어쩔 수 없다 is best memorized as a single chunk rather than analyzed piece by piece.

pattern: ~는 것은 어쩔 수 없다 (klausa dinominalkan) dan 어쩔 수 없는 N (menerangkan kata benda)
meaning: Nominalizing an entire situation with ~는 것 lets 어쩔 수 없다 act on it as a whole ('there's nothing that can be done about the fact that...'); describing it as 어쩔 수 없는 instead lets it modify an upcoming noun ('a N that can't be helped/avoided').

notes.formation: [clause]~는 것은 어쩔 수 없다. [clause]~는 것은 어쩔 수 없는 [noun].
notes.usage: 명성이 깎이는 것은 어쩔 수 없어요 'There's nothing I can do about my fame being tarnished'; 학생들이 저를 싫어하는 것은 어쩔 수 없어요 'There's nothing I can do about the students not liking me'. As an attributive: 부장님을 싫어하는 것은 어쩔 수 없는 일이에요 'Hating your boss is inevitable'; 우리가 어쩔 수 없는 문제에 도달했어요 'We arrived at the problem that we can't do anything about'; 아이들이 사춘기를 지나가는 것은 어쩔 수 없는 일이다 'Going through puberty is something that all kids go through'.
notes.nuance: These sentences are often hard to translate directly into English/Indonesian - what sounds natural in Korean can feel awkward when translated word-for-word, so it's more useful to focus on the underlying meaning ('this situation/fact is unavoidable/uncontrollable') than to force a literal rendering every time.

pattern: 어쩔 수 없이 ('terpaksa/tanpa pilihan lain', bentuk kata keterangan)
meaning: Converting 어쩔 수 없다 to its adverb form ~이 lets it modify a following action, meaning it was done 'unavoidably' or because the speaker had no other choice.

notes.formation: 어쩔 수 없이 + [action done out of necessity].
notes.usage: 부모님께 어쩔 수 없이 진실을 알려줬어요 'I had no choice but to tell my parents the truth'; 응급 환자가 있어서 어쩔 수 없이 기다려야 돼요 'There is an emergency patient, so you will have no choice but to wait'; 용돈이 깎여서 어쩔 수 없이 이번 주부터 아껴 써야 돼요 'My allowance was cut, so I'll have no choice but to start saving from this week'; 부장님이 저를 매일 혼내서 저는 일을 어쩔 수 없이 그만두었어요 'Because the boss would get mad at me every day, I had no choice but to quit'.
notes.nuance: This is the adverbial counterpart to the earlier attributive 어쩔 수 없는 - together, the three forms (어쩔 수 없다 predicate, 어쩔 수 없는 attributive, 어쩔 수 없이 adverb) cover the full range of ways this fixed expression can slot into a sentence, always carrying the same core sense of unavoidability/lack of choice.

pattern: N(이)라도 ('setidaknya N', bukan pilihan terbaik tapi lebih baik daripada tidak sama sekali)
meaning: 'At least/how about N' - attached to a noun, ~(이)라도 expresses that the speaker is slightly dissatisfied the most preferred option isn't available, but somewhat satisfied there's still a decent alternative - 'not ideal, but better than nothing (or many other options)'.

notes.formation: [noun](이)라도, placed where the noun would normally sit in the sentence.
notes.usage: 우리가 빵이라도 먹을래? 'Shall we eat some bread (or something)?' - bread isn't the top choice for either speaker, but it's an acceptable fallback; 배가 고파서 라면이라도 먹어야 될 거예요 'I'm hungry, so I should eat something like ramen' (ramen isn't the first choice, but better than nothing); 여기까지 오셨으니 제가 커피라도 사 드릴까요? 'You came all the way here, so can I at least buy you a coffee?'; 나랑 부딪쳤는데 사과라도 한 마디 안 하니? 'You bumped into me, you're not even going to give me one word of an apology?'
notes.nuance: This is different from ~더라도 (Lesson 99's 'even if') despite looking similar - ~(이)라도 attaches to nouns and expresses a fallback/settled-for choice, not a hypothetical condition. The core feeling is always: this isn't the best option, but it's acceptable given the circumstances.

pattern: Kata keterangan/penghitung + (이)라도/게라도 ('setidaknya sejumlah/dengan cara tertentu')
meaning: ~(이)라도 can attach to adverbs (or adjectives converted to adverbs with ~게) and to counters, expressing that an action happens in a way, timing, or quantity that isn't ideal but is still better than the alternatives.

notes.formation: [adverb](이)라도. [adjective]~게라도. [number+counter](이)라도.
notes.usage: Adverb: 우리가 지금이라도 가야겠어요 'We need to go right now' (better late than never); 그 일을 혼자라도 해야 될 것 같아요 'I'll probably have to do that job by myself'. With ~게라도: 우리가 청구서를 늦게라도 낼 거예요 'We are going to pay the bill, even if it is a little late'; 할아버지 생신 선물로 돈을 적게라도 모아서 드리자 'Let's gather money, even if it is a little, and give it to grandpa on his birthday'. Counter: 그 기사를 한번이라도 보여주면 안 돼요? 'Can you show me that article just once?'; 조카가 하나라도 있었으면 좋겠어요 'I wish I had a nephew, even if I only had one'.
notes.nuance: The same core '不-ideal-but-acceptable' feeling from the noun pattern extends here to HOW, WHEN, or HOW MUCH something is done - the timing/manner/quantity mentioned isn't the speaker's first choice, but is presented as an acceptable compromise.

pattern: 장소에라도 ('ke/di tempat tertentu saja', bukan pilihan pertama)
meaning: ~(이)라도 can attach to a location marked with ~에, indicating the speaker goes to a place that isn't the most preferred option but is better than the alternatives (like staying home or doing nothing).

notes.formation: [location]에라도 + [suggested action].
notes.usage: 우리가 할 것이 없어서 공원에라도 같이 가는 게 어때요? 'We have nothing to do, so how about going to a park or something?'; 비가 내리고 있으니 영화관에라도 갈래요? 'Now that it is raining, do you want to go to the movies or something?'

pattern: Kata tanya + 라도 ('apa/di mana/kapan/siapa saja', berbeda nuansa dari 아무~나)
meaning: ~(이)라도 attaches to common question words to mean 'anywhere/anytime/anybody/anything/anyway' - similar to Lesson 25's 아무 데나/아무 때나/아무나/아무 거나/아무렇게나, but with a subtly different nuance from ~(이)라도's core meaning.

notes.formation: 어디라도 = anywhere; 언제라도 = any time; 누구라도 = anybody; 뭐라도/무엇이라도 = anything; 어떻게라도 = any way.
notes.usage: 저의 여자 친구가 어디라도 간다면 저는 같이 가고 싶어요 'It doesn't matter where my girlfriend goes, I want to go with her'; 언제라도 우리 집에 항상 와도 돼요 'It doesn't matter when it is, you can always come to our house'; 누구라도 그 문제를 풀 수 있어요 'It doesn't matter who it is, anybody could solve that problem'.
notes.nuance: Compare 가기 전에 아무 거나 같이 먹자! (implies anything would be equally satisfactory) with 가기 전에 뭐라도 같이 먹자! (implies there'd be a BETTER option available, but the speaker is settling for something rather than nothing) - the ~(이)라도 versions carry that characteristic 'not ideal, but acceptable' undertone that 아무~나 lacks.

pattern: 편 (kata benda 'sisi', arah dan 'berpihak pada seseorang')
meaning: 편 as a plain noun means 'side' - most commonly combined with direction words (뒤편 'back side', 왼편 'left side', 오른편 'right side', 반대편 'opposite side', 건너편 'other side of a street') - and can stand alone to mean being on someone's 'side' in terms of support.

notes.formation: [direction] + 편. Standalone: [person]의/내/네 편.
notes.usage: 면접하는 곳이 건물 뒤편에 있어요 'The place for the interview is behind the building'. Standalone (support): 친구가 내 편으로 오라고 빌었어 'My friend begged me to come to his side'; 무슨 일이 생기든지 나는 항상 너의 편이야 'Whatever happens, I am always on your side'; 우리 딸은 천사라서 항상 좋은 사람의 편에 설 거야 'Our daughter is an angel, so she will always be on the side of good people'.
notes.nuance: This standalone 'being on someone's side' usage extends the physical 'side' meaning metaphorically to loyalty/support - a natural semantic shift similar to English 'whose side are you on?'.

pattern: Adj~는/은/ㄴ 편이다 ('agak/cenderung...', melunakkan suatu deskripsi, baik positif maupun negatif)
meaning: Describing 편 with an adjective (via the ~는 것 principle) softens the description compared to the plain adjective alone - commonly translated 'on the ... side', humbling a positive trait or lessening the severity of a negative one.

notes.formation: [adjective attributive]~는/은/ㄴ 편이다.
notes.usage: 그 사람이 돈이 많아요 'That person has a lot of money' (could sound like a strong, possibly consequential claim) vs 그 사람이 돈이 많은 편이에요 'That person has a fair amount of money' (softer, more humble). More positive-softening examples: 우리 아이는 똑똑한 편이에요 'Our son is fairly smart'; 저의 남자친구가 잘생긴 편이에요 'My boyfriend is on the handsome side'. Softening a negative trait to sound less severe: 저는 키가 작은 편이에요 'I'm quite short' (softer than a blunt 저는 키가 작아요); 저의 남자친구는 못생긴 편이에요 'My boyfriend is on the ugly side'; 고양이가 할퀸 상처가 꽤 심한 편이에요 'The wound from the cat scratching me is quite serious'.
notes.nuance: The construction works both directions: for a positive trait, it's a way to speak humbly (avoiding a boastful-sounding blunt statement); for a negative trait, it softens how bad the situation sounds ('it's bad, but not THAT bad'). Either way, 편 doesn't change the underlying fact - it just turns down the intensity/directness of how it's stated.

pattern: V~는 편이다 ('cenderung...', butuh kata keterangan agar masuk akal)
meaning: 편이다 can also describe a verb, but unlike with adjectives, the sentence usually needs an adverb to make sense - commonly translated 'tend(s) to...'.

notes.formation: [adverb] + [verb]~는 편이다.
notes.usage: 제가 운동을 하는 편이에요 alone sounds incomplete/odd ('I exercise... fairly?') - it needs an adverb: 제가 운동을 자주 하는 편이에요 'I exercise fairly often'; 제가 운동을 잘 하는 편이에요 'I tend to exercise well'; 제가 운동을 열심히 하는 편이에요 'I tend to exercise hard'. More: 저는 수영을 잘하는 편이에요 'I swim fairly well'; 제가 매일 늦게 자는 편이에요 'I tend to go to bed fairly late'; 그 여자 아이들이 수업 시간에 많이 떠드는 편이에요 'That girl chats quite a bit during class'.
notes.nuance: Unlike the adjective version (where 편 alone provides enough content to soften a complete description), a verb alone with 편이다 lacks a clear dimension being softened - the adverb supplies that missing dimension (how often, how well, how hard), which 편 then softens/qualifies.

examples.hangul: 제가 달리기를 빨리 하고 있는 편이에요

examples.meaning: I am running fairly quickly.

pattern: V~는 길이다 ('sedang dalam perjalanan ke/dari...', hanya kata kerja datang/pergi)
meaning: When 길 (normally 'street/road') is described by a coming-or-going verb (가다, 오다, 들어가다/들어오다, 나가다/나오다, 내려가다/내려오다, 올라가다/올라오다, 돌아가다/돌아오다) and predicated with 이다, it means the speaker is 'on their way to/from' somewhere.

notes.formation: [coming/going verb]~는 길이다. Only works with verbs expressing coming or going - other verbs before 길이다 don't get this special meaning.
notes.usage: 제가 집에 가는 길이에요 'I am on my way (going) home'; 제가 회사에서 오는 길이에요 'I am on my way (coming) from work'; 지금 회사에서 나오는 길이에요 'I'm on my way out of the office'; 이가 매일 시려서 이제 치과에 가는 길이에요 'My teeth are sore everyday so I'm on my way to the dentist now'. Past tense (changing 이다's tense): 제가 산을 내려가는 길이었어요 'I was going down the mountain' - the verb before 길 stays present tense; only 이다 is conjugated.
notes.nuance: Without 이다 completing the sentence, this special meaning disappears - 제가 산을 올라가는 길에 있어요 (using ~에 있다 instead) is just an ordinary sentence meaning 'I am on the road that goes up the mountain', with no 'on my way' implication. It's specifically the [coming/going verb] + 길 + 이다 combination together that creates this idiomatic meaning.

examples.meaning: We are on our way going into the stadium.

Kalimatnya sebenarnya masih punya makna itu
quiz.explanation: Without 이다 completing the sentence, the special idiomatic meaning of [coming/going verb]+길+이다 disappears.

pattern: V~는 길에 ('di tengah perjalanan ke/dari..., berhenti melakukan sesuatu')
meaning: Attaching ~에 (instead of 이다) to 길 expresses that while on the way to/from somewhere, the speaker stops to do something else along the way.

notes.formation: [coming/going verb]~는 길에 + [action done along the way].
notes.usage: 제가 집에 가는 길에 빵을 사 줄까요? 'On my way home, should I buy some bread (for you)?'; 집에 오는 길에 맛있는 것을 사 주면 안 돼요? 'On your way home, can you buy something delicious please?'; 친구를 만나러 나가는 길에 책을 반납할 거예요 'On my way out to meet a friend, I will return the book'; 음식을 가져오는 길에 포크를 갖다 주세요 'On your way back from getting food, can you grab me a fork?'
notes.nuance: This is a direct extension of the previous ~는 길이다 pattern, swapping 이다 for ~에 to shift the meaning from 'I am currently on my way' to 'while on the way, [this other action] happens' - both rely on the same underlying coming/going + 길 combination.

examples.meaning: On my way out to meet a friend, I will return the book.

quiz.explanation: ~는 길에 expresses another action done along the way, while ~는 길이다 just states being on the way.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을 길이 없다 ('tidak ada cara untuk...')
meaning: 'There is no way of/to' - literally 'there is no road/direction to do', but better understood as expressing that an action is simply impossible to accomplish; most commonly paired with 알다 ('to know') to mean 'there is no way of knowing'.

notes.formation: [verb]~ㄹ/을 길이 없다.
notes.usage: 죽은 그 사람이 누구인지 알 길이 없어요 'There is no way of knowing who that dead person is'; 우리 프로그램의 청취자가 몇 명 있는지를 알 길이 없어요 'There is no way of knowing how many listeners our program has'. With other verbs: 기후변화를 측정할 길이 없어요 'There is no way of measuring climate change'; 부러진 조각상을 고칠 길이 없어요 'There is no way of fixing that broken statue'; 해외여행을 할 때 호객꾼을 피할 길이 없어요 'There is no way of avoiding touts when you travel abroad'.
notes.nuance: This is a genuinely distinct usage from the 'on my way' meaning of 길 covered earlier - here 길 metaphorically means 'a way/method/path' to accomplish something, echoing the English idiom 'there's no way to do X' fairly closely.

examples.hangul: 어제 잃어버린 통장을 찾을 길이 없어요
examples.romaja: eoje ireobeorin tongjangeul chajeul giri eopseoyo

pattern: V~는 김에 ('sambil sudah melakukan..., memanfaatkan kesempatan untuk juga...')
meaning: Unlike ~는 길에 (Lesson 113's 'on the way', limited to coming/going verbs), 김에 can attach to ANY verb, expressing that the speaker takes the opportunity to do a second action while already doing the first - because the first action makes the second more convenient now.

notes.formation: [first action]~는 김에 [second action taken as an opportunity].
notes.usage: 새로운 침대를 사는 김에 새로운 베개도 사자 'While we are buying a new bed let's buy some new pillows too'; 다시 식당에 들어가는 김에 빨대도 갖다 주세요 'While you're going into the restaurant again, get me a straw, please'; 계약을 연장하는 김에 퇴직금에 대해 얘기할까요? 'While I am renewing my contract, shall we also talk about my severance pay?'
notes.nuance: Be careful not to confuse this with ~(으)면서 (Lesson 62), which can also translate as 'while' - but ~(으)면서 simply describes two simultaneous actions, without the specific nuance that the first action creates a convenient OPPORTUNITY for the second. ~는 김에 specifically implies 'since I'm already doing this, I might as well also do that'.

examples.hangul: 애기랑 소방서에 가는 김에 소방차를 구경했어요
examples.romaja: aegirang sobangseoe ganeun gime sobangchareul guygeonghaesseoyo
examples.meaning: While going to the fire station with the baby we also took the chance to check out the fire trucks.

examples.hangul: 큰 트럭을 빌리는 김에 제일 무거운 화물을 실어서 보냈어요?
examples.romaja: keun teureogeul billeoneun gime jeil mugeoun hwamureul silreoseo bonaesseoyo?
examples.meaning: While renting a big truck, did we load up the heaviest cargo and send it?

examples.hangul: 저지방 우유의 효과를 설명하는 김에 고지방 우유의 효과는 설명 안 할게요

pattern: 말하는 김에 / 말이 나오는 김에 ('kalau sudah menyinggung soal itu...')
meaning: The same 'taking the opportunity' idea extends to conversation topics: 김에 described by 말하다 ('to speak') means taking the chance to bring up something while already discussing a related topic; described by 말이 나오는 ('the topic came up'), it means seizing the moment right when a topic happens to be raised.

notes.formation: [topic]에 대해 말하는 김에 [related topic to bring up]. 말이 나오는 김에 [action taken now that the topic is up].
notes.usage: 그 남매에 대해 말하는 김에 그 남매의 부모에 대한 문제도 말할게요 'While we're on the topic of those siblings, let me tell you about the problems of their parents'; 돈에 대해 말하는 김에 병원에 대한 기부가 얼마나 중요한지 설명할 거예요 'While we're on the topic of money, I will explain how important donations are to our hospital'. With 말이 나오는: 말이 나오는 김에 그 문제의 해결법에 대해 얘기하자 'Now that we are talking about that, let's talk about solutions to that problem'; 말이 나오는 김에 놀이동산에 언제 갈지 결정하자 'Now that we are talking about it, let's decide on when we are going to the amusement park'.
notes.nuance: Both variants extend 김에's core 'convenient opportunity' meaning from physical actions to conversational topics - 말하는 김에 focuses on the speaker actively taking the chance to add related information, while 말이 나오는 김에 focuses on a topic having spontaneously arisen, prompting the speaker to seize that moment.

quiz.explanation: 말하는 김에 focuses on actively taking the chance; 말이 나오는 김에 focuses on a topic spontaneously arising.

pattern: V~ㄹ/을걸 (그랬다) ('seharusnya saya...', penyesalan tentang tindakan sendiri)
meaning: 'I should have done' - expresses regret that the speaker didn't do something in the past, specifically used for the speaker's OWN actions (not another person's) - often used in self-talk, so it's typically not formally conjugated.

notes.formation: [verb stem]~ㄹ/을걸 (그랬다). 그랬다 is optional, with essentially the same meaning either way. When directing regret slightly outward to a listener, honorifics attach to 그랬다 rather than to ~ㄹ/을걸 itself: 가사를 더 잘 외울걸 그랬어요 (not 가사를 더 잘 외울걸요). Commonly combined with ~나 or ~나 보다 (Lesson 109): ~ㄹ/을걸 그랬나(요)/그랬나 봐(요).
notes.usage: 가사를 더 잘 외울걸 (그랬어) 'I should have memorized the lyrics better'; 공기가 건조해서 로션을 조금 더 바를걸 'The air is dry, so I should have put on a bit more lotion'. With ~나: 가사를 더 잘 외울걸 그랬나 봐 'It looks like I should have memorized the lyrics better'; Person 1: 오기 전에 밥을 먹을걸 그랬나? 'Should I have eaten before coming here?' -> Person 2: 우리가 곧 나가서 곧 먹을 거야! 'We are going to go out and eat soon'.
notes.nuance: This is specifically for the SPEAKER's own past actions - it's not used to say another person should have done something. It's often felt as self-directed speech, which is why formal conjugation feels unnatural directly on ~ㄹ/을걸 - if formality is needed, it's added onto the optional 그랬다 instead.

examples.meaning: I should have used a fruit knife instead of a kitchen knife.

quiz.question: ~ㄹ/을걸 (그랬다) dipakai untuk tindakan siapa?
options: Tindakan PEMBICARA sendiri di masa lalu
Tindakan bersama secara umum tanpa subjek jelas
quiz.explanation: This construction is specifically for the speaker's own past actions, not another person's.

pattern: 안 V~ㄹ/을걸 / ~지 말걸 ('seharusnya saya TIDAK...')
meaning: Negating the verb before ~ㄹ/을걸 (using 안 or ~지 않다/말다) flips the regret: the speaker did something and now wishes they hadn't.

notes.formation: 안 [verb]~ㄹ/을걸, or [verb]~지 말걸 (using 말다, the negative-command word, rather than 않다).
notes.usage: 오늘 학교에 안 올걸 'I shouldn't have come to school today'; 아침으로 초밥을 안 먹을걸 'I shouldn't have had sushi for breakfast'; 그 걸 엄마에게 말하지 말걸 'I shouldn't have told my mother that'; 신장이 안 좋아서 이렇게 단 것을 먹지 말걸 'My kidneys aren't good, so I shouldn't have eaten such a sweet thing'. Combined with earlier forms: 오늘 학교에 안 올걸 그랬나 봐 'I guess I shouldn't have come to school today'; 우리가 동물원에 안 올걸 그랬지? 'We shouldn't have come to the zoo, eh?'
notes.nuance: This is a straightforward application of standard negation (안 or ~지 말다) to the already-learned ~ㄹ/을걸 (그랬다) pattern - all the same optional additions (그랬다, ~나, ~나 보다) still apply equally well to the negated version.

examples.meaning: I shouldn't have brought this heavy bag.

examples.hangul: 그 걸 엄마에게 말하지 말걸 그랬나?
examples.romaja: geu geol eommaege malhaji malgeol geuraenna?
examples.meaning: Should I not have told my mother that?
I should have made questions based on high school content. (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: Kata negasi mana yang dipakai bersama ~ㄹ/을걸 alih-alih ~지 않다?
quiz.explanation: Both 안 and ~지 말다 (rather than ~지 않다) are used to negate this pattern.

pattern: 괜히 ('sia-sia/ternyata tidak perlu', kata keterangan bermakna serupa ~ㄹ/을걸)
meaning: 괜히 is an adverb (roughly 'in vain', though no English word perfectly captures it) marking that the speaker realizes what they did didn't actually need to be done - similar to the previous ~ㄹ/을걸 pattern, but framed as an already-realized fact rather than a regretful wish.

notes.formation: 괜히 placed adverbially in a sentence, before the action that turned out unnecessary.
notes.usage: 나는 무거운 가방을 가져왔어 'I brought the heavy bag' vs 나는 무거운 가방을 괜히 가져왔어 'I brought the heavy bag in vain' (e.g. realizing at the campground that a friend also brought a tent, so bringing one's own heavy bag/tent wasn't needed). More: 오늘 학교에 괜히 왔어 = 오늘 학교에 안 올걸 'I shouldn't have come to school today'; 이 무거운 가방을 괜히 가져왔어 = 이 무거운 가방을 안 가져올걸 'I shouldn't have brought this heavy bag'; 제가 그 자선가가 말하는 것을 괜히 믿었어요 'I shouldn't have believed what that philanthropist was saying (although I did)'.
notes.nuance: 괜히 marks a realization that something was pointless or unnecessary - often because it turns out the situation was already handled another way, or the effort simply wasn't needed. Because of this shared underlying sense, 괜히 sentences and ~ㄹ/을걸 (그랬다) sentences can often convey very similar meanings, just through different grammatical routes - one stating regret directly (~ㄹ/을걸), the other stating the pointlessness as a now-realized fact (괜히).

pattern: V~ㄴ/은 채(로) ('dalam keadaan.../dengan...', keadaan berlanjut sampai dan melampaui tindakan berikutnya)
meaning: 채, described by a past-tense ~ㄴ/은 verb clause, indicates that the STATE resulting from an action continues until (and typically beyond) the following action - distinct from ~(으)면서 (Lesson 62), which describes two actions actively happening/progressing at the same time.

notes.formation: [verb]~ㄴ/은 채(로) + [following action]. ~로 is optional with no meaning change. Common verbs: 신다 (put on shoes), 입다 (put on clothes), 켜다 (turn on), 끄다 (turn off), 덮다 (cover), 앉다 (sit), 서다 (stand), 넣다 (put into), 놓다 (put onto), 감다 (close eyes), 잠그다 (lock), 모르다 (to not know).
notes.usage: 선생님이 모자를 쓴 채 학교에 들어갔어요 'The teacher went into the school with a hat on his head' - this does NOT mean he actively put the hat on as he entered; it simply describes the ongoing state (hat on head) at the time of entering, regardless of when the hat was put on. Compare: 선생님이 모자를 쓰면서 학교에 들어갔어요 (with ~면서) would mean he actively put the hat on AT THE MOMENT of entering - grammatically correct but a strange, rarely-needed meaning. More: 그 남자는 눈을 뜬 채로 죽었다 'That man died with his eyes open'; 미국 사람들은 신발을 신은 채 집에 들어가요 'American people go into their houses with their shoes on'; 슬기는 슬기가 아픈지도 모른 채 일을 했어요 'Seulgi worked without knowing she was sick'.
notes.nuance: The 'and beyond' part matters: 너무 더워서 저는 여름에 속옷을 안 입은 채로 밖에 나가요 doesn't just mean the person goes outside without underwear - it means that state (no underwear) continues even after going outside, not just at the moment of leaving. This 'continuing state' framing is what fundamentally separates ~ㄴ/은 채 from ~(으)면서's 'simultaneous active processes'.

pattern: Bentuk aktif vs pasif sebelum 채로 (끈 채로 vs 꺼진 채로, makna hampir sama)
meaning: When an active verb has a passive equivalent (켜다/켜지다, 끄다/꺼지다, 덮다/덮이다, 잠그다/잠기다), either can precede ~ㄴ/은 채로 with essentially the same overall meaning - the only real difference is whether WHO performed the action is specified.

notes.formation: [active verb]~ㄴ/은 채로 (specifies who did the action) vs [passive verb]~ㄴ/은 채로 (doesn't specify who).
notes.usage: 우리는 불을 끈 채로 영화를 봤다 'We watched a movie with the lights off' (specifies 'we' turned off the lights) vs 우리는 불이 꺼진 채로 영화를 봤다 'We watched a movie with the lights off' (doesn't specify who turned them off, just that they were off) - both describe essentially the same scene. A third variant, 불이 꺼져 있는 채로, is also acceptable with the same overall meaning.
notes.nuance: Distinguishing these three forms matters more when looking at the describing clause in isolation (우리는 불을 껐어요 'we turned off the light' vs 불이 꺼졌어요 'the light was turned off' vs 불이 꺼져 있어요 'the light is off' - each has its own distinct nuance) - but once attached to ~ㄴ/은 채로, all three effectively describe the same overall situation, so the distinction becomes much less important in practice.

pattern: ~더~ (mengingat fakta dari pengalaman masa lalu) + ~던가 (bertanya ke diri sendiri, 'apakah dulu...?')
meaning: ~더~ signals the speaker is recalling (or asking someone to recall) a fact from a past experience - it never appears alone, always combining with another grammar point (~던가, ~더라, ~더니). Combined with ~ㄴ/은가 to form ~던가, it's used to ask oneself a yes/no question about a past experience one should know but can't quite remember.

notes.formation: ~더~ + ~ㄴ/은가 = ~던가 (also combines with ~라 to form ~더라, and ~(으)니 to form ~더니, covered in later lessons). Usually attached to ~았/었 first for a specific past experience: [verb]~았/었던가?
notes.usage: 내가 이 책을 읽었던가? 'Did I read this book?' (imagine pulling a book off a shelf of 100 books you've read over the years, unsure if this specific one was among them - you should know, but can't quite recall). More: 파리를 죽였던가? 'Did I kill the fly?'; 이 옷을 빨았던가? 'Did I wash these clothes?'; 우리가 어제 만났던가? 'Did we meet yesterday?'
notes.nuance: This construction can typically only be used to ask oneself a plain yes/no question - it cannot naturally form open-ended questions like 'what day did I read this book?' (내가 이 책을 무슨 날에 읽었던가? sounds unnatural), since that would require more than a simple recalled yes/no answer.

examples.meaning: Did I take that class?

pattern: Waktu sekarang vs lampau dengan ~던가 (kebenaran umum vs pengalaman spesifik)
meaning: Both present- and past-tense ~던가 are grammatically possible, with a subtle difference: past tense refers to a specific past experience being recalled, while present tense asks about a more general truth being currently applied.

notes.formation: [adjective]~던가? (present, general truth) vs [adjective]~았/었던가? (past, specific recalled experience).
notes.usage: 이 과자가 비싸던가? 'Is this candy expensive?' (asking about a general truth currently applicable) vs 이 과자가 비쌌던가? 'Was this candy expensive?' (recalling a specific past time, e.g. when it was bought) - both sentences essentially convey the same meaning in practice, since something expensive usually remains expensive, but the nuance differs slightly.
notes.nuance: For verbs, present-tense ~던가 (without ~았/었) usually sounds odd, since it implies the speaker can't remember something happening RIGHT NOW (내가 이 책을 읽던가? sounds like the speaker has memory issues about their current action) - so verbs almost always take the past-tense ~았/었던가 form, while adjectives more naturally allow either tense depending on whether a specific past moment or a general ongoing truth is being asked about.

examples.meaning: Is that method effective?
Was the interest always this high?
Wasn't the price always this cheap? (used to show the pattern)

quiz.explanation: Plain present-tense ~던가 on a verb implies memory issues about a current action, which sounds odd.

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate, recalling a specific past moment: 'Was this candy expensive?'

pattern: ~던가 dengan kata tanya ambigu (hanya ya/tidak) + bertanya ke orang lain (informal, jarang)
meaning: Question words like 언제/어디/뭐 CAN appear in ~던가 sentences, but only when functioning ambiguously (Lesson 25's principle) rather than as genuine question words - the sentence still only asks 'did X happen at all', not 'when/where/what specifically'. ~던가 can also, less commonly, be directed at another (usually much younger) person informally.

notes.formation: [verb]~던가? with an ambiguous question word (not a genuine information request).
notes.usage: 내가 이 책을 언제 읽었던가? does NOT mean 'When did I read this book?' - it means 'Did I read this book at some time?' (언제 as an ambiguous 'sometime', per Lesson 25). Similarly: 그 사람이 어디 갔던가? = 'Did that person go to some place?' (not 'Where did that person go?'); 오빠가 나한테 뭐라고 했던가? = 'Did my brother say something to me?' (not 'What did my brother say to me?'). Directed at another person (informal, usually older-to-much-younger): 슬기가 많이 아프던가? 'Is Seulgi really sick?'; 네가 생선을 먹던가? 'Do you eat fish?' - though other question forms (~ㄴ/은가?, ~나?) are more commonly used for this purpose.
notes.nuance: This mirrors the exact same ambiguous-question-word principle already learned in Lesson 25 (뭐 먹었어요? can mean either 'what did you eat?' or 'did you eat something?') - applied here specifically within the self-directed ~던가 construction, where only the 'did it happen at all' reading is grammatically natural.

examples.meaning: Did that person go to some place?
Did you buy a cell-phone?
Did my brother not say anything to me? (used to show the pattern)

quiz.explanation: 언제 here functions as an ambiguous 'sometime', not a genuine 'when' question.

pattern: V/Adj/이다~더라 ('dari pengalaman saya, saya sadar/lihat/perhatikan bahwa...')
meaning: Combining ~더~ (recalling a directly-experienced fact) with ~라 (stating a fact) creates ~더라, attached to the end of a sentence to convey a realization the speaker reached through first-hand witnessed experience - best translated 'from my own experience, I realized/saw/noticed that...'.

notes.formation: [verb/adjective/이다 stem]~더라.
notes.usage: 가방이 무거워 'The bag is heavy' (plain fact) vs 가방이 무겁더라 'The bag is heavy (from my own direct experience of it)' - same conveyed fact, but the second adds the nuance of personal, first-hand realization. More: 이민호는 정말 멋지더라 'Minho Lee is very stylish (from what I experienced)'; 캐나다 날씨가 너무 춥더라 'I realized that Canadian weather is very cold'; 한국말을 배우는 게 힘들더라 'I realized that learning Korean is hard'. With 이다/verbs: 문제는 컴퓨터더라 'From my own experience, I realized the problem is the computer'; 그 학생이 뻥을 많이 치더라 'From my own experience, that student jokes a lot'.
notes.nuance: Since ~더라 specifically requires a first-hand REALIZATION from experience, a sentence like 내가 학교에 걸어가더라 (simply stating one walked to school, with nothing new learned) doesn't work - but 학교에 걸어가는 게 힘들더라 ('I realized walking to school is difficult') does, since something was genuinely discovered through the experience.

pattern: Waktu sekarang vs lampau sebelum ~더라 (menyaksikan langsung vs melihat hasilnya saja)
meaning: Present-tense conjugation before ~더라 means the speaker directly witnessed the action itself happening; past-tense conjugation means the speaker only witnessed the RESULT/evidence of the action, without seeing it occur.

notes.formation: [present-tense verb]더라 (witnessed the action itself) vs [past-tense verb]더라 (witnessed only the result/evidence).
notes.usage: 어제 비가 오더라 'I saw it rain yesterday' (literally watched water falling from the sky) vs 어제 비가 왔더라 'I saw that it had rained yesterday' (e.g. saw the wet ground, but didn't actually watch it raining). More: 여자친구가 식당에서 밥을 먹더라 'I saw/noticed my girlfriend eating at the restaurant' (watched her eat) vs 여자친구가 식당에서 밥을 다 먹었더라 'I saw/noticed that my girlfriend had eaten all of her food' (arrived to find an empty plate, without watching the eating itself); 그 직원이 신발끈을 안 매고 출근했더라 'I noticed that worker came to work with his shoelace untied' (saw the untied shoelace at work, not the actual commute).
notes.nuance: The present tense is more commonly used before ~더라 in general, but the past tense is available whenever the situation specifically calls for describing witnessed evidence/results rather than the live action itself - a genuinely useful distinction for precisely conveying what was actually observed.

pattern: ~더라? ('ah, apa/kapan/di mana ya lagi...?', bertanya ke diri sendiri sesuatu yang pernah dialami tapi lupa)
meaning: Ending a question with ~더라 (rather than a plain question ending) implies the speaker once experienced/knew the answer but currently can't recall it - similar to ~던가 (Lesson 117), the question can be technically self-directed but overheard/answered by a listener present at the time.

notes.formation: [question word] + [verb/adjective]~더라?
notes.usage: 빵이 얼마였더라? 'How much did the bread cost, again?' (implies you once knew the price but can't recall - e.g. checking your wallet at home and trying to reconstruct what you spent) vs plain 빵이 얼마였어요? 'How much did the bread cost?' (implies you never knew at all, e.g. asking mom who bought it). 슬기가 어디 갔더라? 'Ah, where did Seulgi go, again?' (you saw her leave but forgot where) vs 슬기가 어디 갔어? 'Where did Seulgi go?' (you have no idea at all).
notes.nuance: Just like ~던가, even though this question is grammatically self-directed, a listener who was present for the original experience (like a friend who shopped with you) can naturally overhear and answer it - the question feels like thinking out loud rather than a direct request for new information from someone else.

examples.meaning: Ah, when did I graduate again?
Ah, where did I get off the bus, again?
Who didn't win that election again? (used to show the pattern)

quiz.question: Perbedaan antara '슬기가 어디 갔더라?' dan '슬기가 어디 갔어?'?
options: ~더라 menyiratkan pernah tahu tapi lupa; polos menyiratkan tidak pernah tahu sama sekali
Keduanya sama-sama tidak bisa dijawab orang lain
quiz.explanation: ~더라 implies once knowing but forgetting, while the plain form implies never having known at all.

fillInTheBlank.sentence: How much did the bread cost, again? -> 빵이 [BLANK]

constructionQuiz.prompt: Translate: 'Where did I put the paper in the living room again?'

pattern: ~았/었더니 (saat pembicara subjeknya: 'saya mengalami..., dan karena itu...')
meaning: Combining ~더~ (first-hand experience) with ~(으)니 (Lesson 81's 'because/so') forms ~더니. When the speaker is the subject, this typically takes the form: [speaker's past-tense action]~더니 [resulting emotion/feeling/state] - conjugating the clause before ~더니 to the past tense (~았/었더니) sounds far more natural than present tense here.

notes.formation: [speaker's action]~았/었더니 [resulting state, often an adjective/emotion].
notes.usage: 내가 스타박스 커피를 마시더니 기분이 좋아졌어 sounds awkward (present tense) vs 내가 스타박스 커피를 마셨더니 기분이 좋아졌어 'I drank Starbucks coffee, and because of that my mood improved' (natural). More: 논술문제를 열심히 썼더니 손이 아파요 'I wrote the essay question hard, and because of that my hand is sore'; 몸이 아파서 마사지를 받았더니 몸이 더 이상 아프지 않았어요 'Because my body was sore, I got a massage, and because of that my body isn't sore anymore'; 하루 종일 걸었더니 너무 피곤해요 'I walked all day, and because of that I am very tired'.
notes.nuance: A native speaker consulted by the author found 하루 종일 걸었더니 다리가 아파요 and 하루 종일 걸어서 다리가 아파요 essentially indistinguishable in meaning - ~더니 simply adds a slight extra nuance (the speaker personally experienced the first action) compared to plainer connectors like ~아/어서 or ~기 때문에, making the sentence a touch more nuanced without a dramatic change in overall meaning.

pattern: ~더니 saat membicarakan orang lain (pembicara langsung menyaksikan klausa pertama)
meaning: When the sentence describes someone ELSE (not the speaker) with ~더니, it specifically means the speaker personally witnessed the first clause happening - unlike ~아/어서, which doesn't indicate whether the speaker actually observed it.

notes.formation: [witnessed action by someone else]~더니 [resulting outcome].
notes.usage: 슬기가 체육시간에 너무 많이 달리더니 다음 수업을 들을 수 없었어요 'I personally saw/experienced Seulgi run a lot during P.E. class, so she didn't attend the next class' - only someone who was actually there (like the P.E. teacher) could say this, unlike the plain ~아/어서 version which could be said by anyone (even Seulgi's parents, who weren't present). More: 슬기가 2개월 동안 일자리를 구하려고 노력하더니 결국 좋은 일자리를 구했어요 'I personally saw/experienced Seulgi trying to get a good job for two months, and she eventually got a job' (said by someone close enough to have witnessed the whole process).
notes.nuance: This is the key distinguishing feature of ~더니 in third-person sentences: it functions as a claim of first-hand witness testimony, not just a neutral cause-and-effect statement - the speaker is implicitly asserting 'I was there and saw this happen', which restricts who could naturally say the sentence.

pattern: Waktu sekarang vs lampau sebelum ~더니 (keadaan berlanjut vs berhenti)
meaning: As with ~더라 (Lesson 118), the tense before ~더니 matters: present tense doesn't necessarily indicate the first clause's situation has stopped, while past tense (~았/었더니) specifically implies that situation has ended.

notes.formation: [present-tense verb]더니 (situation may still be ongoing) vs [past-tense verb]~았/었더니 (situation has specifically stopped).
notes.usage: 어제 비가 오더니 오늘도 비가 온다 'I saw/experienced that it was raining, and it's raining today too' (correct - the rain continued from yesterday into today) vs 어제 비가 왔더니 오늘도 비가 온다 (INCORRECT - the past tense implies the rain had stopped, contradicting 'it's raining today too'). Both of these, however, work: 어제 비가 오더니 오늘 하늘이 맑아요 'I saw that it was raining, and/so now the sky is clear' and 어제 비가 왔더니 오늘 하늘이 맑아요 'I saw that it had rained, and/so now the sky is clear' - nearly identical in this context since both fit with the rain having ended.
notes.nuance: This is the same underlying present/past distinction already established for ~더라: present tense leaves open whether the situation continues, while past tense specifically asserts it has stopped - so whichever tense you choose must remain logically consistent with whatever comes in the second clause (a continuing situation can't follow a past-tense 'it had stopped' clause).
